Chapter 3: The Steppe

The campus sprawled across a mesa overlooking the Pacific. The winding coastal highway crested Torrey Pines hill past a gliderport where paragliders slid along thermal winds rising from thousand-foot sandy cliffs. The place was massive, a world unto itself. The only thing I remember from orientation was a student guide standing before the incoming class of freshmen and saying, "Find your balance." If you'd told me then that the sun-bleached UC San Diego campus would put me on horseback living with nomads in Mongolia within a few years, I'd have thought you were crazy. But that's how it happened.

I declared aerospace engineering, "rocket science," I told my mom, as if difficulty itself could prove something. But once classes started I found myself slipping into anything that caught my eye, opera, philosophy, geophysics, modern world history. It helped that there were almost no girls in engineering, so wandering into other departments served multiple purposes. Suddenly I could invent myself in any form.

By my second year I'd gravitated toward an equally eclectic materials science professor named Mark Meyers, a former Brazilian military officer turned poet and explorer who told stories of trekking the Amazon with the same ease he described atomic lattices and quantum entanglement. He would charge into a lecture hall like he was going into a battle, frantically scribbling equations that defined the properties of our material world and then slip into cheeky tangents of grand adventures in the jungle. I was hooked. I asked him for a job. He brushed me off at first, but I kept showing up, sweeping floors and polishing microscope samples, until I'd worked my way into the lab. Meyers ran his graduate students like a military unit, walking in each morning at nine sharp saying, "Where are my little rabbits? The old fox is here," he would say with a sadistic joy.

Also, for the first time in my life, I had my own crew of friends. Kids from around the country who'd arrived at a campus overlooking the beach, all of us starting our lives on our own terms. We'd build bonfires at night and try to learn to surf under a full moon. On weekends we'd pile into someone's car and drive to the desert to climb or down forty-five minutes south to Mexico where we could go to bars underage and eat street tacos for fifty cents. On breaks, when other students went home to families, I went to the mountains. By graduate school the crew had deepened. My best friend Derek turned the forest behind the faculty club into a giant labyrinth of packing wrap, a hammock garden built into the middle of it with a projector playing Baraka on repeat. When money got tight we'd forage like it was a sport. I fashioned a blowgun from lab supplies and hunted rabbits on the campus lawns. Derek called it an "art project" to avoid uproar, and somehow a photo of me holding a rabbit and the weapon ended up framed in the graduate advising office as a cautionary tale of what happens when you go off the deep end. We were a band of misfits who had finally found each other, and the energy of that was intoxicating.

But while my mind was expanding in every direction, something else was pulling at me. I'd been the earthquake kid, the Cambridge kid, the Palo Alto kid. I could study the atomic structure of a self assembling abalone shell under an electron microscope, but I still didn't know where I came from, why I felt the way I did as a human. That winter, after a lifetime of sacrifice and a fractured family my mother decided it was time. She gathered my siblings and me for a trip to Hong Kong to reconnect with the side of my family I had never truly known.

We arrived to piles of red envelopes filled with cash from every Chinese New Year we'd missed, saved for us by relatives who had been waiting. My mother's parents lived in a 450-square-foot flat in one of Hong Kong's towering residential blocks, a space that had once held five siblings, a piano, and my uncle's chickens. Now a dozen uncles, aunties, and cousins squeezed between faded yellow walls that held decades of memories, most of them unknown to me. My grandmother offered us sliced fruit and cookies and sweaters she'd knitted for two weeks straight until she vomited, her telling us this expression of a dormant love was so intense it left me speechless.

My Mandarin had rusted from disuse, and it didn't matter anyway because most people in Hong Kong spoke Cantonese. Because she knew it and thought it would be more useful to us in life, my mother had taught us Mandarin in our earliest years. But even without words, being there felt like something waking up from within. People looked like me. They behaved and moved like my mother. The mannerisms and views I'd grown up with in our California home, the respect she had longed for from us, suddenly made sense.

Then I met my grandfather, my mother's father, deeply aged but carrying himself with a gentle dignity. His slow, deliberate English became a bridge to the whole side of the family I'd been cut off from. He would pause between each word, in a staccato-ed cadence. "I - am - glad - you - came...". One afternoon, sitting in that tiny living room with the towers of Hong Kong pressing in from every window, he told me about his life. How he'd been a student when the Japanese bombers came. What he saw as he walked across a thousand miles of war-torn China to find his family, arriving nearly dead of dysentery. Attending the Geneva convention and the signing of the Accords as a photojournalist for the only English translated newspapers coming out of Hong Kong at the time. How he'd met my grandmother in the ruins of Nanking. As he spoke I could see the weight of lived memories in his eyes. On my father's side, his father had traversed some of the same lands as a scholar during the Cultural Revolution. Both families had passed through versions of China that existed now only in fragments and memory.

Then, out of the blue, he pointed to his lower back. He said our family all had the "blue spot," a birthmark that recedes a few years after birth. A sign, he said, of an ancient heritage often referred to as the Mongolian spot.

"We all come from somewhere far back." He leaned forward with a half smile. "Maybe we come from the North."

My mother, siblings and I returned to Hong Kong for several winters after that, we walked amongst the dizzying maze of modernity and antiquity, the intwined layers of the incredibly unique city that my mother had grown up in, slowly piecing together her world and through it a larger world I belonged to. Then one year my brother Ed, who had always been the first to go all in on our ideas as kids, used money he had saved day trading out of his Berkeley dorm room to buy us two tickets to Tibet. "I've always wanted to see the top of the world," he said, "let's go!" over an unexpected phone call. That was when I saw the power of deciding just to go, and it was also the first time I saw a living ancient world that had never really disappeared.

I remember arriving in Lhasa and feeling the altitude in every ounce of my body, watching a woman on the street fold dumplings with the speed of an F1 pit crew, her hands a blur while monks filed past in saffron robes. We spent only a few days in the intrepid city, under the shadow of the Patala Palace before embarking on our goal, a trek to Everest Basecamp to look upon the top of the world with our own eyes. A week later, through the most grueling walk I had ever known, where each step felt like a mountain, we stood at seventeen thousand feet in a makeshift village of food and tents beneath the highest point on earth.

"We call it Chomolungma," said a younger Sherpa boy I'd become friends with over the days we lived at basecamp. "Goddess Mother of the World." On our last night an enormous windstorm whipped through the camp, and we all rushed to tie down the ropes that held the canvas tarp roofs on the various canteens, half laughing and half grimacing. The next day my friend pressed a small medallion into my hand. It bore a Sanskrit symbol that looked like a number three with a hooked line extending from its back.

"What does it mean?" I asked.

"Ohm," he said.

I wore it around my neck without understanding its significance. Back in San Diego, I'd find myself turning the medallion over in my hands between classes, contemplating the fact that that world, now so far away, was still spinning without me. Had it really happened?

In the summer of 2006, I convinced my research advisor Mark Meyers to let me take the summer off by appealing to the explorer's heart he wore on his sleeve. He agreed, but hesitantly. "The enemy never sleeps", he reminded me implying my intellectual competitors would not be taking a break. This time I would be going where my grandfather's words had lingered. "Maybe we come from the North."

I scraped together funds from odd jobs, campus mail delivery, and writing the department newsletter, and bought a plane ticket to Beijing. The plan was ridiculous, but audacity was what I was learning to trust. I would take the Trans-Siberian Railway to Ulaanbaatar, buy a horse, ride into the wilderness, find a nomadic camp that would take me in, live with them until it was time to come home, then ride back, sell the horse, and fly out. I had a handheld GPS and had read that under an ancient Mongolian code called the Yassa, failure to offer a fellow nomad hospitality was punishable by death, which I found reassuring given my graduate student budget.

Derek's response was to track down obscure videos of Mongolian throat singing and grin encouragingly. Years later, I would perform it at his wedding.

Within the first hour in Beijing a taxi driver scammed me out of a hundred dollars, a substantial chunk of my entire budget. The train station was a city under a roof, loud and endless, every sign a wall of Chinese characters I couldn't fully read. Jet-lagged and adrift, I guessed my way from counter to counter until somehow I had a ticket for a bunk in a four-berth cabin the next day.

I found my cabin early and walked down the narrow passage between berths, my backpack slung over my shoulder. A large man barged through with two huge bags of rice on either shoulder and slammed into me. Rancid cigarette breath washed over me as he screamed at me to get out of his way. I didn't understand his curses well enough to take offense, but his anger was obvious. He threw the bags of rice into my berth. Two Mongolian women were right behind him, looking shocked. I stepped aside and he glared ready to fight, but finding only confusion on my face. Then he left. The women stared at me as I sat down. In broken English they apologized for their "friend," who was actually their guide in Beijing. "We know you're not Mongolian," one said, "because you didn't fight."

Their names were Bayaraikhan, BiBi for short, and Inga.

The train slowly left the station. I stuck my head out the window and watched fragments of the Great Wall go by. Eventually the forested mountains surrounding Beijing gave way to the desolate Gobi, the landscape opening up until there was nothing but brown earth and sky in every direction.

BiBi and Inga had come to buy medicine for one of their mothers and bags of high-quality rice not imported into Mongolia. Their high cheekbones and features looked slightly Russian, their words sounded like whispering from the sides of their teeth. Over boiled eggs and cards, I told them about my grandfather's words about the Mongolian spot.

BiBi's face lit up. "Then you are Mongolian! We are family!" She laughed and squeezed my arm. Inga nodded approvingly.

I told them my plan to buy a horse and live with the nomads.

"That's nice," BiBi said, her expression shifting. Her skepticism was no longer masked.

We became friends quickly. They tried to tell me what to expect, and I told them everything I knew about the country from books, which wasn't much. At night we converted our seats into bunks and I dozed on the top one, hugging my bag after having read about thieves who duplicated conductors' keys and filled cabins with sleeping gas.

At the border the train stopped in the middle of the desert at 2 AM. Speakers blasted patriotic Chinese marching band music as huge spotlights shone down on our cabins. Guards with bayonets searched the compartments and stuck their weapons into the ceilings to catch stowaways. Some passengers were thrown from the train screaming, left stranded with piles of their belongings. When the guards reached our cabin, I said "I'm with them, I'm an American and they're my guides," and the ruse worked. But watching other passengers dragged away, I realized the liberty I took for granted was not universal.

By the time we crossed into Mongolia, the horse plan had been firmly vetoed. BiBi grew serious. "Albert, you will die if you do this. Mongolian horses are very wild. They will leave you in the desert."

Using a small brick-like cell phone she called her brother. His name was Amaraa, and when we arrived in Ulaanbaatar he was waiting in the crowd with a hat that said "California" and a smile that took over his whole face. He grabbed the bags of rice, and helped BiBi and Inga towards his truck. With no actual plan other than the one I had dreamed up, I threw my bag into his weathered Land Cruiser. He smiled and said in a strong raspy voice with a Mongolian accent, "Come on, let's go!"

I had no idea Mongolia even had a movie industry, but I quickly learned that Amaraa was building it. I had randomly ended up with one of the most famous actors in the country. On the drive through the streets I saw him on a billboard for a film about Genghis Khan. But fame sat lightly on him. Over the next few days, as we drank at a bar and he told me stories about digging frozen sheep out of the snow during the dzud, the brutal winters when ice locks the grass beneath the snow and animals starve by the thousands, I began to understand that his generosity wasn't performance. It was principle. "This world is small," he told me. "We have to put good energy into it. For our children and our children's children."

Then one evening he suddenly announced he'd take me himself. "You can't go alone. There are wolves. Your horse will run away and you will die. What will I tell your mother?" He laughed, then grew serious. "Stay at my extra apartment. In two days when the car is fixed, we'll go. I will take you to the countryside to see my Uncle the nomad." I didn't feel right accepting such generosity. "It's okay," he said. "I'm your friend. Don't refuse."

When we left Ulaanbaatar two days later, his mother and BiBi walked us out and sniffed our faces. "This is how we kiss in Mongolia," Amaraa explained. "We smell the soul." As we pulled away, his mother threw cups of milk into the sky for good luck.

We drove all day in Amaraa's old Toyota, which he'd nicknamed Dusty. The only music was Mongolian folk music, Boyz II Men and Neil Diamond, and we sang along with gusto, filling the sweeping skies and golden fields with American R&B and ancient throat singing harmonies. Along the way he explained the customs. If you see a wolf, good luck. A fox, bad luck. Horses walking toward your car, very good luck. Wherever we passed someone on the road, Amaraa would stop and greet them as if they were old friends. He'd give rides to anyone who needed one, help push a stuck vehicle, share whatever food we had. Everyone seemed to know him, or at least to trust him on sight. There was a magnetic quality to him, a combination of strength and compassion and humility that reminded me of the stories I was reading about Genghis Khan.

At sunset, Amaraa scanned the horizon the way a migratory bird finds home. He turned off the road and drove through tall grass, over hills and through valleys, no road at all, the truck gliding across the steppe like wide skis over fresh snow. We arrived at a small camp of five gers. His uncle, a tall older man in a cowboy hat with a sun-bleached face, came out to greet us.

I ducked through the felt door and stepped into a different world. Firelight in the center, carpets on the ground, beds lining the perimeter, a dry-aging goat carcass hanging overhead. They handed me a bowl of flour noodles boiled in milk tea with fragments of jerky. It was delicious. Then came the fermented milk candies. Plates and plates of them. I smiled politely, took one, and quietly slipped it into my sleeve.

The next morning Amaraa handed me a set of reins. The Mongolian saddle was a piece of wood covered in the thinnest of cloth padding, and the stirrups, he explained, were invented by Genghis Khan so warriors could ride standing and shoot arrows at the same time. I sat bow-legged, fumbling for stability, while a little girl circled us effortlessly bareback, giggling. After a few hard falls, I was bruised but finding something like rhythm. We rode out to bring in the herd, and as my horse galloped across land that stretched endlessly around us, I felt part of something I'd been looking for without knowing what it was. But truthfully, I was barely in control. Where Amaraa led, my horse followed.

Days turned to weeks. At night I'd rise from my cot to relieve myself outside, and my eyes would adjust to a sky so dense with stars it felt like I was floating in space, weightless amid a cosmos scored by the murmurs of 500 sheep. The smell of burning yak dung filled the air with a sweetness that I came to associate with home. In the mornings, Amaraa's aunties would stir a tall vat of airag, fermented mare's milk that had a hint of bubbles to it, and we would drink from a silver bowl passed hand to hand through the center of the ger like spokes of a wheel.

One afternoon, riding back from bringing in the herd, Amaraa and I stopped at a well in the middle of a valley. We pumped water and splashed it over our faces and necks, smiling and laughing at nothing in particular.

"This is life," he said.

He told me that a lot of people go to Ulaanbaatar looking for jobs, but they'd realize how much they miss the old ways and return to nomadic life. It was getting harder, he explained. Fences were going up as companies bought mining rights, displacing the boundless ancient ways. My back was sore from the wooden saddle and my skin was raw, but as the evening light stretched across the endless grass and my horse lurched forward with a gentle squeeze of my legs, I felt like the truest version of myself in that moment.

Later that week Amaraa's uncle asked us to help him brand the baby horses of the year. After an intense afternoon of hoofs and the smell of singed hide, we rode to neighboring camps to invite them to a celebratory feast. Stopping at each one for another silver bowl of vodka, which I learned turned into several bowls passed around, I was eventually riding across the plains of Mongolia completely drunk. At least it loosened my back. That night a community gathered in Amaraa's uncle's ger, singing the ancient Mongolian songs about horses, family, and the land. I started to hear something familiar in them, a cadence that reminded me of Native American songs in documentaries I'd watched as a kid. I wondered if I was hearing echoes of a time when ancestors crossed the Bering Land Bridge tens of thousands of years ago, carrying their songs with them.

One evening, a nomad who'd been sizing me up all night said something to Amaraa.

"He wants to wrestle you."

The man was smiling like he didn't trust me. He stood up and walked toward me. I stood up too.

Amaraa said, "Albert, you shouldn't do this. These guys are strong. Every day they're working the land." But I knew if I backed down I would truly be out. Even if I lost, it was better to try.

We walked out of the ger. A throng of excited nomads poured out with us. First person to touch their knee or elbow to the ground loses. The guy squared up, shirtless, so I took my shirt off. Then everything around me began to blur. The cheers, the stomping feet, the landscape. All I could hear was my heartbeat. I wasn't on the steppe anymore. I was back in high school wrestling matches, in childhood scraps with my siblings.

He was stronger than I was. But I had one chance. I shot forward, low at first, arched my back, swung behind him, and dropped him to his knee.

For a moment I couldn't believe it. Then the quiet in my mind shattered and the roar came flooding back. Everyone jumping, cheering, clapping. Amaraa ran over beaming. "You won! Now you must do the eagle dance!" I raised my arms like a bird with leaping arches in my legs. A man poured airag down my back.

That night, the silver bowl was passed with bigger smiles and talk of the eagle dance. Years later, when I'd return to Mongolia, Amaraa would name me NaChing, the eagle.

As the weeks passed, Amaraa told me about Genghis Khan. Not the barbarian caricature of Western textbooks, but to him the greatest nomad to have ever lived, a man who had risen from nothing to forge the largest contiguous empire in history. He told me about the sacred mountain, the Burkhan Khaldun, where the young Temüjin had stood at his lowest moment and somehow willed his fate into existence. He told me that nobody knew where Genghis Khan was buried, that his tomb had never been found, and that Mongolians believed it carried the spiritual power of his people.

Amaraa spoke too about Mongolia's struggle to hold back foreign mining companies intent on extracting gold and uranium, poisoning the rivers that had sustained his people for generations. He wanted to defend the land the way his ancestors had. It wasn't just history to him. It was alive and under threat.

One day, driving across the steppe in Dusty, Amaraa said, "Let's be andas." An anda is more than a friend. It's a brotherhood chosen by fate, a bond that goes beyond blood. I said yes without hesitation.

Before I left, he gave me a curved Mongolian sword from one of his movie sets, engraved with the words: "To my brother, we wish all the best to you in your life. Your Mongolian family."

I flew back to San Diego with it tucked in my checked bag, walked into a burrito shop near campus, still smelling like yak dung and fermented mare's milk and blinked in disbelief. The fluorescent lights felt alien. A week ago I'd been galloping across the steppe. Now I was ordering a California burrito and trying to remember my lab access code. But the curved sword on my wall and the scar from the wooden saddle said it had all been real. Meyers welcomed me back with a hearty handshake of a fellow explorer, told me to make a presentation of the journey to the lab meeting that next Friday, and then told me to get back to work. The deal held: the road fed the work, and the work earned me the road. But the bug had bitten.

The next summer I went back to Asia, this time to retrace my family's journeys during the war and traverse the Chinese heartland. My grandfather on my father's side had moved back through these lands as a scholar of political science during the Cultural Revolution. My mother's father had walked across a thousand miles of them to survive. But there was not much in the way of our family story beyond that, at least not that I knew. I wasn't wandering. I was following severed threads, trying to see if they still connected to anything.

I traveled along the Silk Road that both of my grandfathers had described, again overly ambitious with that GPS as if it was a beacon home if I got lost. Mosques flew by the double-decker bus window. The giant mountains of the Karakoram rose above me. Ethnically diverse Chinese kids ran through ancient trading towns with blond hair and hazel eyes beneath felt hats. I was struck by how much more diverse China was than anything I'd imagined growing up, as if the monolithic image from my childhood was shattering into a mosaic with each mile.

In a market in the far west I met a French wayfarer, tall and wiry and gray-haired, his clothes patched and faded from decades on the road. He'd spent twenty years drifting, never more than two months in the same place. We shared a bowl of soup and traded stories. I told him about Mongolia. He told me about a village deep in the mountains of central China where people still lived in traditional tree houses. There was something melancholy about his solitude, a life spent searching but never landing. I wondered if that would be my fate.

I boarded an overnight bus headed south, spending eleven hours wedged into an upper bunk while the driver hurled down back roads at terrifying speeds and speakers blasted 1980s Arabic music. When it got too cold to continue west I kept going south, watching through the window as China transformed beneath me, from the camels that roamed the high deserts of the North to the snow-covered peaks of Sichuan, and finally into the rolling rice terraces and humidity of the South. Eventually I found myself in a village called Dali, nestled in the mountains of Yunnan. Cobblestone streets and terracotta roofs and red lanterns, but alongside the ancient architecture was a subculture of young Chinese rebels who had walked away from the relentless grind of expectation in favor of folk music and poetry and cheap rice wine.

I walked in and sat at the bar. The bartender had a Pulp Fiction haircut, a stern face, and wore all black. When I ordered in English she said, "Why aren't you speaking Mandarin?"

Her name was Maya. I was instantly attracted to her.

Every time I tried to switch to English, she refused. "You're Chinese, look at your face." But when a Frenchman walked in and ordered in English, she responded in a perfectly California accent. It was just me she was demanding Mandarin from.

Over the next two weeks, she introduced me to a community of young Chinese castaways I had no idea existed. They were artistic, passionate, independent, nothing like the obedient archetype I'd seen typecasted in the West. They had rejected the grind of competition and expectation in favor of this little enclave where they played heartfelt guitar riffs in smoky rooms as the music floated into the streets that had been paved 600 years before. In the evenings we cooked meals that tasted of my mother's cooking over coals. It felt so natural and we quickly became a crew. They didn't fit in either.

Maya and I fell together quickly. She gave me a haircut in her tiny apartment, a minimalist room with blank walls and nothing but a mattress on the floor. She cooked vegetables and rice on a portable propane burner while I showered off weeks of road grime. We spent the night together, and I lost myself in words of passion spoken in my native tongue. The words shaped the feeling, and the feeling reshaped the words. I was experiencing love in a language I'd never used for it before, and it unlocked a version of me I hadn't fully known. I spoke Mandarin daily, and eventually in my dreams.

It was a parallel life, the one I would have been living had my great-grandfather not left for North America a hundred years before. The longer I stayed, the more real that parallel became, and the harder it was to remember my other reality.

One day she took my hand and led me to a lake surrounded by rice fields so green they looked painted. We borrowed a fishing boat, which she insisted on calling "borrowing," and rowed to the middle. She could sense the conflict in me, that I was already beginning to pull away even as I wanted to stay.

"Look at these mountains," she said. "They've been here for millions of years. Our worries, they're superficial. You will come and go. I will come and go. We will be long gone. And yet these mountains will still be standing here." That was Maya. She'd spend an hour brutally teasing me about my accent, then drop something like that without blinking.

On my last night, an international group of musicians staged a concert in one of Dali's ancient gatehouses, the towering stone structures that had once been built to keep outsiders from entering the city. Now the gates were thrown open and people from everywhere danced inside them, drums and didgeridoos echoing off walls that had repelled invaders for centuries. Maya and I had agreed to work the tickets and bar, I needed any cash I could get. It was blissful to ignore what was coming, but the truth wouldn't wait. I thought of the French wayfarer in the North, his twenty years of drifting, the loneliness in his eyes. I didn't want that. I had a half-finished PhD, a crew of friends, a lab with a old fox who expected his rabbits back by September. This was not my home, as beautiful as it was. I had another life, and it was waiting.

We fought. She didn't want me to leave. I stood on the cobblestones under her window in the rain, flicking rocks at the glass. Finally, a text: "If you're going to leave, just leave." I boarded the bus at 5 AM, pulled my hood up, and sobbed the entire way. The other passengers stared. I was leaving behind a version of myself that I would never find again, but I also knew I had to keep going.

Two days later, in a train station hundreds of miles away, my phone buzzed.

"Hey California, why are there so many dogs in this train station?"

I looked up and there she was. She'd bought a plane ticket to intercept me. We ran into each other's arms. She said, "I know you have to go, but we couldn't say goodbye like that."

For the next two nights, on a rooftop overlooking the camelback mountains of Guilin which fade into the mist like echoes of thought, she taught me to meditate for the first time, showing me how to quiet my mind and let the horizon come to me instead of chasing it. On our last morning she handed me a book.

"You should read this," she said.

The cover read Siddhartha. The story of a man who searches the world for meaning, and discovers, at the end, that everything he sought was already inside him.

Before I flew home, I followed the French wayfarer's directions into the mountains of central China. After days of trains and buses and a motorcycle ride into increasingly remote terrain, I found the hamlet he'd described: a cluster of traditional tree houses in a forest above the clouds. I arrived alone, and as the sun set I sat in a rice field playing my guitar, badly. A few kids came over. Most of them spoke Miao, an indigenous language as distinct from Mandarin as the Uyghur I'd heard in the far west near Pakistan, or the Mongolian I'd tried and failed to learn on the steppe. In these early journeys I'd encountered more versions of being human than I'd known existed, and I was beginning to sense that this diversity wasn't the exception but the rule, that beneath the borders and languages and customs, something universal was holding it all together. A ten-year-old girl who happened to speak Mandarin appointed herself my translator. She and her friends brought me to the one-room tree house where she lived with her family, the women in black dresses with colorful triangle patterns, her father squatting with a long powder-loaded rifle, smoking a pipe. They welcomed me, fed me vegetables from their farm and tilapia from a nearby pond and a fermented drink that tasted like old gym socks. We played music together on a flute one of the women brought out. That night we all bedded down in the small hut among the clouds, pigs sleeping in the farm below, a wood fire burning in the center. It felt just like the gers of Mongolia, a clan huddled together in each other's warmth.

As I drifted off, reading the first pages of the book Maya had given me, my phone buzzed. A text from my roommate in San Diego: fires were sweeping through Southern California, everyone was being evacuated, they'd packed my things in a box. The message ended, "Also, Happy Halloween."

That world seemed so very far away.

A few days later I landed in San Diego to find my belongings piled under a pool table, the air still smelling of smoke. While I'd been searching for who I was on the other side of the world, the life I'd left behind had been stuffed in a box and nearly burned to a crisp.
title: Chapter 3: The Steppe

content:
Chapter 5: Burn the Ships

I gave myself one year. I pinned a timeline to the wall above my desk and told everyone who would listen: We're going to locate the tomb of Genghis Khan. It sounded like a child saying he'd be an astronaut. But someone does become that astronaut. So I kept saying it, until I almost believed it.

The economy had just tanked. I had no job, no income, no home, and no credibility for what I was attempting to do, it was not something anyone would expect of an engineer. So I burned the ships, metaphorically. I sold nearly everything but a guitar and some clothes and moved into my Mazda hatchback. I pushed my clothes and guitar to one side, laid the back seats flat, shoved the passenger seat as far forward as it would go, and built myself a bed. It felt like a tent, which I was used to from all the camping and climbing trips. The hardest part was crawling out of it each morning, convinced everyone walking by was staring at me. At first I told myself it was romantic, like some outlaw poet. The romance wore thin fast. Every night was a hunt for somewhere to park without being ticketed or towed. In a city manicured like a lawn, I was the weed hoping not to be plucked.

Two things kept me going: the timeline taped to my car window, and my friends. Each night before sleep it was the last thing I saw, each morning the first.

They lent me parking passes and couches, would let me take showers in their apartments from time to time. Derek, still finishing up his degree, would hang a fake sign reading "Sleep Study in Progress" on a conference room door so I could nap. If I was exhausted from a rough night in the car, Nate would carry me on his handlebars back to campus where I still had a library card and was using it to tap into the entirety of the UC collection of rare books, a valuable resource for the search.

Without any income I made scrounging for food into an art form, literally. The campus salad bar charged by the bowl, so I'd engineer these towering structures, carrots laid horizontally as scaffolding, cucumbers as buttresses, piling the thing so high it looked like a miniature architectural project. The cashiers would stare. I'd smile and hand them my dollar fifty. It worked till they changed the policy to charge by the ounce a few months in. I hit every free dinner at every student club that would have me, regardless of affiliation.

Everything was precarious. One morning, after sleeping on Shay and Nate's couch, I blurted, "I just want a fucking closet." Without a word, they emptied theirs and pointed at the bare shelves. "There. Your closet." Then they sat down and helped me hack together a project website using open-source tools only because we couldn't afford any software. That was the kind of friendship that kept the ember alive.

Underneath it all, in the long hours when I couldn't sleep, I wondered if I was delusional. Everyone I knew was building careers. I was living in a parking lot, chasing a tomb that had been hidden for eight centuries. The whole thing could collapse tomorrow. But then I'd look at the timeline on the window and think: maybe the tomb has stayed hidden precisely because no one had been crazy enough to seriously go looking for it.

Nate was all in from the start, never doubting, even when I doubted myself. Shay played devil's advocate until I told him I needed him to believe it or leave, the way we'd believed in each other on the wall. That shifted something, like a ship clearing seaweed from its keel. Kostas dove into centuries-old texts, piecing together clues from Persian chronicles and dusty archives. We called ourselves the Valley of the Khans Project and made a ridiculous anthem on my ukulele:

"He wants to fiiiiind... the lost tommmmb... of Genghis Khaaaaan... using geo-phy-sy-cal techniques!"

We were planning our own impossible mission with duct-tape resources and big, foolish innocent audacity. Omri, an undergraduate obsessed with robotics, agreed to build makeshift drone prototypes from scrap materials for aerial photography, years before anyone had heard the word "drone" applied to anything outside science fiction. A young Spaniard named Alex Novo agreed to be our geophysicist for the price of a flight. Each person who joined had somehow convinced their real job that this was something they had to do. None of them were paid. Slowly we were transforming from a ragtag group of engineering doctoral students and climbing buddies into something that almost looked like an expedition team.

The institute where I'd heard Seracini's lecture gave me an unpaid desk wedged amongst the administrative staff. It wasn't much but it was a start, an institutional home to build from and that was enough. That cubicle became my command post. Towers of history books rose higher each week. The accountants around me watched, first amused then perplexed, as a framed poster of Genghis Khan appeared over the piles like a flag planted in foreign ground.

Kostas and I became detectives. We'd meet at the cubicle with coffee and spread photocopied pages across the desk, chasing fragments of a trail that was eight centuries cold. We had friends in the graduate community translate ancient Arabic texts. We powered through Paul Pelliot's rare three-volume Notes on Marco Polo, a French sinologist's obsessive annotations that cross-referenced every claim. Each source offered a glimpse, but their contradictions only deepened the mystery.

The Chinese chroniclers, writing more than a century after the Khan's death, offered conflicting accounts. The Yüan Shih described a secretive burial at a hidden valley where the imperial hearse was raised for interment, the ground meticulously restored so no trace remained. Another text described how the site would have been trampled by thousands of horsemen and left for nature to reclaim. The Persian historian Rashid al-Din wrote that Genghis Khan had selected his burial site beneath a lone tree, a place so sacred it was guarded by an elite force and shrouded by dense forest.

But the Mongolian sources were the most compelling. The Secret History offered no burial details, but described in vivid poetry the power of the Burkhan Khaldun, the sacred mountain, placing it at the source of the Onon and Kherlen rivers. Later chronicles pointed to a location known as the Ikh Khorig, an ancient forbidden precinct somewhere in the Khentii Mountains, declared sacred by Genghis Khan himself. During the Russian occupation, travel to this region had been forbidden as part of the effort to suppress Mongolia's history. Even now it was classified as highly restricted.

All the sources agreed on one thing: the burial site was not just hidden but deliberately obscured. And all clues pointed to the same place, the sacred mountain, somewhere in a sprawling, untamed range on the Mongolian-Russian border. Kostas looked up from the papers and said what we were both thinking: "We need to go there."

When a university writer did a short story on the project, it snowballed into coverage from the Union-Tribune and NBC. One morning, riding on Nate's handlebars in a dress shirt because I couldn't afford a parking pass, my phone buzzed. "This is Mark Brender from the GeoEye Foundation. I just read the article about your project, we want to support you. Just tell us where to point the satellites." We whooped in the middle of a construction site like lunatics. I was simultaneously commanding satellites in orbit while riding on the handlebars of my friend's bike because I couldn't afford my own. I couldn't tell anymore if I was living the dream or losing my mind. Possibly both.

Then came the card. I'd stitched together every token of the project's legitimacy into a binder that I carried everywhere like Excalibur: GeoEye and UCSD logos, letters on letterhead, the project plan. When I learned that Maurizio would be walking Terry Garcia, EVP of National Geographic, through a tour of the campus, I found their itinerary and set an ambush. At the exact minute their route cut through the student center courtyard, I stepped through the stream of bodies in my one button-up shirt and suit, looking entirely out of place among a sea of board shorts and hoodies, folder in hand, and delivered the best elevator pitch of my life.

Terry listened, flipped through the binder half distracted by an inbound call on his phone, placed a card into my hand and said "Follow up."

I stared at that little paper rectangle as if it were the key to my entire future in cardstock form. When I brought it back to show Nate and Shay we jumped for joy then stared collectively at it like we had found a winning lottery ticket. "You better write to that guy every day!" Nate proclaimed. We settled on weekly updates. There weren't replies at first. But the emails never bounced back, and that was enough.

Around that time I met Kara. She worked at a center for virtual reality on campus, had a real job, a real apartment, a real life. I ambushed her in a hallway the way I'd ambushed Terry Garcia, only with less preparation and more stammering and no binder. She saw right through me but she laughed, and that was enough to get a coffee in the shade of the university buildings. I told her we should collaborate. She looked at me with a smirk and said, "What does that mean?" She was smart, that was obvious. But she had a cute, go-with-the-flow attitude that actually masked a stubbornness in a way that was endearing. Her face had the composure of a duchess, but she was eager to go rock climbing and camping with me in the desert. I was living in my car with a poster of Genghis Khan taped to the wall of a borrowed cubicle, and she didn't seem to mind. More than anything, she made me believe in myself. At a time when most of the world would have told me I was delusional, she told me to keep going.

After dozens of unanswered emails, I wrote Terry one more time, telling him I was going to Mongolia with the remainder of my funds to secure permissions. Finally he responded. "Why don't you come by the Society before you go and present your plan?"

Terry offered a date for the presentation in DC, two days after I was to be the best man at Derek's wedding. Derek and his fiancee were expecting a baby, and I was to be godfather. To save money I'd do it all in one trip: rural Ohio for the ceremony, DC for Nat Geo, then straight to Mongolia.

It was snowing when I arrived in Ohio. Derek's dad Bob, an eccentric giant of a man who'd made his fortune in land prospecting, met me at the airport. On the drive to their estate I told him about the search for the tomb. Later, between toasts for the bride and groom, he pulled me into his office and started poring over my maps, his hand shaking violently up and down. "Dowsing," he said. Abruptly he proclaimed, "Before you go, you will catch a fish!"

The snow had become a full-blown blizzard. I had a flight to catch. It seemed insane. But he was the boss. The next morning, still legendary hung over from a night of champagne and banjos in tuxedos, I was dragged to the river without pity. The wind yanked at my fly rod like it wanted to carry me off. I cast into the white void, the fly smacking uselessly against the freezing current. Everything suggested this was pointless except Derek's dad, who kept yelling through the wind, "There's a fish out there! I can feel it!"

The line went taut. Hands trembling, I reeled in a monster of a trout. I hadn't really caught it. The wind had dragged my hook into the fish's fin, purely by chance. But whether or not I believed in dowsing, it was a good omen. I gave Derek a hug, then left for the airport with his father's blessing, still stinking of fish guts.

The next morning, in a dingy roach-infested hotel, I put on my only suit and walked past the monuments of Washington toward National Geographic headquarters. Fred Hiebert, the archaeology fellow, met me in the lobby and gave me a tour. We passed the offices of legends: Mike Fay, who'd crossed Africa on foot. Sylvia Earle, one of the first female deep-sea pioneers. Bob Ballard, who'd found the Titanic. I was a kid among my heroes, and I didn't have a fixed address.

Fred took me to a small room where about thirty editors with notepads trickled in. The communications director gave an unflattering introduction that amounted to "we have no idea who this guy is." Then I stood up and told them everything. The story of Amaraa, the steppe, the Secret History, the sacred mountain, the technology that could look without touching. "I'm flying to Mongolia tomorrow to establish permissions to enter the forbidden zone," I said. "I would be deeply honored if National Geographic would support this project."

When the room emptied, Fred turned to me. "You know what you really need? A dazzler." He crafted a vaguely supportive letter, slapped a golden Nat Geo seal sticker on it, and just like that, my binder leveled up.

That evening I was invited to the home of Tim Kelly, president of Nat Geo Global Media. Stunned, I sat in his living room holding a glass of wine, surrounded by Emmys and photographs from expeditions that had changed the way people understood the world. "I was in the back of the room today," he said with a soft-spoken authority. A few days ago I'd been trying to figure out where to shower. Now Tim's wife Susan was smiling at me and saying, "One day, you'll write a book about this." I laughed because it was the only honest response I could muster. Then across the treetops of Washington D.C.'s Rock Creek Park a Lion's evening roar washed over their rooftop patio where we had migrated to. Was I dreaming? The distance between my actual life and the life that was unfolding around me had become so vast I couldn't process it. I kept waiting for someone to realize I was just a kid who lived in his car.

A few days later my plane circled over Ulaanbaatar, forced into a holding pattern while prevailing winds pushed the smog from the intense charcoal factory stacks that powered much of the city. My dazzler binder, a borrowed suit and suitcase from friends, and whatever was left of my savings were all I had. It was minus twenty degrees when I walked through the airport doors.

It was amazing to be with Amaraa and BiBi again, only this time it was winter and my quest had evolved significantly.

"You're going to need permission from the foreign office, the minister of culture, and members of Parliament," they told me. "This is going to be very political."

BiBi's husband's father had been a historian, and he introduced me to Professor Bira, an elder statesman of Mongolian history who had risked his life preserving manuscripts during the Soviet occupation, when speaking the name of Genghis Khan could get you killed. His lieutenant Ishdorj had spent his career fighting for the same cause. These were not men looking for a paycheck. They had their own reasons for wanting this story told, reasons that ran deeper than mine. For decades, Mongolia's history had been suppressed, its greatest figure erased from its own textbooks. The tomb wasn't just an archaeological question to them. It was the keystone of a cultural identity they had spent their lives defending. Over a cold-cut lunch near a square with statues of Genghis Khan and Lenin, I showed them everything and cited their own work back to them. They were cautious but intrigued, not so much by the binder but by what it said about the approach. No excavation. Revelation without desecration.

Within a week, through a chain of introductions that moved faster than I could follow, and before I could believe it I found myself walking through the large marble atrium of the Mongolian equivalent to the Whitehouse and past a large staff with white horse feathers adorning a speared tip. "The Sulde, it's the Soul banner" I was told. I would know its significance later. Eventually I was granted an audience with the foreign policy advisor to the president. An hour later, he signed a letter of support. I sent a copy to National Geographic. The distance between who I'd been six months ago and who I was pretending to be now was getting harder to measure.

Before I could return with a full team, I needed to get as close as I could to the mountain to retrieve GPS coordinates for the satellites. I asked Amaraa to help me organize a small group to drive north toward the Ikh Khorig, the ancient forbidden precinct that I had read about and that most Mongolians knew about from their own childhood stories. At its edge, guards with rifles stood watch, descendants of the Darkhads, hereditary protectors who had guarded this threshold for centuries. My binder meant nothing here. We offered cigarettes, drank tea. Hours passed. What mattered wasn't paperwork. It was whether the purpose behind our presence could be felt.

The gate lifted. Not with fanfare, but with the quiet scrape of wood, an old hinge groaning. And suddenly we were driving into a landscape that had been for the most part sealed for eight hundred years.

It was historic. And we knew it.

We followed the frozen Kherlen River deep into the range, past snow covered ovoos of prayer flags on the ridgelines. In the distance I could see a mountain taller than any other in the valley, its peak shaped like a cap, as if it had been terraformed. I got my GPS out with frantically shivering hands and recorded the coordinates. At the base of the ridge, next to the icy river, we made camp. That night, under a sky so dense with stars it felt like the universe was pressing down on us, Amaraa and his friends began singing and telling stories about their families, these Mongolians who had brought me into their sacred land. There on that river, in a place that had once been the speculation of the world, I had slipped through time.

A few days later I was back in Ulaanbaatar, then on a plane to San Diego, once again in disbelief at all that had transpired. When I landed I went to pick up my car and it wasn't there. Towed weeks earlier, unnoticed. My only home and everything I owned, gone. I tracked it to a tow yard and used the last of my money to get it back. That night I cried myself to sleep in the car, the GPS coordinates of a sacred mountain stored in a device on the passenger seat, and not a dollar left to get back to it.

The next day, a message from Fred. "Good news. Nat Geo wants to sponsor you. You've been approved for a fifteen-thousand-dollar exploratory grant."

I sat in the car and stared at the screen. I had the coordinates. I had the grant. I had a team of friends who believed in something no sane person would bet on. And I had seen the sacred mountain with my own eyes.

The hardest part was still ahead. I just didn't know yet that it would begin with the words, "Guys, we're fucked."
title: Chapter 5: Burn the Ships

content:
Chapter 7: The Break

In the spring of 2016, four years after I had met the shamans on the Burkhan Khaldun, I found myself loading Charlie and Millie into a small rented RV. Millie was barely three, still in diapers when she slept. Charlie was six, already starting school.

Mini camp chairs, microscopes, toy cars, princess dresses, rock hammers, model rockets, mac and cheese packets, carpets, sun umbrellas, even a ceramic chiminea found their way into that small home on wheels. Did I have enough diapers. Did I have enough food. Would the kids be bored, would they be scared. They were toddlers, and I was going as the lone adult, the three of us into the unknown. It wasn't until I pulled out of the driveway of our half-built house that it struck me: I had no plan and no destination. Just the road and a desperation to go. The passenger seat was empty. I had never imagined it would be.

The kids played as our little home on wheels labored up the familiar freeways. I drove alone up front, the loud hum of the engine drowning out their yelps from the back as they played and fought in equal measure. The rattle of pots and pans against the steady vibration of the road was so loud that I handed them an expedition walkie talkie so they could talk to me while staying safely in the back. Outside, the city thinned and the desert opened up, I could breathe again, and in that expanding space my thoughts overwhelmed me. How did this happen, and what would come of us now.

--

For a while, everything had felt like a surreal dream. I'd shown up on that quiet San Diego street with a broken VW pop top and a baby hours from being delivered, and we became a community almost instantly. Our neighbors Rich and Katrina became the family we didn't have, Kara and I having both left fractured ones behind when we went to college. Their daughter Pearl adopted Charlie like an older sister. The oldest nursery in the city sat on one side of us, free range chickens wandering through its aisles, and on the other an old cemetery that had been turned into a park. Only a handful of tombstones remained, pushed to the edge as a reminder of a time before anyone alive could remember. Only a few generations had passed since those names were living people, but time had churned on and their lives were now one-line summaries on stone that ghost tours would gawk at and kids would skateboard past on their way to their favorite climbing tree. On summer evenings young parents would lay out blankets in the park and listen to free concerts while their babies crawled in the grass between the headstones. A tomb hunter turned stroller pusher couldn't have asked for a more fitting home.

Toys and strollers were scattered down our small front porch and into the tiny yard with its hammock that stretched the full width of it. When Charlie was a newborn I'd sit in an old thrift store reclining chair with him asleep on my chest, about the size of a large melon, and we'd gently snore together, my chest rising and his rising with it, his tiny heartbeat against my skin. As he grew he was playful and mischievous like any boy, but there was a compassion to him, a selflessness and care that seemed to come from somewhere older than his years. We made home movies with anyone we could wrangle from the surrounding houses. Katrina became an ancient sorceress. Charlie and Pearl gathered sticks for a potion to be brewed in a cauldron that was really an old pot we'd found in the canyon. On warm evenings I'd set up a projector in the driveway and we'd watch Indiana Jones in the open air with the folks from the houses below and behind us. We'd walk next door to the nursery and buy cartons of ladybugs, which Charlie and Millie would scream with delight as they were opened and their world was suddenly covered in small charming flying beetles.

On Wednesdays I'd come home from the university where I was still planning and building for the next expeditions, and Kara would roast a chicken, sprinkling smoked paprika over it and baking it on low. I'd carve it around a table of my expedition mates, Shay, Nate, Kostas, whoever was available, like we were having Thanksgiving dinner. We'd make boisterous toasts about the wind in our sails and the sun against our faces, and the fact that when faced between two choices we would always pick the more adventurous one, sometimes evoking old English accents to mimic the speeches we imagined officers would make in the days of the age of sail. Drones stacked next to changing tables. Expedition maps pinned above the bassinet. Kara designed patches and stitched them to our jackets as if we were astronauts preparing for launch. We turned the crowdsourced satellite platform from the Khan project into a startup we called Tomnod, Mongolian for "eye in the sky," and to our surprise the eye we had built for one mountain began turning toward the rest of the world, eventually helping six million people join the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. At night I would read volumes of the Master and Commander series to Charlie and Millie as they fell asleep to the incredible detail with which Patrick O'Brian could build the life on a ship of the line into our imaginations. When the book was closed I'd linger in the room they shared, partly scared to trip over the sea of toys sprawled around me like the booby traps purported to protect the First Emperor's tomb. One false step and a Lego piece would be wedged into my heel. Kara's Danish desserts made it nearly impossible to get them to sleep, and any move was a risk. So I'd sit there in the silence, trapped in a sea of toys and domestication, a book of adventure in my lap and a future of unknowns all around me. This is how it went for a long time, through the heart of the Mongolia years and in their wake.

--

The desert opened around us. I could feel the road pulling away from the city, from everything, the way it always does on the 395.

--

After the final expedition, and days before we were to publish a story on what we had found, the phone rang. The Mongolian Minister of Culture explained that most of our findings from the mountain had to be embargoed. It was not said directly, but implied that my foreign status and Chinese last name had turned our work on the sacred site into a political liability. Through Baika I heard the worst part: even Amaraa was feeling the pressure, as Baika suggested I remove photos of us together from the internet to lessen the fallout.

I hung up and watched Charlie playing in our six-foot by ten-foot grass patch of a garden through the window. The shaman's words came back. Respect the old ways. The mountain wasn't mine to define. I compiled all the results, had them translated into Mongolian, submitted the report to the government, and let it go.

But it was painful. For Amaraa and Ishdorj, my Americanness and the blue spot story had been how I'd shown up. I had ridden with them, wrestled with them, stood on the mountain with them. But my last name carried eight centuries of weight between two nations whether I claim it or not. For Mongolians, a Chinese surname signals centuries of conflict, the erosion of land and language, the monasteries burned during the Cultural Revolution. History is not something of the past. It shapes the way we see each other right now, and it was shaping the way my work was being seen, regardless of who I actually was or where I had actually come from.

I had come to Genghis Khan's story with excitement and defiance. Western history had left him out or reduced him to a barbarian, and I saw in my own blue spot a belonging to something far more extraordinary.

The project itself hadn't failed. The whole search had been rooted in the promise of looking without touching, and we had kept that promise. The storm-torn roots had shown us more than we expected to see, and the geophysical scans hinted at what lay beneath. But on that mountain we had made the critical decision not to go any further. It wasn't ours to decide what happened next. The shaman's words had reminded us of that. The will for secrecy around the burial site had survived eight hundred years, proof that this was living history, not the dead kind. And I had to accept that what I was looking for could never be confirmed from the dirt, not under the promise I had made. What the mountain had really been showing me was that some secrets can remain, and the sacred part I was meant to share with the world was the reverence itself, not the secret it protected.

So I let it go. Just as the approach had been non-invasive, so would the response. To push back would be to hurt the very thing I was hoping to honor. It was hard, but it was a simple truth bigger than me.

What stayed with me wasn't the embargo or the lost findings. It was that our journey had become a source of pain for the people it was supposed to celebrate. That's what broke me. Amaraa never said a word about it to me directly. He didn't have to. Our brotherhood would survive it, and he would one day be at my side in a way I couldn't yet imagine.

But I was complete with the search. The most significant thing I had found on that mountain wasn't in the ground. It was in the people who had become my family, and in the understanding that what I'd find in the years ahead wouldn't come from tombs alone. It would come from the memory and spirit of the living.

And then Millie came. And whatever had been lost was eclipsed by what arrived.

--

The road climbed through dry hills. I checked the mirror. Both kids still out. Millie's mouth was slightly open, her Elsa doll clutched to her chest even in sleep.

--

She'd been born under a full wolf moon. I'd woken at 3 AM to find Kara reorganizing the entire pantry in a frenzy of primal nesting, and by morning she was in labor. When I held my daughter for the first time, something in me that had been reaching and striving and chasing for years went still. Her entire palm gripped my finger as if I were some kind of giant. On her lower back was the same blue spot Charlie had been born with, the mark my grandfather had pointed to on his own skin in that tiny Hong Kong apartment years ago. I had my boy and my girl. Charlie walked into the room with a bright red firetruck we'd arranged for Millie to "bring him from the other side of existence," and instantly they were best friends. For a while I just held her. The expeditions, the startup, the mountain, all of it shrank to the scale of this tiny person breathing in my arms.

The next day, my cofounders commandeered an empty delivery room down the hall, carrying briefcases. The Tomnod deal had come through, a buyout that came with golden handcuffs, four years of corporate work in Boulder. It was a wild juxtaposition, the birth of one baby and the release of another. But I looked at Millie, asleep in the bassinet a wall away, and the decision wasn't hard. If I wanted my kids to know a life led by their passions, I had to live that life myself. I left most of it on the table, said goodbye to my closest friends, and kept building a life as an explorer, as ridiculous as that sounded.

Not long after, Gil disappeared in the Peruvian Andes. He'd been with us just a few months before, holding Charlie on his lap. His laugh and grungy untethered spirit had always made him seem like a wolf amongst dogs, and seeing him hold my kid in our quirky domesticated setting with a big smile on his face was something I'll never forget. "Maybe this is the next step?" he said, looking down at Charlie with the frightened awkwardness of a man seeing change looming on the horizon. He'd once written, "Perhaps mountain climbing has become a way for me to recover all the beautiful things I have lost. Perhaps it is the manifestation of my search for truth. Perhaps I expect to find a clue which will lead me towards the meaning of life. But all I ever find are more mountains to climb."

When the guys turned Tomnod's satellite eye toward the mountain to search for him, it found his final tracks in the snow. He had fallen. I stared at those tracks on a screen and thought about all the places our friendship had taken us, and how the mountains that gave us so much could also take everything.

--

The road kept climbing. I passed a sign for Lone Pine. Not far now.

--

Millie was fierce from the start. As Rich put it, she was always ready to fight for her seat at the table. She lived in an Elsa dress so long that it would end up in tatters, and before you knew it there was a small pile of shredded blue dresses that made up the majority of her hamper. No one would tell her otherwise, and no one could. If there was one word for her it was determination. But beneath the will was a kindness that matched her brother's, just expressed differently, like the same song played in a different key. Charlie was easy, gentle, curious. Millie was a force. Together they were everything.

With the money from the sale I began to build us a home from the ground up. My sister Jane had become an architect, and with her guidance I set to work on the house. Charlie and I made pirate ships from leftover wood. Millie swung from whatever wasn't nailed down. I was building the life my parents hadn't been able to hold together.

New expeditions were calling. National Geographic sent me to Guatemala, then China. The expeditions fed my soul, and so did my children. Both were desire, and the situation made me choose between them.

----

The 395 stretched ahead in the darkness, the kids long asleep. A truck passed going the other way, its headlights sweeping across the cab and then gone.

--

The truth is I don't know when the marriage started to go wrong. It wasn't a single moment. It was more like the dishes that piled up in our sink, spreading from the basin to the countertops until the mess was everywhere and neither of us could remember who was supposed to clean it up. The fights grew more frequent. The silences between them grew heavier. We argued over the decisions that poured into any young family, but underneath was something neither of us had words for yet.

I was gone too much. That was part of it, and it was the part I could see. Each expedition took me further into the world, and each homecoming required a longer adjustment back into a life that had kept moving without me. Most of the career explorers I'd met at Nat Geo headquarters had been divorced. I told myself we'd be different.

We were driving back from a weekend in the mountains when it happened. The pine trees thinned as we descended, and the city appeared below us, highways branching in every direction, headlights glowing in the setting sun. The kids were asleep in the back seat, so we couldn't really talk, but it was clear she didn't want to anyway. The tension sat between us. I remember the road curving through the last of the foothills, the way the light caught the windshield, and the feeling that something was about to be said that couldn't be unsaid. I kept my hands on the wheel and my eyes on the road. Neither of us spoke for the last twenty minutes. The only sound was the kids snoring gently in the back and the tires on asphalt, and in that silence the marriage was already over. I just didn't know it yet.

When we got home I carried Charlie to his bed, then Millie. I tucked them in the way I always did, pulling the blankets up to their chins, and stood there for a moment watching them sleep. Then I closed the door and walked into the kitchen where Kara was waiting. The fight that had been building for months broke open, and in the middle of it she said something that rearranged my understanding of the previous five years. She'd been living a lie, she said. She'd realized she was a lesbian, and she couldn't suppress it any longer.

The person I'd known seemed to vanish overnight, replaced by someone I didn't recognize. I don't say that to diminish her courage. 'Coming out' must have been terrifying, and I can only imagine the loneliness of carrying that secret through a marriage and two children. But in that moment I couldn't see her bravery. I could only feel the floor disappearing.

I had promised myself I would never walk away from my family the way my father had walked away from his. I never imagined she would be the one to leave. The pattern I'd spent my adult life trying to break had repeated itself, only from a direction I never saw coming. My parents' marriage collapsed when I was seventeen and it shaped everything. Now my kids were three and six.

That night I drove to the house I'd been building a few blocks away. It was just framing and sawdust, no exterior siding yet, the cold night air coming straight through the walls. I stood in the hallway alone for a long time. There were no children breathing on the other side of a wall. There was no one. Just the wind through the bones of a house that was supposed to hold everything, and didn't hold anything yet.

The first night, my friends helped me build a bed. Shay and Tom were there, along with a few others from those days. But later, as it settled in that this was not going away, the lonely nights came. There was no front door yet. Wind blew through the open frames and reminded me it was a construction site. I'd plug my amplifier into the unfinished walls and play guitar until my hands bled. A crowbar next to the bed where the dream of a wife had been.

Rich handed me a surfboard. "Surf it out," he said. And I did. But more than surfing, I built. I built the house by day. Played guitar alone at night, Johnny Cash on in the background, plywood under my feet.

The kids traveled between Kara's place and mine, carrying themselves between two versions of home with a grace that no child should have to summon. But they were each other's rocks. Millie would boss Charlie around and Charlie would let her, and then they'd curl up together and the world outside their little circle would stop mattering.

On my weeks with them, I cooked mac and cheese on a camp stove in the one finished room and we all piled together to sleep. One evening, as I was heating dinner and trying to hold it together, Charlie watched me quietly. I told him that he and Millie were my best friends.

He looked at me with those steady eyes and said, "More than friends. Family."

I had to turn away so he wouldn't see my face.

--

The highway was empty now. Just the center line and the headlights and the hum of the engine pulling us north.

--

I turned to my guitar, and then to the people who showed up with instruments of their own. Jamie Shadowlight played electric violin the way weather moves, unpredictably, in sweeping patterns that felt less composed than channeled. We built battery-powered amplifiers and carted them out to the desert to play for the stars alone. We called ourselves the Infinite Vortices, and our only fans were rocks and cactus and the occasional desert rabbit. But the music was putting me back together.

The wounds healed. The house took shape. Kara and I chose forgiveness, not for ourselves but for the kids.

My father had been reaching out for years, and I had refused to answer. But now, holding my own children through a fracture that mirrored the one he'd caused in my life, I began to understand that pride can build like a mountain over time. I didn't want Charlie to grow up without a grandfather because I was trapped in a cycle of resentment. So I picked up the phone. The conversation was awkward and halting and nowhere near enough. But it was a beginning.

And then, a few months before the accident, I met Bruna. A media coach suggested coffee at a nearby shop. What he didn't tell me was that he knew there was a beautiful woman behind the counter. I walked up and ordered a black coffee. She asked how I was doing.

"I've just been preparing," I said.

"Preparing for what?"

"I'm going to China to use near-infrared satellite imagery to survey a two-thousand-year-old tomb that housed thousands of terracotta warriors, created to carry the first emperor into the afterlife."

She handed me my coffee, leaned forward, and gave a smile that took my breath away. Derek picked me up for Burning Man that summer, and amidst forty thousand people in the desert, there she was, covered in dust, running toward me. We locked eyes, and tears and laughter came for reasons neither of us could explain. Back in San Diego a week later Charlie and Millie bonded with her instantly. For the first time since the divorce, I could see a version of the future that wasn't just me holding on alone.

---

The headlights found a sign: Diaz Lake. I pulled off the road and killed the engine. The kids were still asleep in their camper beds. I stepped out into the cold air and looked up at Mount Whitney rising in the moonlight, the same mountain I'd climbed with Gil years before. I was alone, but not. All of it had led here, to this road, with these two sleeping kids, and the feeling that we were going to be alright.

The next morning we fished for trout and had one for breakfast. Then we turned east into Death Valley.

We entered that vast desert with nothing but each other, rolling past sand dunes and dried lake beds and salty hot springs that bubbled up with primordial fish. Dust storms kicked up tornadoes across the alluvial plains, and we put on ski goggles and played in the howling wind. Whenever there was a nice view we'd stop, unfurl a carpet and sun umbrellas, and make nature our living room. Time slowed. The stress dissolved. The further we went, the more insignificant all my fear and confusion began to seem.

One evening, we came to the edge of a vast sea of sand dunes. Millie climbed onto my shoulders as we made our way toward the tallest one, miles from where we'd parked. These weren't mountains of stone but mountains of sand, shaped by millions of years of wind, their beauty born from the storm. Charlie turned to me, wise beyond his years, and said, "Dad, we're going to be okay."

We sat at the top of the highest dune and watched afternoon give way to evening. As the light faded we lay on our backs with our feet in the air, pretending we were astronauts floating through the universe. Then we slid down side by side, laughing all the way to the bottom, golden sand clinging to our skin.

Days later I dropped the kids at their mom's. Millie's hair was full of dreadlocks. Charlie was covered in bug bites and scrapes. Kara gave me a knowing smirk and asked me to learn how to comb the tangles out of Millie's hair. Other than that, she was happy for us. And from that moment on we found a new stride. We were different people for our kids, but we chose to trust that those differences would fit together to help them become whoever they were meant to be.

At least for a few months. Until a car flipped on its side and crushed me beneath it.
title: Chapter 7: The Break

content:
Chapter 8: Limb Salvage

I woke to beeping. A heart rate monitor somewhere to my left, steady and mechanical, reducing my body to a number on a screen. Fluorescent lights buzzed overhead. I tried to move and couldn't. I tried to remember, but it felt like I was trying to remember a dream within a dream.

It came back in pieces. Each time I surfaced from the sedatives, another fragment would appear. The golden afternoon at the bay. Millie's fish. The Rhino climbing the dirt track, Adam steering in playful arcs. And then the tilt, that slow-motion shift where time seemed to stretch and I could see everything that was about to happen but couldn't stop it. My foot shooting out as if one leg could push back two thousand pounds of rolling metal. The sound. The dust. Millie screaming. The strange silence that followed, where I lay staring at the sky and saw, in a single terrible flash, every version of the future I'd been building collapse at once.

Then darkness. Bruna's hands wrapped around my head as she chants. Then a surgeon's face above me, calm and steady, saying something about doing everything they could. Then darkness again. X-rays. Metal rods driven through shattered bone. Hoses flushing the dirt that had been ground into my flesh. I'd surface for a few seconds, long enough to register Bruna's face beside me, and then slip back under.

When I finally came to and stayed, I looked down and saw what I'd become. My leg was impaled with metal fixators and wrapped in bloody bandages. The thing at the end of it didn't look like a shin anymore. It looked like something that had been taken apart and reassembled by someone who'd only seen a limb described in a textbook.

There was Bruna, waiting as if she'd never left. How long had it been? Days? I had no idea.

I was told they were working on "limb salvage." The word hit differently than I expected. Not rescue, not recovery. Salvage. Like a ship that's already gone down and you're just trying to pull what you can from the wreckage.

The days that followed settled into a rhythm that felt less like healing and more like endurance. Every morning the nurses unwound layer after layer of gauze while I gripped the bed rails and tried to breathe through it. Every afternoon the physical therapists arrived. "Just try to stand, put a little weight on it." Every time I tried, the blood rushed down into my leg, swelling it until the pain wiped out every thought except "make it stop!". We'd try again tomorrow.

Between attempts, I lay there. The ceiling became the most familiar surface in my world. I memorized the pattern of the acoustic tiles, counted the tiny holes in them, traced the seams where they met. But amidst the uncertainty, there was also a strange sense of relief, all the swirling energy of my life had been forced to a halt. Fate had grabbed me by the neck and said stop. For the first time in years, I wasn't going anywhere. Literally.

Objects started appearing around me. Cards covered the windowsill and spilled onto the floor. Someone brought my guitar from the house. Paint sets and brushes appeared, gifts from friends who knew I liked to draw but didn't know my hands shook too much to hold a brush. An explorer who can't walk. Would I even be able to work again?

Then the visitors came. My mother arrived from one direction, my father from another, the two of them navigating the awkwardness of being in the same room for the first time in years because their son was in a hospital bed. Old climbing partners showed up with red eyes and tight smiles. Everyone I'd ever known filed through that room. It felt, in the strangest way, like I was attending my own funeral. They draped my bed with bright decorations, strung up lights, brought scotch that the doctors immediately confiscated. They turned the sterile room into something that looked more like a festival camp than an ICU recovery ward.

I remember looking down at my one remaining foot sticking out from the bottom of the hospital bed and being embarrassed at how mangled it looked. Years of climbing and expeditions had done a number on it. I wished I'd taken better care of it. Bruna looked at it and said, "At least now you'll get to pay half price for a pedicure." Explorers don't get pedicures, I shot back.

She slept in the chair beside my bed every night, with a blanket the nurses brought her. She managed visitors, changed my bandages, chased down nurses when the pain spiked. It was an intense way to fall in love, but that's exactly what was happening. The empty passenger seat from a few months before wasn't empty anymore.

Kara brought Charlie and Millie. The moment they walked in, the room changed. Charlie was careful around the equipment, studying everything with his quiet, cataloging attention, asking the nurses what each machine did. Millie grabbed at whatever she could reach. They climbed over the bed and wrapped my face in bandages like a mummy, and their laughter cut through everything. I did my best to make it an adventure. Look at all these cool machines. Look at Dad's robot leg. I made faces and told jokes and let them draw on my cast with markers. But beneath the performance was a fear I couldn't speak: that the father they deserved, the one who carried them on his shoulders and drove them into the desert to camp under the stars, had been crushed under the roll cage with the rest of my bones. What kind of father would I be now? When Charlie hugged me goodbye that day, he did it so gently, so carefully, as if he understood that his father was something that could break. He was six years old.

At one point, while Bruna was carefully peeling back my bandages, Kara caught sight of my leg and fainted. After the initial awkwardness of their first meeting, I think she was relieved Bruna was there. Having someone else to share the weight of what was happening was better than carrying it alone.

One night Bruna climbed into the hospital bed with me. Within seconds every heart rate monitor in the room started going off. Nurses came running.
