We tried to play it off awkwardly, Bruna smoothing the blankets like she was just adjusting pillows, me staring at the ceiling with an expression that fooled no one. The nurses looked at us, looked at the monitors, and left without a word.

About two weeks in, the doctor who'd first operated on me stopped by for a quieter conversation. He closed the door and sat on the edge of the chair and looked at me for a long time before he spoke.

"The truth is, you can go through years of surgery and it will destroy your body and consume your life. But from what I saw in that operating room, you'll never get back the leg you remembered." He paused. "I think you should consider amputation."

The word didn't register at first. I had no frame of reference for it. In my mind, amputation was something out of a Civil War documentary, bearded surgeons and biting down on leather. It wasn't something that happened to thirty-five-year-old explorers in San Diego.

But I was in so much pain. Day after day in that bed, watching my life shrink to the size of a hospital room. How much worse could it really be?

When I told friends and family I was considering it, the reactions were immediate. My mother and father were both shaken, in their own different ways. My friends were shocked. But Derek was the first to push back hard.

At first he'd been running around doing whatever needed doing, fetching my guitars from the house, bringing things Bruna asked for, always arriving with his hands full and his smile already going. But once Bruna was in command of the bedside, Derek reverted to the way we'd always been. He got curious. He started asking questions about the fixators, the oxygen chambers, the failure rates of different procedures. He worked the phones. He called every doctor he knew, every friend of a friend on the UCSD medical faculty. He reminded me that Eli, who was part of our circle, could be my attending infectious disease specialist.

"You're exhausted and you're in pain and you're making the biggest decision of your life from a hospital bed," he said. "How could you make a decision as drastic as cutting off your leg without at least trying everything?"

He was right, and I knew it. My family wasn't ready either. None of us were.

Reluctantly, I agreed to the transfer.

UCSD was different, it was a research hospital which meant we could try unconventional things. The doctors were good and they knew me, which made the clinical distance feel less cold. They wheeled me into a series of new surgeries and operations, each with a specific target: cleaning out infection, stabilizing the fixators, trying to coax blood flow back into tissue that was giving up. I spent hours in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber shaped like a giant submarine with gauges and wheeled handles that looked like something out of Jules Verne's mind, lying inside it while pressure built around me, willing my cells to cooperate. The curved ceiling was inches from my face. Condensation formed and dripped. The hum of the machine was the only sound, and in that sealed metal tube, with oxygen pumping into my bloodstream, I was truly alone for the first time since the accident. There was no one in there to look strong for. My mind would wander and I'd pretend I was an ocean explorer, a captain in some vessel from Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea. I brought the Master and Commander books I'd been reading to Charlie and Millie at bedtime, and in that pressurized capsule, separated from the world by sheets of metal, I lost myself in Patrick O'Brian's ship of the line. The irony wasn't lost on me. A few months ago I'd been reading these adventures to my kids after the Indiana Jones projector nights and the ladybug releases. Now I was reading them alone in a metal tube, the adventure books becoming my only way out while my body was being pressurized back together. Between chapters I'd lie there and wonder if my world as I had known it was over.

Because of the pain medication I required, they moved me to the high-level ICU where I could be monitored more closely. It was there, on a long night after one of the surgeries, that the pain found a new register.

Bruna was in the chair beside me. The doctors had explained that pain management was about getting in front of it, staying ahead of the wave so it never fully crested. She'd set her alarm for every hour so she could wake before the latest IV infusion of pain meds wore off and click the dispenser to allow more to arrive. Every hour through the night. Click. Sleep. Alarm. Click. But somewhere in the long hours, the wave got ahead of us. I was writhing, gripping the rails, my whole body clenched against a pain so total it erased thought. I fought it the way I'd fought everything in my life, with resistance, with will, as if I could overpower it by refusing to submit.

But the resistance was making it worse. Every muscle I clenched amplified it, sent it ricocheting through my body until I was fighting myself as much as the pain. I don't know when exactly I gave up. Not in the way of defeat but in the way of a fist unclenching. I stopped fighting. I didn't have a choice. There was nothing left to fight with.

And when I stopped, the pain didn't go away. But it changed. It was still enormous, still consuming, but it was no longer crushing me because I was no longer pushing back against it. I lay there breathing, tears on my face, and the pain moved through me instead of against me. Bruna's hand on mine. The beeping of the monitors. The fluorescent hum.

I have many gaps in my memory from that time. The pain medication blurred days together, erased conversations, rearranged the order of events until I couldn't be sure what had happened when. But that night stayed with me. Something in my understanding of my own body had shifted, the lesson was somewhere in my bones: the resistance was its own kind of suffering, separate from the pain itself.

As the weeks ground on, the broader pattern became clear. Each surgery seemed to buy a little less than the one before. The infections came back. The tissue wouldn't hold. I could see it in the doctors' faces, that slight hesitation before they said "let's try one more thing." A loop of diminishing returns that was consuming what was left of my strength.

I started to understand what limb salvage actually meant in practice. It wasn't a plan to make me whole. It was a plan to harvest pieces from the rest of my body, transplant the muscles of my back, graft skin from my thigh, all to Frankenstein some semblance of a foot back together. The nerves were shattered. The circulation was compromised. The bones were held together by metal rods doing the work that calcium no longer could. Even in the best case, I'd end up with something I'd have to protect for the rest of my life, not something I could live on.

Mark Meyers came to visit. My old professor, the Brazilian military officer turned poet who'd first let me into his lab after weeks of sweeping floors. He sat at my bedside and we talked not about the leg I was losing but about the one I might build. He framed the whole thing as an engineering challenge, the way he'd framed everything since the day I'd met him. What materials, what design, what interface between biology and machine. For the first time since the accident, I felt the engineer in me stir. If I amputated, I was removing the variable I couldn't control. Everything after that was not up to the doctors, it would become a design problem, and design problems were what I'd been trained to solve.

The fork in the road came about three weeks after the accident. The surgeon sat me down and laid it out plainly. Option one: the back transplant. Take muscle tissue to rebuild the soft tissue around the rods. Multiple additional surgeries. Months more in the hospital. No guarantee it would hold. Option two: amputation.

The choice was mine alone.

I thought about it for days. I thought about it while they changed my dressings. I thought about it while Bruna was asleep in the chair and the corridor was quiet and the only sound was the beeping that had become the metronome of my new life. I'd stare at the ceiling and run the same loop. If I keep the leg. If I lose the leg. If I keep it. If I lose it. I thought about my kids. I thought about the steppe. I thought about the sand dunes in Death Valley, Millie on my shoulders. I thought about my dreams of backpacking with Charlie, now seemingly gone.

What would I become?

Then Brent came to visit. He'd been with us at the bay on the day of the accident. While everyone else had been focused on saving my leg, Brent had been quietly looking forward.

He'd found a prosthetic clinic that looked more like a gym than a hospital, run by a guy who built legs for Paralympians and veterans. Machines and carbon fiber and people learning to run again. And he'd found a photograph, which he brought to my bedside.

In the photo, a one-legged surfer named Mike Coots was riding a barreling wave, his bright yellow prosthetic slicing through the water, his face lit with pure joy. Coots had lost his leg to a tiger shark at seventeen and never stopped surfing. He'd just switched to a shorter board.

I held the picture and stared at it. Will I ever surf again? I'd asked the doctor the night of the accident. What I'd really meant was something bigger. Will I carry my kids? Will I run with them? Will I climb those dunes with Millie on my shoulders again? Will I still be the father they need?

For weeks I'd been staring at a mangled leg and imagining years of surgeries to preserve something that was already gone. This photograph showed me something else. A man who'd lost the same thing I was losing, and who looked more alive than I felt.

I gathered my friends and family. My parents. Derek. Bruna. The people who had carried me through three weeks of limbo. I told them I'd made my decision.

"I can't cling to the past," I said. "It's gone. I need to do this."

The room was quiet. Adam, who'd been driving the Rhino when it flipped, looked destroyed. The guilt had been eating at him since the day of the accident, visible every time he visited, in his eyes, in his voice, in the way he couldn't quite look at my leg. I told him it would be okay. That what had happened was an accident, and we'd leave the regret behind with the rest of what was about to be cut away. I told him that the pain of regret was something we could fix, and we needed to fix whatever we could out of the wreckage.

The doctor brought me a consent form. One page. I stared at it for a long time, at everything that single piece of paper represented. The irreversible act of signing the death of my former self. Then I signed it, and reached for the guitar.

I started playing something loose and bluesy, making it up as I went. Told everyone this was the Goodbye Leg Blues. The room shifted. Someone laughed, then caught themselves, then laughed again when they saw I was smiling. Bruna and Tim Kelly filmed it with a smile on their faces. Derek leaned against the doorframe shaking his head with that look he got when I did something he thought was both insane and exactly right. My mother wiped her eyes and tried to sing along to a song that was finding its words on the fly.

It wasn't gallows humor exactly. It was something closer to a wake. A sendoff for the body I was about to leave behind. I played until my fingers hurt and my voice cracked, and for a few minutes the hospital room felt like every campfire and jam session and midnight kitchen table I'd ever sat around, a circle of people I loved, nobody wanting to be the first to stop.

Then the doctor rushed in and the music stopped. My latest labs had come back. The bone infection that had been lurking was spreading fast. If they didn't operate now, it could kill me.

The celebration was over. It was time.

They wheeled me down the hallway to the operating room. The fluorescent lights slid past overhead, one after another. I saw Charlie in the corridor. He was holding Millie's hand. He looked at me with those steady, serious eyes, and I tried to project a strength I didn't feel. Millie waved. She didn't fully understand what was happening, but she could feel it, and she waved the way she waved when I dropped them at their mom's, a wave that meant she trusted I'd come back.

My mother's face. My father's, tight and pale. Adam, who couldn't look.

Charlie held my gaze as the gurney rolled past. I held his back. The last thing I wanted him to see was fear.

In the operating room everything was bright and cold. The surgical team moved around me in scrubs and masks. The anesthesiologist prepared a cocktail that Derek had helped coordinate with my pain doctors. It contained ketamine, a dissociative that could reduce the risk of phantom limb pain by disrupting the brain's map of the body before the body was altered. That was the theory. Nobody knew for certain.

Bruna held my hand. Charlie's face was still in my mind, those steady eyes in the corridor. Millie's wave. I tried to hold all of it as the drugs took hold and the room began to dissolve. The ketamine carried me somewhere else entirely.

I was flying among pyramids, and then I was the pyramids. Geometric forms built and collapsed and rebuilt around me, an infinite avalanche of shapes in constant motion, crystalline structures assembling and shattering and reassembling. Chaos and order locked in a struggle so vast that I was nothing inside it, a speck of awareness tumbling through an architecture that didn't care whether I existed. I was afraid. The chaos felt like it would grind me to dust, reduce me to the particles I was made of and scatter them into the void.

And then I realized there was nothing I could do about it. I couldn't fight it. I couldn't outrun it. The only choice left was to stop resisting.

The avalanche didn't stop. But it stopped feeling like destruction. What had been terror became warmth, an immense, engulfing presence that I can only describe as love. Not the love you feel for another person. Something more fundamental, more like the medium everything was suspended in, the way water holds a fish without the fish ever knowing it's wet.

Somewhere in the middle of it, my father's voice came back to me. He'd told me once about the first instant after the Big Bang. Nearly equal amounts of matter and antimatter, created simultaneously, annihilating each other on contact. For every billion particles that collided and destroyed each other, one extra particle of matter survived. From that remainder, that margin so small it shouldn't have mattered at all, came everything. Every star. Every ocean. Every hand that ever reached for another hand.

Was that what I was feeling? The trace of something that outlasted the destruction, not by force but by the slimmest of margins? I don't know. I don't know what any of it was. But it was the most real thing I've ever experienced.

While my mind moved through whatever space that was, my body lay on the table. With scalpel and saw, the surgeons removed my leg below the knee. The tibia and fibula I'd run with as a kid, climbed trees on, urged horses across the Mongolian steppe with. The leg that had carried my son on my shoulders and spun my daughter in the living room of a house I'd built with my own hands. All of it, separated from me and taken away.

I surfaced just once, briefly, as the nurse wheeled me out of the operating room. Through glazed eyes I saw her face above me. I heard my own voice, distant and strange, say something I hadn't planned. I told her I'd seen whatever God is, and it was just love, and it wins. I don't know where those words came from. They didn't sound like mine. Then my eyes closed again.

Hours later I woke in my hospital bed. The room was full of flowers and cards. Family and friends who'd been waiting for the sedatives to wear off filled the chairs and lined the walls. Their faces were careful, watching me the way you watch someone who might shatter.

I looked down at my body.

Where there had been a mangled limb full of rods and tubes and bloody bandages, there was nothing. A smooth white wrapping where my shin used to be, and then air. My leg was gone. Not temporarily, not in the foggy way it had been gone under anesthesia, but truly, permanently, irreversibly gone. The space it had occupied for thirty-five years was just space now.

The realization broke over me. Under the gaze of everyone who loved me, I wept. I wept for the leg and for the life attached to it. For the mountains I'd climbed and the waves I'd surfed and the horses I'd ridden across the steppe with my best friends beside me. For the version of myself who had walked into this hospital three weeks ago still believing he might walk out the same man. For my children, who didn't ask for any of this. I wept until there was nothing left.

Charlie and Millie climbed up onto the bed. Charlie moved carefully, avoiding the tubes and the wrapping, settling in on one side. Millie scrambled up on the other, less careful but just as certain, tucking her head under my arm. I looked down at my two kids pressed against me, their small bodies warm against mine, and I said what I could think to say.

"Hey. When life gives you lemons, you make lemonade."

Derek was filming on his phone. I've watched that video since. From the look in my eyes I'm not sure I fully believed what I was saying. But I said it. And Charlie and Millie looked up at me and nodded, because they were six and three and their dad had said it would be okay, and that was enough for now.

A few days later, National Geographic sent a gift basket in the shape of a foot. Bruna and I stared at it, then at the space where my foot used to be, then back at the basket. We laughed the kind of laughter that lives right next to tears and you can't always tell which one it is.

I was thirty-five years old, starting over with one leg and two kids and a woman asleep in a chair who had chosen to stay. Millie's fingers were wrapped around the collar of my hospital gown, and she was holding on, and so was I.
title: Chapter 8: Limb Salvage

content:
Chapter 9: The Ghost

The visions I'd experienced during the amputation were profound, but there was something terrifying about them too. As I returned to consciousness, I carried a dizzying memory of having glimpsed an infinite filing cabinet of realities, and an unsettling sense that I couldn't know if I'd been placed back into the same drawer.

Was I still in the same reality?

It didn't feel like it.

In the days following the operation, I was like an infant. I couldn't accomplish the simplest tasks without help. I'd try to stand on crutches and the blood would rush down to the wound, filling it with a pressure so unbearable I'd vomit and crawl back into bed. I was on button-released doses of opioid painkillers, spaced out with intervals that made real sleep impossible. Bruna stayed up through the nights, pressing the button so I could rest. Everything I had been, the man who'd led expeditions into forbidden mountains and climbed three thousand feet of Yosemite granite, was reduced to a person who couldn't get to the bathroom without help.

A week later they discharged me. They wheeled me outside with a bag full of medication, and for the first time in a month the sun hit my face. I breathed air that hadn't been circulated through hospital vents, and the feeling of it, the warmth, the wind, the smell of grass, was so overwhelming it nearly knocked me over.

Before going home I asked Bruna to take me to get a haircut. After a month in the hospital I looked like some cross between a marooned sailor lost at sea and a person just released from a medieval prison tower. The barber stared at my wheelchair and my leg and my wild eyes and didn't ask questions. When she was done I looked almost human again. It was the first normal thing I'd done in weeks.

When I got home, the first thing I noticed wasn't the bed transplanted to my living room or the wheelchair waiting at the bottom of the stairs. It was the silence. No beeping monitors, no shuffling nurses, no fluorescent hum. Just the creak of my own house and the distant sound of traffic on the street outside.

The second thing I noticed was that my house had become an obstacle course. Doorframes I'd framed with my own hands were too narrow for the wheelchair. The bathroom required a production, crutches wedged against the counter, my body balanced on one leg, every basic function an engineering problem. Rich, my old neighbor from when the kids were born, came into the house and installed handicap bars where I would need them. I remember thinking, the leg isn't going to grow back, so make the changes to the house permanent. I couldn't carry a glass of water across the room because both hands were on the crutches. I couldn't pick up Millie when she ran to me because I'd fall over. The stairs to the second floor might as well have been Everest. My world had shrunk to the ground floor, the wheelchair, and whatever Bruna could bring within reach.

Amaraa had flown in from Mongolia. When I saw him standing in my doorway with that wide, weathered grin, it took me a moment to realize who I was looking at. This was the man who had taken me into his family on the steppe, who had knelt beside me on the summit of the sacred mountain with his belt draped across his neck and his hands raised to the sky. He had traveled halfway around the world to carry me into my own house. He and Derek and a few others lifted me out of the wheelchair and brought me inside, navigating the doorframes and furniture with the awkward tenderness of people handling something fragile. I could feel them trying not to jostle me, their hands careful, their jokes a little too loud, covering the fear underneath.

That night they sat around my bed in the living room and threw a party that nobody quite knew the rules for. It wasn't somber and it wasn't celebratory. It was something new, a room full of people who loved me trying to figure out what came next. Bruna handed me my guitar and wrapped her arms around me, her chin resting on my shoulder. Flowers from well-wishers crowded every surface, so many the room smelled like a florist's shop. Derek found a bottle of something. Amaraa told stories about his uncle back home, how they'd asked about me, how the mountain was still standing. I played badly and nobody cared.

Was I still in the same reality?

In the weeks that followed, something I hadn't expected started happening. Three-year-old Millie started waking me each morning with my clothes laid out for the day and her best attempt at a breakfast tray. Six-year-old Charlie took on the chores of cleaning the dishes and taking out the trash, without being asked. The people I was supposed to take care of were taking care of me. I was watching my children become something the events of our lives were shaping them to be.

A few weeks after coming home, the Challenged Athletes Foundation hosted a triathlon in La Jolla. Friends of friends were involved, and someone insisted I come. It would be the first time I'd left the incubator my home had become since the amputation.

As Bruna and Derek drove me into town, I felt a self-consciousness I wasn't prepared for. I was in a wheelchair, missing a leg, and this was the first time anyone outside the people who loved me would see what I'd become.

Then I saw them. A group of amputees running the race, moving with fluid strength, part human, part hardware. Their prosthetics caught the light as they ran. Among them was Mike Coots, the one-legged surfer whose photograph had shifted everything for me in the hospital. The image that had been a lifeline just weeks before. And now, incredibly, he was standing right in front of me on the same carbon leg I'd studied in that picture.

Someone introduced us. He pulled me into a hug and said, without hesitation, "We'll be surfing in a year."

That night, the special I'd filmed in China about the first emperor's tomb premiered on television. The kids and I crowded around Adam's couch with his family to watch. It was strange, watching a ghost of myself. There I was on screen, running around ancient burial sites like it was nothing, two good legs carrying me wherever I wanted to go. Charlie and Millie kept looking from the screen to me and back, trying to reconcile the man on TV with the one beside them on the couch. I couldn't reconcile it either.

That was when the phantom pain began.

It started as sharp, electric darts, like lightning bolts firing from the place where my foot had once been. I'd look down and see nothing but air. The sensation was startling, almost surreal. Then it started taking over.

It triggered a pain that felt as if someone had lit my leg on fire, folded it in half, and pulled every tendon and muscle fiber apart. Except there were no tendons, no muscle fibers, no bones. There was only the ghost of what had been, screaming into the void. When I instinctively reached for the source of the pain, I found myself grasping at nothing, my mind glitching at the disconnect between what it expected and what was there.

Try this: close your eyes. Without looking, touch your toes. Wiggle your fingers. Feel where your body ends and the world begins. You can do it because your mind holds a map of itself, an ingrained understanding of where every part of you is at all times. Now imagine that map is wrong. Imagine your brain insisting that a part of you is still there, clenched in agony, burning, being crushed, and when you reach for it you find nothing but air. You can't scratch the itch. You can't rub the muscle. You can't put ice on the burn. The pain is real but the source of it no longer exists, and there is absolutely nothing you can do about it. That was my life. I was haunted by my own ghost.

The phantom grew stronger by the day. What had started as something triggered by specific movements became increasingly spontaneous, arriving without warning, without cause. It felt like a kind of drowning. I wasn't thinking about surfing with Mike Coots one day. I had two hundred and fifty thousand dollars in outstanding hospital bills, a still-unfinished house, and a career that was very much in jeopardy. But I couldn't think about any of that either. The pain superseded everything.

When it hit, I'd clutch my stump and seize up as if someone were electrocuting me. It would stop me in any moment, at any time, a cringe of pain that froze me until it passed and left a look of shock fading from my face. But the worst part was the bathroom. The nerves that had once run down my leg passed through my groin, and any activity associated with the lower half of my body triggered agony so severe I stopped wanting to drink water or eat. The fear of what was coming on the other end was enough to make me avoid the basic mechanics of staying alive. I was a man starving himself to avoid a pain that didn't technically exist. And the kids saw it all the time. It was impossible to hide. I'd be in the middle of dinner or reading to them and it would hit, and I'd freeze while they watched, not knowing what to do, waiting for their dad to come back.

Make it stop.

Make it stop.

Makeitstopmakeitstopmakeitstop.

I tried to find moments of levity, especially for the kids. When Halloween came around, I looked at my stump and then at Charlie and Millie and said, "I think Dad's going to be a pirate this year." I put on an eyepatch, strapped on a wooden peg leg, and handed out candy to neighborhood trick-or-treaters who hadn't heard about the accident. They kept trying to figure out how I was pulling off the illusion. "How is your leg doing that?" one kid asked, poking at it. Charlie and Millie thought this was the funniest thing they'd ever seen. I told the kid's dad that we were just really committed to Halloween this year, he laughed awkwardly. A few weeks later we went to Disneyland and discovered the first real perk of amputation: we never waited in a single line. "Dad," Millie said, "you should have done this a long time ago." There would be more of these moments as the months went on, small victories of absurdity. But the phantom didn't care about my sense of humor.

They'd sent me home with a list of medications that looked like I was running a pharmacy for a small village. But how could any drug fix something that wasn't actually there? The phantom had no address. It lived in a map my brain refused to update, and no pill was going to redraw that map.

At some point the dots began to connect. What was happening was in my mind, so I needed to find ways of reshaping my mind. I lay on the bed that had been brought downstairs for me, laptop open, and began to search. It was the only kind of expedition I could go on. I couldn't walk to the bathroom without help, but I could dive into the research, and the engineer in me treated it the same way I'd treated the search for the tomb: systematically, obsessively, pulling on every thread I could find.

I read about neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to rewire itself. I read about Kundalini yoga and transcendental meditation and float tanks. I read about how the Mazatec people of Oaxaca had used psilocybin for centuries as a portal to healing and understanding, and how María Sabina, the curandera whose ceremonies had brought this tradition into global consciousness, spoke of the mushrooms as a way to see "with the heart." I read about how roughly ninety percent of the world's cultures had institutionalized some form of altered states of consciousness, and that shamanism appeared built into virtually every society on earth, living and ancient. The shaman's drum that had vibrated through my chest on the sacred mountain in Mongolia, the Ohm that Bruna had chanted over me in the dirt, the mantras the Sherpa had pressed into my hand in Tibet, these weren't isolated practices. They were variations of a species-wide exploration of the mind, technologies of consciousness that had been developed and refined across tens of thousands of years. I started wearing heart rate variability monitors, trying to tune my body into parasympathetic resonance, the meditative state where the brain quiets enough to be rewritten. Ramesh Rao, the director of the UCSD center where I'd built the Genghis Khan project, showed me that through various states of meditation he could measurably shift his own bio-response on the HRV monitors. He introduced me to a lab at UCSD called the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination. What I needed to do was figure out how to imagine a new reality, and here was a place that studied exactly that. They helped me build visual feedback loops that could take the meditative states deeper, and Ramesh wanted to see if multiple people could converge their mind states simultaneously, synchronized flow, he called it. It was all about maximizing what psychologists called "flow states" to reach a point of neuroplasticity where the brain could accept new input. I asked Jamie and Leo, the same crew I'd been playing desert music with since the divorce, to wear the monitors during our jams. We'd play in open tunings, eyes closed, ears and hearts open, the variability sensors tracking what our bodies were doing beneath our awareness. Our only rule was to never play the same thing twice. Jamie on her violin, Leo on his drum synth, me on the guitar, finding synchronized streams of consciousness through spontaneous riffs that flowed in and out of each other. Sometimes we sounded awful. But there were times when our minds would let go entirely and I had no idea what my fingers were doing, the music playing itself through us rather than by us. Those were the moments when we'd look at the monitors afterward and see the signals converging, three separate hearts falling into the same rhythm without anyone leading. The Infinite Vortices had become a laboratory as much as a band. My living room looked like a California hippy research facility on hyperdrive. Bruna's crystals and sage and palo santo next to my laptop and VR goggles and biosensors. The woo-woo nature of some of these things wasn't lost on me, but they were all focused on a place that science and medicine couldn't reach alone, the mind. These were cultural clichés, but they were also rooted in older discoveries from cultures that had been studying consciousness as a science for thousands of years.

It was during this search that Derek and other friends reached out into the community and found that San Diego was home to the world's leading expert in phantom limbs: a neuroscientist who had written the book Phantoms in the Brain. His name was V. S. Ramachandran, but everyone called him Rama.

Tom Levy, the head of the archaeology department at UCSD, connected us. The next morning, Bruna wheeled me to his office. The hallway smelled of chalk dust in a way that reminded me of the labs my father had worked in. A sign said The Center for Brain and Cognition. I knocked and he appeared: a tall, elderly Indian man wearing a golfer's hat.

"You must be Albert," he said.

His office was a cabinet of curiosities. Brains floating in jars, artifacts from every continent, a dinosaur skull perched on a shelf beside stacks of papers. Graduate students orbited him like disciples. He was old and frail in his body, but as he talked a childlike wonder emerged in the knowing smiles and long stares. After introductions, he leaned forward with one of those smiles.

"Where do you think the body ends and the mind begins?"

He took me to a wall covered in mandalas. These intricate geometric patterns, he explained, were once understood as technologies of the mind, visual tools for focusing attention and inducing altered states. They weren't decorations. They were instruments. Different cultures, different centuries, same engineering problem: how to open a door in the mind that the mind doesn't know is there.

I began reading everything I could about the science behind what I was experiencing. The mind holds a geospatial map of itself, an ingrained understanding of where every part of the body is at all times. But my map was wrong now. Every time my nervous system tried to rely on it, it got lost. My brain interpreted that wrongness as pain so immense and intangible it left me helpless.

Rama had spent his career studying the border between body and mind, and had proposed that the same mirror neuron system that caused my phantom pain was also the mechanism behind human empathy, the ability to feel what another person feels, to literally mirror their experience in your own brain (ref: Ramachandran, V.S., "Mirror neurons and imitation learning as the driving force behind the great leap forward in human evolution," Edge.org, 2000). He had invented something called the mirror box, the first tool, he claimed, to actually remove a phantom limb. It looked like a wooden guillotine with mirrors inside. "You put your good leg here, your stump here," he said, demonstrating with his hands. "The mirror tricks your brain. Shows you two whole legs again. The phantom disappears because your mind believes what it sees. I am famous for removing something that isn't actually there," he said with a laugh.

Bruna helped me position my good leg on one side and my stump on the other. I looked down into the mirror. And there they were. Two legs. Two whole, intact, normal legs. I knew it was a reflection. I knew my left leg was gone. But my brain didn't care. It saw two legs and it believed. The phantom, which for weeks had been clenched in a position of agony, a foot that was on fire, a shin that was being crushed and folded in half, began to release. I could feel the muscles I no longer had unclenching. The burning cooled. The crushing eased. For the first time in weeks the screaming in my nervous system went quiet, and I sat there staring at two legs in a mirror and crying because the absence of pain, after so long, felt almost as overwhelming as the pain itself.

Then Rama lifted the mirror away. The fire rushed back like a door slamming shut. My brain had been shown a new story of itself. It just wasn't ready to hold it on its own.

Bruna kept driving me back. Each visit, Rama tried something new. He'd have Bruna sit next to me and put a blanket over our midsections so it looked like her leg was extending where mine should have been. She'd move her foot to mimic what mine used to do. All of a sudden I was a man with two legs, although one was significantly more beautiful than the other. It was imprecise, but real enough to fool my brain for a moment.

Some of the exercises bordered on the absurd. He'd gone to a Halloween store and come back with a bag full of severed plastic limbs. He placed one where my leg had been and then slowly pulled out the fixator pins that had been stuck in my real leg for weeks. As each one slid free from the rubber, I exhaled deeply, my body releasing tension it had been holding since the hospital. "Very interesting," Rama said with gravity, studying my face. Then he'd slide the fake leg away, forcing me to watch its disappearance over and over, training my brain to accept the absence. He also brought a lamp with a fan built into it and strips of orange fabric cut to look like flames, from the same Halloween store. He held it under the spot where my foot had been, trying to see if my phantom could feel the heat of a fake fire. I was an experiment of Halloween freakishness. But I laughed, and Rama laughed, and the graduate students scribbled notes and tried not to laugh, and for a minute the absurdity of a world-renowned neuroscientist waving blood-smeared rubber limbs and fake fire at an amputee explorer was the best medicine I'd had in weeks.

And then I'd return home, to the real torment. Towers of pain pills stacked on the counter. The phantom folding in on itself, set ablaze, crushed in ways no body could bear. I longed to be whole again, to move as I once had, to dance in the desert and chase my kids across the yard. Instead I was being leveled by a pain that lived only in my mind.

Bruna made each trip to Rama's office feel less like a medical visit and more like an adventure. And she'd smile at me with a love that carried no trace of pity.

But it wasn't all hospitals and phantom pain. On the good evenings, we'd buy packs of canvas and park my truck against the cliffs at sunset, sitting in the bed with paints and brushes, doing our best to capture whatever images were in our minds and never quite perfecting the art. It didn't matter. It was about being there. The truck had a canvas cover over the bed, and when the stars came out I'd fold it down and we'd lie there staring up, our own bedroom on wheels. She felt like the innocence of youth, a spirit that had emerged from Brazil with a passion that could transform anything into a moment of joy. She would see a full moon and stop everyone around her, strangers and friends alike, screaming in astonishment at its beauty in a way that you couldn't help but smile and join in. But that same passion we shared could turn the other direction just as fast, jealousy and fighting that burned as hot as the love. The intensity of our connection that had saved me in the hospital was the same intensity that would eventually make it hard for us to find level ground. I didn't see that yet. I only saw the stars and the paint on her fingers and the feeling of being alive beside someone who refused to let the world be ordinary.

One day she suggested we take a trip, our first since I'd left the hospital. She drove us to Joshua Tree. At the campsite there was a handicap parking spot. It was the first time I'd ever needed one. Someone was camped in it who clearly didn't qualify, and as I hobbled out of the truck on one leg, they shamefacedly packed their things and left. I watched them go and thought about this new separate existence I was in.

Bruna set up the tent while I sat in a camp chair and watched. I couldn't help. I couldn't hammer a stake or carry a bag or walk to the water spigot. Every time I needed to move, I'd plant the crutches in the sand and heave myself up, then swing my body forward in the lurching gait that had become my only way of getting anywhere. The crutches sank into soft ground. The sand got into everything. I'd been a climber, a surfer, a man who lived in his body. Now I was a spectator in the desert, watching someone set up camp for me because I couldn't do it myself. But years before, when I'd spent every weekend here with my crew of fellow climbers, someone had shown me a hidden cave tucked behind a few loose stones. I'd gone back to it whenever I could, just to sit in the quiet and look up. Knowing where to look, I could see the blackened marks left by ancient fires that once burned within, ghosts of another time, another body, another life.

We moved a few stones aside and crawled on our backs through the narrow opening. The air inside was cool and heavy, carrying the mineral smell of old stone. Above us, the ceiling revealed a story thousands of years old: petroglyphs and red markings that looked like some kind of calendar or celestial map, traces of a painted starscape from a time when someone had sat in this same darkness and looked up. People had come here to mark what they saw with nothing but pigment and stone.

Bruna started chanting. The same sound she'd chanted over me in the dirt the day of the accident. The same sound I'd first heard from a monk in Tibet who pressed a medallion into my hand. She held a string of 108 beads, passing them between her fingers, repeating the mantra she had learned on the banks of the Ganges during her travels through India, just before she entered my life.

I know how it sounds. A Brazilian woman chanting Indian mantras in a cave marked by Indigenous North Americans, while a one-legged Chinese-American engineer lies on his back trying to rewire his brain. In California. It's easy to dismiss. But the pain dissolved. For the first time in weeks, lying in that darkness, the phantom released its grip and I could breathe without bracing for fire. Whatever was happening wasn't bound to any single tradition or culture. It was the same door the shaman's drum had opened in Mongolia, the same door Rama's mandalas pointed to, the same door that ninety percent of the world's cultures had found their own way through across thousands of years. The tool didn't care who was holding it. It worked because the brain it was working on was human, and humans have been opening this door since before we had language for what was on the other side.

Lying in the dark with the ancient markings above me, I felt the research I'd been doing on the bed at home converge with what was happening in my body. The mirror had offered my brain a new story, a version of reality without pain, but my mind wasn't plastic enough to hold it. The moment the visual trick ended, the old map reasserted itself. What I needed was the mirror and a state of heightened neuroplasticity at the same time. The brain's map isn't hardware. It's software. The phantom limb was my brain imagining a leg that wasn't there, and the pain was real because imagination isn't decorative, it's how the brain constructs reality. I needed my brain to imagine a different body and believe it. The pathways could be rewritten, but only during windows when the brain was open enough to accept new input. The mirror provided the input. I needed something that could open the window.

The research had already pointed me in a direction. Doctors at Johns Hopkins had published work on psilocybin, the active ingredient in certain mushrooms, showing that patients with terminal illnesses could face their mortality through what they described as transformative spiritual experiences. In a sense, that's what I needed too. I had to accept the death of what was to step into whatever came next.

The continuity of agony was so unrelenting it had started to make me think I should have just died in the accident. María Sabina had spoken of seeing "with the heart." I needed to see with mine. But I was lost in a broken map of myself, and the only way I could think to redraw it was to go deeper than any research paper or mirror box could take me.

Bruna obtained the mushrooms from friends. One month after the amputation, in mid-November, she drove us a hundred miles off road into the most remote section of Death Valley. My leg was propped on a pillow in the passenger seat. The cab was cluttered with medications, a mirror, Bruna's beads, supplies for a few days in the dunes. I still hadn't gotten a prosthetic. My leg was too raw, stitches still holding together muscles and flaps of skin folded over sawed-off bone. If something went wrong out here, there was no hospital, no wheelchair ramp, no one to call. I was a one-legged man on crutches in the most remote stretch of desert in America, and the only person who knew where I was had driven me there.

On the drive I told Bruna something I hadn't said out loud. The pain had become so chronic and lasting it was like being underwater, unable to breathe. I wondered if it would have been better to have died that day of the accident. I thought about Charlie and Millie and couldn't understand how that thought could even exist in my mind, but the pain was drowning me. It was my lowest point.

Bruna set up camp and spread a blanket for me to lie on beneath the wide, empty sky.

I didn't know how the psilocybin would affect me. It was intimidating to release my final illusions of cognitive control, but I knew I needed to go big, what researchers at Hopkins called a "hero's dose."

As the mushrooms took hold, a tingling spread across my chest, faint at first but growing stronger. Forty-five minutes in, I went to urinate, and for the first time since the accident, the ghost of my leg didn't scream out in agony. The phantom pain was gone. Just gone. Leaving only a weightless relief, the absence of something that had been so constant I'd forgotten what silence felt like.

The world began to change. The desert, which I'd always seen as vast and empty, was suddenly teeming. Every grain of sand had texture. The mountains breathed. I could see the heat rising off the ground in patterns that looked like music.

It was disorienting at first. My rigid former self fought to maintain control. But then Bruna said a single word.

"Succumb."

In the ICU, on that long sleepless night when the pain got ahead of us, I had learned that resistance was its own kind of suffering. Now I heard it again, from her lips in the desert. I let go.

I took off my bandages and my clothes and lay there staring at my naked body for the first time since the surgery. The catastrophic wound had healed over, leaving only a stump where my shin and foot had been. It had been covered and wrapped and hidden since the surgery. Now it was out in the open, and the vulnerability of it, this raw, tender thing that had always been shielded, was almost too much.

I lowered it into the sand. The sand was cool against skin that hadn't felt anything but gauze and bandages in weeks. I flinched. Then I let it settle. And as the grains covered my leg, a memory arrived that I wasn't expecting. Millie burying me on the beach. Not long before the accident, maybe weeks before, she'd piled sand over my legs while I lay there pretending to be trapped. "You can't move, Dad! You're stuck!" Both legs under the sand, her little hands patting it down, laughing.

Now I buried what was left in the same sand and slowly pulled it out. I watched the stump emerge. I watched my brain register the shape. And there was no pain. Not a flicker. For the first time since the amputation, my mind saw what was actually there and didn't scream. It just looked.

Bruna danced through the dunes, moving like part of the wind. We laughed until the laughter turned to tears, until the tears turned to something deeper. I had been living in fear of pain, and here, that fear had no place. Fear and resistance were the very things that had been giving the pain its life.

I did a handstand in the sand. Who needed legs if I could walk around on my hands upside down? I was joking, but only half. I rolled and tumbled through the dunes, laughing like a kid who'd just discovered what a body could do. My body, flawed and incomplete, felt alive in a way I hadn't thought possible since the accident. But the peak of it wasn't a moment I can point to in time. It was the feeling of being inside the world rather than looking at it, the way a fish doesn't know it's in water until it's taken out. The sand, the mountains, the light, Bruna, the pain I'd left behind, the body I was learning to inhabit, all of it part of the same thing. The question of what I'd lost simply stopped being the right question.

We sat under a beach umbrella as the sun traced its arc and the moon rose to take its place. For the first time in months, I felt whole.

We spent a couple of nights there under the stars, in the slowly fading glow of a small fire, hundreds of miles from anyone. On that blank slate of sand and sky I could imagine my life as an explorer again. In a place called Death Valley, I was reborn.

On the last night, my friend Tom Garrison appeared with his partner, on their way to the hot springs. I hadn't seen him since the jungles of Guatemala, back when I still had two legs. As we sat around the fire, Tom shared that he'd been raising a major fund to launch a massive LiDAR survey of the Maya lowlands. "It's going to be big," he said with a smile. In time I'd learn how right he was.

Bruna and I drove back down the 395, past hot springs and dry lake beds and granite peaks and rivers winding through the valley floor. As the last effects faded, aspects of the phantom pain lingered. But it was diminished. Less excruciating. It no longer had me wishing I'd died. I could hold it now.

Two days later I met with Rama and my pain doctor at UCSD and explained what had happened. They were shocked, but also excited. They suggested my experience could be written up as a case study. Eventually that case study would lead to a clinical trial, and the founding of the Center for Psychedelic Research at UCSD. But that was all in the future. We were in strange territory, and none of us had a map for it.

With Bruna's help, I began a regimen of psychedelics paired with mirror therapy and other techniques aimed at inducing the kind of openness that would allow my brain to let go and accept its new map. With each journey, the phantom diminished further. What had been an inferno became a flicker, still present, still a reminder, but no longer the thing that defined my days.

Questions of pain and memory and the relationship between the two still linger for me. There are whole stretches of that time I can't account for. Pain pills, psychedelics, trauma, it all blurred together, eroding my sense of continuity. Pain itself is a memory, and I was training my brain to release it. But in chasing that release, in pursuing ego death on repeat, I sometimes wondered: the ego is also the self, the anchor of who you are. If you erase too much, what remains?

Was I still in the same reality?

I don't know. I'm not sure anyone who goes through what I went through comes back to the same one. But the map of the self is not fixed. That much I knew now. The same brain that had imprisoned me in phantom fire was the same brain that could set me free.

The clinic didn't look like a hospital. It looked like a gym that happened to have prosthetic legs hanging from the walls. Brent had found the place back when I was still in the hospital, the same day he'd shown me the photo of Mike Coots on that wave. It was run by a prosthetist named Peter Harsh, an Ironman athlete who treated every patient as if he were building an athlete, not repairing a broken person. San Diego's proximity to the naval and marine bases had made the city home to one of the most advanced prosthetic communities in the world, and Peter's clinic was at the center of it.

When Bruna rolled me through the door, the first thing I noticed were the people. Young, athletic amputees moving around the space, some former soldiers still in uniform, all of them carrying themselves with a confidence I hadn't felt in months. It was a mental shift I wasn't expecting, seeing what was possible reimagined right in front of me. I think Peter understood something that took me longer to see: it all started in the mind.

He took a plaster mold of my residual limb and crafted a temporary socket, shaping and reshaping it until it held my full weight through nothing more than vacuum. The idea of loading the biggest injury of my life with everything I had was terrifying. Every instinct said don't. But I gripped the parallel bars and pressed down. My leg slid into the check socket and as I stood my eyes began to tear up. Not from pain. From a milestone I hadn't realized my mind needed so badly.

From across the room, one of the other amputees yelled over with a big grin, "It's just a paper cut!" He was missing his leg above the knee. In this room, that made me the lucky one.

Then Peter showed me a shelf. A motorcycle-specific foot designed to grip pegs. A dive foot that rotated downward to fit a fin. A ski foot engineered to clip straight into bindings. Possibilities of what I thought was gone, sitting on a shelf waiting for me to step up. Literally.

I spent weeks on those parallel bars, a little more confident each day. Sometimes Millie and Charlie would come with me, turning the clinic into their personal playground, jousting each other on wheelchairs. "Let's go to the leg shop!" they'd say whenever it was time. Finally, Peter said I could walk from one side of the room to the other. In the video Bruna took that day, I'm limping, wincing, and smiling with pure joy. Later that afternoon, the check socket was replaced with a sleek carbon fiber prosthetic. I put phoenix wing stickers on each side, looked in the mirror and thought: this is my new identity.

Life itself became therapy. Being a dad of two curious kids was my workout. I went to a parking lot and taught myself to drive with my left foot. When the kids were with Kara, Bruna insisted we test the limits. One weekend she took me to Mammoth to try skiing. It took an hour to wedge my prosthetic into a ski boot. My leg nearly fell off on the lift. Every bump was agony. But then the wind hit my face, and for the first time since the accident I felt real movement, not just survival but flight. The mountain didn't care that I had one leg. I knew I'd bring Charlie and Millie back as soon as I could.

By spring, six months had passed since the accident. The debt was piling up, and I'd started contemplating selling the house. But the legs were moving, and that was everything. I took the kids back to Death Valley, alone this time. We hiked to the top of the tallest dune, Millie and Charlie charging ahead while I limped behind them. At the summit they turned to me, breathless and grinning, and repeated every encouraging thing I'd ever said to them back at me. "See, Dad? When you believe it, you can do anything." They were six and three, parroting their father's own parenting tropes at him on a sand dune, and it was the funniest and truest thing I'd heard in months.

Then the world came calling.
title: Chapter 9: The Ghost
