Chapter 10: El Robotico

National Geographic asked if I wanted to go to Guatemala. I was barely out of crutches, still learning to trust the prosthetic. But there was no question.

Tom Garrison's consortium had flown a plane armed with LiDAR over every inch of the Petén jungle, one of the largest remaining tropical forests in Central America and the ancient heart of the Maya Empire. The first results showed digital fingerprints of what appeared to be plazas, pyramids, roads, and entire cities sprawling across the forest floor, all of it hidden beneath the canopy. If the data held true, it would reshape what we knew about the Maya.

The Maya had captivated me since I was a kid. There's a photo that still hangs in my house of my siblings and me with our parents on a beach in Mexico, the last trip before my father left. We're bent over a pile of sand, building a pyramid, because days earlier our parents had taken us to Chichén Itzá. That stepped pyramid could summon a serpent out of sunlight, casting a shadow that slithered down the staircase as the equinox sun crossed the sky. It was engineering and astronomy and mythology fused into a single stone structure, and as a boy who'd spent countless nights stargazing with his father, I was in awe. Now LiDAR was pulling their lost cities back out of the earth.

I'd actually been to the Petén before. In 2015, when I still had two legs, Tom and I had tried to rig balloons and drones with LiDAR equipment to survey the jungle canopy from below, using the Engineers for Exploration program I'd started at the university in the wake of Mongolia. It didn't work. The jungle was too dense for a helium balloon to navigate without getting tangled, and our early-stage drones weren't dependable enough. We kept pushing until one of our sensors, worth more than any of us made in a year, vanished into the green with a malfunctioning GPS drone. We had to rethink everything. Then I lost my leg. While I was learning to walk again, Tom kept chasing the vision, and now he'd pulled together the consortium known as the PACUNAM Lidar Initiative that made it real.

Nat Geo wanted me to be the thread that tied the story together across the scattered camps in the jungle. I appreciated that nobody asked about my leg or questioned whether I could handle it. I'm sure conversations about my readiness happened behind the scenes, but outwardly they left the choice to me, and that made all the difference.

A map of an undiscovered world had been created with lasers in the sky by my friends. The explorer in me was not a phantom.

I packed the usual gear: tent, headlamp, snake gaiters, machete. But for the first time I also packed prosthetics, walking sticks, and silicone covers to keep my stump from getting infected. I genuinely didn't know if my body could handle the jungle. But I had to try.

Bruna and I arrived in the Petén on a late spring day. Tom picked us up in Flores, the last waystation city before the uncharted depths of the forest, and leveled with me.

"Albert, I'm kind of screwed," he said. "The Guatemalan archaeological community has held up everybody's permits. We're all in limbo."

Why does every expedition seem to start with this line. With everyone stuck waiting, Flores had become something like an Olympic Village for archaeologists, all of them in a holding pattern. Renowned scholars who'd spent their careers in the jungle were crammed into little hotels and bars, trading rumors about permits over rum, their machetes and field gear piled in corners while bureaucracy ground forward. The energy was a strange mix of frustration and giddiness, like climbers stuck at base camp staring at the summit.

In a little bar on the waterfront, Tom pulled out his laptop and showed us what would become an iconic map. LiDAR works by firing millions of laser pulses from an aircraft toward the earth, each one timing its return to build a three-dimensional picture of the surface below. The magic is in what it can ignore. Even in the densest jungle, a fraction of the light slips through gaps in the canopy to strike the ground. Strip away every return except that bottom layer, and the forest floor appears bare and legible, as if the trees have simply vanished.

What Tom showed us on that screen took a moment to process. Topographical data painted in greens and reds, revealing the subtle rises and falls across a landscape no one had ever seen. Speckled throughout were the footprints of ancient lives. Pyramids and celestial observatories connected by long causeways. What appeared to be a great wall encircling vast neighborhoods. And this was only one slice. Other archaeologists were bringing back scans from their own sectors of the forest, each one revealing a constellation of previously unknown sites. People who'd spent their careers hacking through this jungle on foot had walked right past all of it, the foliage so dense it swallowed temples whole. We sat in that bar staring at the screen and it felt like looking at a treasure map that no one in history had ever possessed.

Then a legend walked into the bar. I'd actually met Stephen Houston on the flight down, though I'd embarrassed myself by mistaking him for another legendary Mayanist, David Stuart, his longtime collaborator. He laughed. Dave was his friend and they were meeting for dinner that night at their favorite restaurant in Flores. We'd all go. Houston was one of the foremost Maya epigraphers alive, a scholar who'd spent decades deciphering the glyphs carved into temple walls and stelae across the Maya world. For centuries those carvings had been dismissed as decoration. Houston and his colleagues had proven they were a written language, and he could look at a carved stone and read it the way you'd read a letter, real kings, real wars, real dates. Short, stout, and crackling with energy, he had an unapologetic drive for knowledge that made you feel like anything that wasn't discovery was wasting his time. Like everyone else, he was frustrated by the permit delays. Unlike the younger archaeologists, he wasn't about to sit around knowing he had to return to his home university for teaching responsibilities in a week.

He turned to me. "We don't have to be that official. Why don't you, Bruna, one of my students, and I go for a 'tourist hike' through the jungle? It won't be to excavate or anything. Let's just take a walk."

I didn't need to be asked twice.

Tom arranged for a couple of jeeps and a soft-spoken, machete-wielding crew boss named Don Antonio to go with us. Don Antonio had grown up in the jungle. In his youth he'd fought and survived machete battles with rival communities, but you'd never guess it from his calm, earnest eyes. If we were going off trail, at least he'd be there with us.

The first time I'd come to the Petén, Tom had explained that literally everything in the jungle was trying to kill me. Every bug, every snake, every crocodile. "Just don't step off the trail," he'd warned. Now I was with Steve Houston and his LiDAR map. The whole point of our "little walk" was to go where there was no trail.

The drive from Flores took us through muddy roads strewn with fallen trees and ruts that rain had turned into small lakes. We used one jeep to pull the other out of the mud more than once. As we got deeper, the air thickened and I worried about keeping my stump clean. There was no sterilized water, and baby wipes could only do so much.

We reached El Zotz, "The Bats," a field site named for a grand bat cave that must have been there in the time of the Maya. The last time I'd been here, the place had been bustling with activity. Now, with Tom still stuck in Flores, nobody had been there in months. It was nothing more than an abandoned hut in a clearing, surrounded by screaming howler monkeys and a helicopter pad for emergencies. Bruna's eyes were wide. We strung up our hammocks.

It was the first time I'd slept in the field since the accident. I'd packed spare leg parts alongside snake gaiters and my sleeping bag, not knowing how the humidity would affect me. Peter had made the socket a bit oversized so I could adjust my fit with different sized leg socks as the stump swelled. When I climbed into the hammock I realized there was an unexpected advantage: without a foot on that side, I could curl up without it poking against the hammock wall. The bigger problem was keeping the liner clean, a silicone sleeve that rolled onto my stump to provide the cushion I needed before sliding into the prosthetic. In the middle of the night, needing the bathroom, I sat in the hammock doing my best to put the whole contraption on without falling out of the swing, then looked up with my headlamp to see the reflection of a million eyes staring back at me from the darkness. Every insect in the jungle, frozen in my beam.

The cacophony was like nothing I'd ever heard. A thousand species all screaming at once, every one of them trying to eat something or avoid being eaten. I lay there listening to the howlers and the occasional crack of a branch under something heavy, and tried to sleep.

I woke in the morning to Steve sitting in a chair on the helicopter pad, already poring over maps, compass in hand, trying to find a GPS signal.

"We're going to go twenty kilometers that way," he said, pointing into the wall of green. "And we'll see what we find."

Twenty kilometers through untouched jungle. Even with two legs that would be brutal.

I didn't know what to say other than "Okay." My anxiety may have shown on my face. Steve, misreading my concern entirely, tossed me a bottle of Gold Bond powder. "I know it's hot out here. Great for the humidity. Put it on everything."

We started down a side trail and almost immediately the forest consumed us. Even with the LiDAR map in hand, nature forced us back to basics. GPS was useless without a line of sight to the sky. All we had were paper maps marked with waypoints, but in the dense undergrowth the contours of the land were invisible.

"I guess we're going to have to use the old tools," Steve said, pulling out a weathered compass that looked like he'd carried it since he was a student. We'd arrived with cutting-edge laser data and were navigating by dead reckoning, estimating our position by direction and distance traveled. We figured we'd head two kilometers out to where there should be a bend in the path, then northeast along a ridge to the cluster of anomalies revealed in the data.

Don Antonio hacked away the vegetation with a casual efficiency that made the jungle look easy. We hiked roughly in a line so as to minimize the snake risk. Steve was in front of me, Bruna right behind. I felt unsteady on legs I still barely knew. I wanted to use my machete to clear the vines that kept snagging my carbon ankle, but Steve glanced back with a half-joking smile. "The most dangerous thing in the jungle is a gringo with a machete." It could bounce off a vine and hit me in the leg, he explained. I looked down at my prosthetic. "I'll use it on this side," I said. Don Antonio, who rarely spoke, added quietly that the snakes would have a harder time with me now.

In the jungle, they say the third person in line is the one that gets killed. The first wakes the creatures up, the second scares them, the third gets bitten. At least I had one less ankle for a snake to find.

We pushed on without daylight to mark the hours, climbing over logs and fallen trees, rolling through so many spiders and scorpions that any squeamishness quickly became pointless. I was on some level aware that I was in pain, my stump hot and swollen inside the socket, the prosthetic ankle catching on every root and vine. But the jungle has a way of narrowing your focus to the next step, the next vine, the next obstacle. There was no room to feel sorry for myself because there was no room to feel anything except forward. The density of closely packed trees played tricks on my mind, and soon everything looked the same. We were deep off trail, in the middle of nowhere. Steve, heedless of anyone's pain but his own, kept pushing ahead. Am I going to be able to keep up? I kept the doubt to myself.

Then Steve stopped. "This looks like a looter pit." We peered into a decades-old trench where someone had once dug for artifacts. At the bottom was a coral snakeskin, freshly shed. Coral snakes are aggressive and incredibly deadly. If the skin was there, the snake wasn't far. We climbed out fast and pushed on.

A few more hours of hacking and climbing. Then Steve came to a small hillside and pulled up short.

"My God," he said. His voice shifted, the flat determination giving way to something I hadn't heard from him before. "See? You see the rise here? You see the rise there?"

All I saw was overgrown moss. But he pulled up the LiDAR map and pointed to a large rectangular anomaly, then pointed to a subtle rise in the ground before us. For a moment I could see the world through his expert eyes: how what looked like an innocuous hill was actually the remnant of a building, buried for a thousand years beneath the jungle floor.

He knelt and lifted the moss. Beneath it were ancient limestone bricks, one on top of the other, marking the edge of a structure the LiDAR had predicted would be there. It felt like finding the tiles in the tree roots in Mongolia, that electric jolt of genuine discovery.

"Look, there's more up here." He pointed to the topographical map. If we followed a steep cliff, we'd reach a mountaintop where the data suggested more structures. We started climbing. It was hard going, the cliff face slippery with moss and loose rock, but the potential for discovery overrode the pain in my leg.

Then a giant tree appeared across our path, its trunk the size of a house. I threw the walking sticks in my pack, grabbed vines as thick as arms, and pulled myself over it. On the other side I found myself balancing along the trunk like a balance beam, one real foot and one carbon foot picking their way across the bark. The jungle was forcing me to move the way it demanded, and what it demanded was everything I had. The sticks weren't going to work here. So I left them behind.

We ascended a ridgeline and the forest fell away below. In the distance, one massive ceiba tree rose above the canopy as howler monkeys called from somewhere deep in the green. I had forgotten everything else around me, including the pain. The jungle was doing what the mirror box and the psilocybin had tried to do, putting me so fully inside the present moment that there was no room left for the ghost. It was hypnotic, and I realized that nature itself could create the altered state I'd been searching for in the months before.

At the top we found an enormous watchtower-like structure, and from that height the landscape finally revealed itself. Pyramid towers emerged from the jungle canopy. Pottery fragments were everywhere underfoot. A raised path that the LiDAR suggested had once been a great wall seemed to surround the city below. The wails of howler monkeys echoed across the treetops, calling from the rooftops of a city that once had been.

All the subtle rises and falls of the terrain that we had been climbing over for hours were part of a vast, hidden infrastructure beneath the foliage. As we moved from ridge to ridge, trying to crudely map the site, Steve read the landscape the way he read glyphs on temple walls. A royal court here. A solar observatory there. A defensive fortification along the ridge. He explained that in the time of the Maya, the plazas would have been covered in white plaster, the buildings painted bright reds and blues, all the trees cleared for miles for wood to build and burn. Where I saw overgrown moss, he saw a city of tens of thousands. Where I saw a gully, he saw a reservoir engineered to capture rainwater for a population with no rivers. He knelt beside a stone cylindrical pit and explained it was where they stored food to keep it cool, an ancient Maya refrigerator. The Maya hadn't just built in the jungle. They had harnessed it and reshaped it on a scale nobody had guessed until LiDAR stripped the canopy away.

And then there was the wall. A structure so massive that archaeologists had always assumed it was geological, a natural ridge running through the forest. But the LiDAR had revealed its geometry, perfectly straight edges that nature doesn't make. It was a great wall between the territories of Tikal and the surrounding city-states, and from the escarpment where we stood we could see, in the distance, the ruins of Tikal, one of the few Maya cities the world had known about before all of this. Steve's voice dropped. We were standing in the footsteps of the Snake Kings, a dynasty that had waged war against Tikal across generations. The glyphs he'd spent his career deciphering spoke of conflicts so devastating they "crushed the stars." The causeways we'd walked had once carried armies. The watchtowers we'd climbed had once held sentinels scanning the horizon for the fires of an approaching enemy. How many wars could a people wage upon themselves before it all came crumbling down? The answer was around us, buried in the same jungle that had swallowed their grandest achievements.

But juxtaposed against the violence was another story. Steve pointed to where the pyramids aligned with the horizon. "See that notch? That's where the sun sets on the solstice. These buildings weren't just political. They were a clock. The whole city was a machine for tracking the relationship between earth and sky." He explained that the Maya had a concept called K'uh, a sacred energy that flowed through all living things. Their rituals, even the blood sacrifice that horrified the Spanish, were attempts to maintain the cosmic balance, to keep the cycles of death and rebirth turning. The ballgame courts, the calendar, the pyramids themselves, all of it was an effort to stay in harmony with forces larger than any single human life. The Maya hadn't just built a civilization. They had built a way of understanding existence. Time wasn't a straight line to them but a wheel, cycles of death and rebirth repeating across the ages. I hadn't been able to picture that as a teenager staring at a pyramid on a beach in Mexico. After everything that had happened to me, standing in the ruins of a world that had risen and fallen and been swallowed by the jungle it grew from, I could.

We spent a few more days using the camp as our base until supplies ran low and Steve's student got sick with dysentery. Then we packed up and headed out.

Other than sores and blisters, my leg survived. Somehow, despite the muck and bugs and humidity, it didn't get infected. That first return to the wilderness was the closest thing I got to physical therapy.

The day after we returned to Flores, Tom's permits came through, and there was a palpable energy among the archaeologists, a giddiness at the prospect of charging into the jungle with machetes in hand to find whatever was out there. In the year that followed, a staggering sixty thousand new Maya structures were found. Pyramids, plazas, entire cities. The New York Times headline read "Lasers Reveal a Maya Civilization So Dense It Blew Experts' Minds." LiDAR had revealed a Maya world an order of magnitude more vast than anyone had imagined. Tom said the history of archaeology would be split between the time before LiDAR and the time after.

National Geographic arranged a helicopter for me, and I was off. I flew from camp to camp across the Petén, documenting the discoveries as they unfolded. Old military pilots would drop in low, our tail rotor barely clearing the big ceiba trees as we descended into small clearings. These landings were risky even for veterans. Years later, on a return trip, I learned one of those pilots had died in a crash.

Other times we'd drive as close as we could on old muddy half-roads. One afternoon, lying in the back of a truck bed talking to my director Ben, we drove straight through a massive spider web spanning the width of the path. I looked over and saw a spider larger than my palm crawling across his forehead. He froze. I tried not to laugh. Another time we stirred up a hive of killer bees that sent us tumbling down an escarpment. And when thunderstorms stranded me in the jungle past my scheduled return, I had to call Kara on the satellite phone to explain I wouldn't be home in time to take the kids according to our parenting schedule. I'm not sure which was scarier, the deadly animals or the wrath of an angry co-parent.

Before I put my prosthetic on each morning, I was still completely disabled. But the moment I donned it, I was running around the jungle like I'd had too many cups of coffee, volunteering to take the lead through the brush because snakes couldn't bite carbon fiber. One night at camp, drinking celebratory beers, Tom told me that everyone gets a nickname from the Guatemalan crew. Mine was El Robotico. I leaned into it. A robot explorer with a map created by laser beams in the sky, hacking through a jungle full of lost cities. It felt very sci-fi for a guy who'd been reading Master and Commander in a hyperbaric chamber a few months earlier.

Then one afternoon, my crew and I pulled into a small village on the outskirts of the jungle. We needed water, beer, and supplies. We must have looked like aliens descending on their world, our caravan of lifted trucks and large cameras rolling into a town of chickens and a single wood-shack market by the side of the road.

The moment I stepped out, eyes turned to my leg. Children pointed. Adults stared. Then my gaze landed on a man across the street.

He was an amputee too. His leg taken by a snakebite. But unlike me, outfitted in carbon fiber and titanium, he balanced on worn wooden crutches, every movement slow, precarious, exhausting. We looked at each other. I saw in his eyes that he was looking at my prosthetic the way I might look at something from another planet. He lived in this village, with these snakes, and this was what they'd cost him. There was no Peter Harsh. No parallel bars. No check socket shaped and reshaped until it fit. Just crutches, and the rest of his life on them.

The pride I'd been carrying curdled. I'd credited my grit, the jungle, the drive to reclaim myself. But the truth was simpler and harder. I was enabled by a prosthetic that cost more than anyone in that village would earn in years. The same snakes I joked about had left this man permanently disabled. For me they'd become a punchline. For him they'd rewritten his life. The only thing separating us was the accident of where we'd each been born.

I went to him and tried to relate, but we were living worlds apart in our realities and circumstances. We got back in the trucks and drove away. Nobody said anything about it. I sat and looked out the window, and the silence in the cab was different from the silence before we'd stopped.

I learned later that the vast majority of amputees worldwide will never have access to a well-fitting prosthetic. The number is staggering, somewhere around ninety-five percent. When I got home, I asked the students in the Engineers for Exploration program to work on using the same photogrammetric technology we'd applied to archaeology to map people's limbs for lower-cost 3D-printed prosthetics. It became Project Limbitless.

When the footage from Guatemala rolled in, National Geographic saw the potential for something larger than a single film. They wanted me to be their person for exploring the ancient world. Not a one-off, but an entire series devoted to genuine discovery. And so began Lost Cities.
title: Chapter 10: El Robotico

content:
Chapter 11: The Sound of the River

The career was taking off. National Geographic had paired me with a brilliant producer named Lucy Van Beek, and together we were building what would become Lost Cities, an entire series devoted to genuine discovery. What I couldn't see, in the momentum of all that was being built, was what was quietly falling apart behind me.

That November, a few months after Bruna and I broke up for the last time, I bought a ticket to India.

Our love had been forged through the year of becoming, and the fire that saved me was the same fire that burned us. We broke up and came back together more times than I could count, drawn by a bond that was inseparable from the crisis it was born in, driven apart by a jealousy over things imagined when we were in our separate worlds. She had a life without me when I was away, and I had one without her. The intensity that had made her hold my head in the dirt and press the pain button every hour through the night was the same intensity that could turn a quiet evening into a brutal fight on a hair trigger. Kids feel everything, and mine had felt enough upheaval already. Eventually she moved away, off to live in another country, and that was that.

I was heartbroken once again. She had saved my life and I will never be able to fully repay her for that. But my mind kept returning to that single hour of eternity, when her hands cradled my head in the bloody dirt as we waited for the ambulance, chanting a single syllable until it ceased to be a word and became a kind of primordial music.

Ohm.

What was that sound? It had followed me across the world. Each time it appeared, something in me opened. Was it a prayer? A frequency? A technology older than language?

When I'd asked her about the mantra, she said she'd learned it in India. She told me of a city that sounded almost mythical, an ancient place of ritual on the banks of the Ganges, home to an eternal fire that never goes out, where Hindus burn their dead and shepherd them into the next life. It has many names: Benares. Kashi. Varanasi.

I wasn't going for work. National Geographic hadn't sent me. There was no expedition, no crew, no LiDAR map to follow. I was going because the woman who had saved my life had left me with a sound I didn't understand, and she'd told me it came from this city on the banks of the Ganges. As I boarded the flight, I felt like I was chasing a sound the way other people chase a person.

As I walked down the aisle of the plane, I saw a woman in the back row. She was Indian, and some of her limbs were short, with attached prosthetics. She had a backpack covered in buttons with slogans like "Free Tibet" and "Vote, Fuckers." One said "I Love My Body."

The seat next to her was empty, so I took it and smiled. One prosthesis-wearer next to another. She was so friendly and self-assured, with none of the self-consciousness that still clung to me. I'd been nervous about traveling in India with a disability, but her fearless demeanor put that to rest.

Then a flight attendant interrupted us. The crew, he said, had been so moved by "our vibes" that they'd baked us a chocolate cake in the little oven at the back of the plane. They presented us cake and cocktails with a card that read, It was a pleasure having you onboard. It was such an auspicious welcome it almost didn't seem real.

We landed in Delhi, then took a short flight to Varanasi. The airport lies an hour outside the city, but even there it felt like I'd stepped into a threshold to another realm. The sky hung in a deep, smoky red, and I couldn't help but wonder if the hue came from the cremation pyres whose fires have defined this place for centuries.

When I called around for a room, everything was full. In Varanasi there seems to be a festival every day, but this time it was Diwali, the great celebration of light's triumph over darkness. The largest festival of the year, and the city was overflowing. I finally found a vacancy in a hole-in-the-wall hostel with a shared bathroom. I handed my phone to the cab driver, hoping the hostel staff could direct him better than I could. I had no plan, only the sense that an open heart could carry me a long way.

As we drew nearer to the city, a tuk-tuk slid in front of us. Hanging from its back window was a familiar shape: the same Sanskrit symbol that had adorned the medallion given to me by the Sherpa in Tibet all those years ago.

Ohm.

The traffic grew denser as we neared the city, until it became a great, slow-moving river carrying every vehicle imaginable. Cars and tuk-tuks, motorcycles with three people on them, entire families on horseback. Cows and donkeys wandered between the lanes. It grew tighter and tighter until people were pushing off each other's cars, making gaps to squeeze through. It looked like chaos, but there was a deeper harmony to it. I probably imagined it but it seemed peaceful, serene even.

A haze hung in the air. Everything smelled of incense but maybe the haze was from the burning pyres which were constant. The sun was setting. There were so many people that they blended together into a wide pastel sea. Deepening shadows cast by three-thousand-year-old temples cloaked buildings built right on top of each other in a grand pileup of mud brick and wood and stone. All those souls were headed in the same direction: the great bend in the Ganges. But I couldn't see it yet. Those ancient roads were built long before automobiles, and as night fell and neon lights came on, my driver stopped in the middle of an impassably crowded street, signaling this was as far as he could go.

"Where do I go from here?" I asked.

He didn't speak English, but he took the phone and called the hostel. He gestured for me to wait. Soon a man came running over. "Come with us," he said.

I grabbed my bag, thanked the driver, and stepped out of the cab's protective bubble into that raging river of movement, trying not to be swept away as I followed my guide. He took me through tiny cobblestone alleyways that led to a crumbling guest house. It looked condemned. Electrical cords everywhere. Monkeys crawling through the windows, which made me think of Charlie and Millie and I called them to tell them about it. People yelling on corners outside. The shared bathroom had a bucket shower and no safety bars, and I had no idea how to manage it with my prosthetic.

But there was a small room with a bed on the third floor, so I could put my bag down. I ate some curry for dinner and went to sleep for a few hours.

At five in the morning I woke to my alarm. I walked out of the guest house and down streets still buzzing with activity in the pre-dawn darkness. Before I could see the river, I could hear it. Not the water itself but the sound that rose from the ghats to meet the morning: temple bells, conch shells, the low murmur of prayer, and somewhere beneath it all, the notes of a raga played on a sitar, a melodic pattern designed specifically for dawn. Varanasi has been the heart of Indian classical music for centuries, a city where sound is not entertainment but theology, where the right vibration at the right hour is believed to attune the human mind to the rhythms of the cosmos. The city had been waking to these sounds for three thousand years. I'd come chasing a single syllable, and I'd arrived in a place built entirely out of sound.

And then I saw it.

The Ganges.

One of the great arteries of human civilization. The holiest river in India, and deeply polluted by the very rituals that venerate it. Pilgrims bathe in it. The dead burn beside it. Temples with huge staircases called ghats lead down to the riverbank. This entire city, one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world, had been built around it like an enormous stadium of worship.

There was no wind. The river lay still, an expanse of suspended glass reflecting the grayish blue of night, shot through with the soft pinks of the coming dawn. The only ripples came from little rowboats chugging in all directions. People milled about, starting their day by brushing their teeth and washing their faces with water from the river. The sounds of a thousand meditations poured from tiny temples pockmarking the ghats.

I walked to the bank and found a man with a rowboat. With hand gestures and some money, I asked him to take me onto the water so I could see the city as the sun rose. We pushed off. When I looked back, I saw smoke rising from a temple at the edge of a great staircase surrounded by enormous piles of wood.

"Burning ghat," the ferryman said. "That is where the dead burn."

Even from the boat I could see human shapes atop the woodpiles, smoldering to ashes that flowed down into the river we floated on. A strange thought surfaced: a part of me had already been burned to ash. My leg, taken in a hospital, had likely been cremated somewhere without ceremony. Some of me was already in this state, already reduced to what these pyres reduced everyone to. I asked him to bring me back to shore.

I walked up the steps of the city that rose from the water. There was a man meditating: an ascetic who'd given up earthly possessions in pursuit of enlightenment. Long dreadlocks, white marks on his head and arms, beads around his neck. He looked at my leg. His eyes widened for a moment, then he returned to his meditation. I sat down beside him in silence. I pulled out my worn copy of Siddhartha and read. The wind picked up. Kites started appearing over the city, kids battling them against each other in the sky, and I thought of Charlie and Millie. I could hear children playing somewhere above.

I decided to walk toward wherever the kites were flying from. But as I was making my way there, past chattering monkeys and cows and a procession of mourners holding their dead on their shoulders, a young man with a confident, almost gangster-like demeanor stopped me in my tracks.

"Hey man, where are you from?"

Wary of being hustled, I tried to brush him off.

"You want marijuana?" he asked.

"Not interested," I said.

He looked down at my leg. His attitude shifted. He left me alone for a minute, then returned with some friends: young Indian men in their twenties. I felt outnumbered, but they didn't seem hostile.

"Let me help you, my friend. What do you need?"

"I don't need anything. I'm just here to read my book." I was still unsure of his intentions. He'd have to be a real asshole to con a one-legged wanderer. I decided to open my heart and see where it would take me.

"If you can show me where we can get onto a roof to watch the kites, I'll buy us a drink."

He said something to his friends in a language I didn't understand. He was clearly the leader. Then he turned back to me.

"I am Baba Lutlo. I know where to take you."

He led me into the backstreets of the city, past markets full of people buying fruit and vegetables. We wound through alleyways, hidden staircases, and even through people's homes. Everyone we passed seemed to know Baba Lutlo. He was like the Fonz of Varanasi: the cool, streetwise leader, constantly reciting catchphrases of his own invention. "24 hour Shiva Power!" and "The Lutlo Way!"

We came to a rooftop at the top of the city. Kids were flying kites. People were washing and hanging their laundry. One of Baba Lutlo's friends stood there waving a flag and whistling to a flock of pigeons that seemed to obey his commands. He threw something in the air and the flock descended to their little rooftop home. There were a few chairs and a table in the corner, and as we sat down, he poured some tea.

"Do you have beer?" I asked without thinking. In this Hindu city, of course there was no beer. Or at least there wasn't supposed to be. But Baba Lutlo had his ways. Somehow he obtained one. I poured it into two glasses and took a long cool sip in the hot evening air.

He asked me what I was doing in Varanasi.

I told him everything. How I'd lost my leg, and how a beautiful woman had wrapped her hands around my head and started chanting Ohm. How I'd come to believe that mantra was an ancient technology for opening the mind to new realities, and traveled here to find where it came from.

As I spoke, something in Baba Lutlo shifted. The catchphrase-spouting, hash-selling character faded, and his expression turned serious. He began to share his own beliefs about karma, reincarnation, and Shiva, the god who embodies both destruction and transformation. Impermanence made divine. He told me he would take me to Shiva's temple, hidden beneath the great burning ghat. But first he had to meet some friends.

"Come to the burning ghat tonight," he told me. "Ask for me."

"What does Baba Lutlo mean?" I asked.

"That's my name. Baba means guru." I knew that much. "Lutlo means thief." He flashed a big, toothy smile. "Because I steal hearts!"

Guru Heart Thief. It suited him.

I walked back to the guest house to change. The sun was high by then and a haze had settled over the city. Markets were bustling and bells were ringing. I saw a line of men getting their heads shaved. Some guys were building a huge boat in a makeshift boatyard. Nearby, women were making ball-shaped food and handing it out to everyone who passed. A crowd of kids played with a goat. I paid for a cup of chai and rested at the hostel. I checked my phone and saw a text from Bruna.

Bruna's name was on the screen. I looked at it for a moment, then put the phone down and decided to leave it behind. Varanasi was calling me for reasons that felt larger than mending a broken heart. Just be present.

When I left again, it was evening. I'd planned to retrace my morning route to the burning ghat, but the city had changed. The time for business had passed with the setting sun, and now was the hour of ritual. Every ghat had been given over to ceremony. Enormous crowds were lighting candles in celebration of Diwali. People painted mandalas on the ground. Each street was filled with processions of music and drums. The city was in its trance.

I meandered along the cobblestones, looking for a less crowded route. There was none. Just more, everywhere. Finally I arrived at the burning ghat and saw a few familiar faces from Baba Lutlo's crew.

"Where's Baba Lutlo?"

They pointed up to where he stood by the pyres of wood. He beckoned me over.

"Ah, man. Come, come. I want to show you something."

He started climbing over rafters and through construction sites and up gates like some kind of parkour master while I did my best to keep up on my prosthetic. We came out on the temple roof, looking down on the ancient crematory with its stacks of platforms for the dead.

Then he brought me to a tiny room that felt more like a cave than a man-made space, looking out over the burning ghat through a missing wall. Three old gurus sat inside, tending a modest fire in the middle of a truly massive bed of ash. Baba Lutlo lit a cigarette and talked with them for a while.

He told me in a hushed voice that this fire has been burning for thousands of years. That it is the heart of Varanasi, the fire of Shiva, the destructive force that returns all things to ash. The men tending it were Dom, a hereditary lineage of fire-keepers who had passed the responsibility from father to son across more generations than anyone could count. Every cremation pyre on these ghats must be lit from this flame. Without the Dom, there is no fire. Without the fire, there is no passage. They had kept it through floods that submerged the ghats and monsoons that lasted months. If this fire ever went out, Baba Lutlo said, Varanasi would cease to be Varanasi.

It was fully dark by then. He led me down through the temple, then beneath it, to where the bodies burned.

We passed so close to the pyres that I could see a skull burst open and brains sizzle out. The flames were uncomfortably hot against my skin. An acrid, queasy scent filled my nostrils. No one was crying. Baba Lutlo told me they believe tears stop the soul from departing. So the living watched the dead with meditative solemnity. We passed through a crowded doorway, then deeper and deeper underground.

We came at last to a huge shrine to Shiva illuminated by candlelight. Men were beating drums, led by a guru who stood on one leg, never letting the other touch the ground. Baba Lutlo told me that was part of his meditation. He'd chosen to use only his left leg for his entire life.

Just like me. I'd made the same choice when I opted to amputate over limb salvage. Seeing that decision mirrored back at me, in a shrine beneath a burning ghat on the banks of the Ganges, felt like something I didn't have a word for. We took our shoes off and stepped onto the marble floor. Baba Lutlo knew the temple keeper and asked him to let me join. I hesitated, but the desire to feel the vibration in my hands was stronger. Someone handed me a drum. It was wood and leather, its handles hard-wrapped leather that felt like they'd been covered in wax from years of hands before mine. I started beating it, spinning it and pounding it with my palms.

Boom. Boom. Boom. Boom. Boom. Boom.

I beat it harder. The sound filled the underground chamber and merged with the other drums until the walls seemed to vibrate with it. I couldn't tell where my heartbeat ended and the drum began.

BOOM. BOOM. BOOM. BOOM.

I was in a trance. I couldn't be sure how long I'd been there. Minutes? Hours? The drum was doing what the shaman's drum had done on the sacred mountain in Mongolia, what Bruna's chanting had done in the Joshua Tree cave, what the psilocybin had done in Death Valley. It was opening a door. Not a door to a place, but to a state, a way of being in which the rigid boundaries of the self dissolve and something larger rushes in. These were the same tools, separated by thousands of miles and thousands of years, all doing the same work on the same human brain.

Finally, Baba Lutlo grinned at me. "Let's get out of here."

I left that place almost in a state of shock.

As we walked to the riverbank, Baba Lutlo told me this was where he'd grown up. His father was a Brahman holy man, and his family had lived here for six generations or more. He knew everyone because this was his home.

We met up with his friends and smoked some hashish. We were all curious about each other's lives, the conversation ranging from what Shiva represented to girls. I spent all night with them, visiting one temple and crematory after another. One stood perched above the primary ghat, looking from a distance like a human-sized birdhouse wedged between the endless scaffolded ancient buildings that rose around it. Its darkened gray stones were caked in candle wax from what must have been centuries of flame. Inside, another drum ceremony was underway. It was the drums that kept pulling me back, bringing me into that trancelike state I'd felt underground.

BOOM.

BOOM.

BOOM.

It was so dark in there. I was aware of people moving below, there were people everywhere in this city, but in that birdcage of a temple it was just me and the drum. The rhythm was fast and explosive, like the crescendo of the shaman's drum in Mongolia except this crescendo never ended, it just kept building and building. The beat grew and grew and grew, just as it had in Mongolia, a steady pulse building in intensity until the room felt like it would rupture. Then an explosion of energy, and it was over. Silence rushed in.

I don't know if it was an hour or three. When I finally looked down at my hands, I saw what I'd done. My palms had split open. I hadn't noticed. I hadn't felt it. My body had detached from itself somewhere in the drumming, and the pain had simply not registered, as if the trance had done to my hands what the psilocybin had done to my phantom leg. Blood oozed from the wound, mixed with cow dung, temple dust, and the muddy river water that carried the ashes of the dead. If I didn't clean it, it would certainly get infected.

"Baba Lutlo, I need to find a place to clean this."

He led me back to the stacks of wood piled high for the pyres. Next to the wood was a little door. He opened it and invited me into the home his family had lived in for generations. There was an older woman inside, and a little girl. Baba Lutlo introduced them as his mother and daughter. He picked his little girl up and spun her around. Once again his entire bearing shifted. He was no longer a thief or a guru. He was a father and a son. Like me.

His daughter was six. She'd been coloring in a drawing when we walked in, and she ran up to him and jumped into his arms. I thought of Millie and Charlie on the other side of the world. His mother washed my hand with clean water and rubbing alcohol, then bandaged me up. They offered me food.

When I was ready, Baba Lutlo said, "Ok, let's go back out." He opened another door, and there they were, right on the other side. The burning bodies.

I realized that every day of Baba Lutlo's life, he'd woken up, opened this door, and come face to face with the smoldering remains of people whose families had traveled from every corner of India to bring them here. He'd watched flesh turn to ash and join the river and the air. He'd seen mourning and celebrating, laughter and tears and fights. The entire circle of life, just a few feet from the house where his daughter was born.

In a city of pilgrims who'd come with holy purpose, it was the thief who truly belonged here, perhaps more than anyone. Next to him, even the gurus were tourists.

It was dawn when we went back outside. We walked along the riverbank as the sun rose, stopping here and there to linger around mandalas painted in the street from the night before.

"Diwali is where we celebrate light winning over darkness," Baba Lutlo said as we passed scores of spent candles.

We sat for a while overlooking a central square as the city woke. I still owed him a drink.

"Let me buy you some chai." His favorite chai stand was a few ghats over, but when we got there and I reached for my wallet, I realized I didn't have it. I'd left it near where I'd first met Baba Lutlo. I rushed back through the busiest city I've ever seen, hoping against all odds. And to my astonishment, it was there, unbothered in the hazy sun. No one had taken it, as if some force had decided to save me from my most careless mistakes.

Baba Lutlo and I had our tea.

In the days that followed, I stopped sleeping in the hostel and started living on the streets with Baba Lutlo and his crew. I ate where they ate and we sat along the ghats all night long, climbing over the city like we belonged to it. They did. It had only been a few days, but in a place that worshiped impermanence, time didn't measure the way it did elsewhere. I existed entirely in the moment.

Baba Lutlo asked some of his late father's friends, Brahman priests, to perform a ritual to Shiva for me. We borrowed a long boat and went onto the river for the ceremony. As we drifted on the water, he pointed to the far side of the Ganges, opposite Varanasi. An empty expanse of sand dunes where dark figures wandered. Those were sadhus who practiced black magic, he said. They fed upon the charred and rotten remains of the bodies burned across the river. He told me he'd gone once to those banks and fallen ill for days. The illness, he said, was metaphysical rather than biological. Varanasi stood perched on the border of the afterlife. A realm beyond.

On my last morning, Baba Lutlo and I went to the riverbank and sat together as the sun began its arc from behind the ancient brick dwellings and temples that rose above the ghats. People appeared through tiny alleyways at the bottoms of buildings like wormholes, emerging to stretch and clean themselves and wash their clothes. Deep red pigments from last night's ceremonies bled into the Ganges. Kids played among the boats, not twenty feet from the burning pyres of the dead. Hindus believe that dying in Varanasi grants moksha, liberation from the cycle of reincarnation entirely. People travel from across India to spend their final days here, not in hospitals but in hospices overlooking the river, waiting for the ghats to receive them. There are places in this city where the elderly check in with the understanding that they have come to die. The living and the dying share the same streets, the same water, the same sunrise, and nobody pretends otherwise.

"Maybe they'll find some leftover gold teeth, if they are lucky," Baba Lutlo said.

He took the bead necklace I'd bought from around my neck. His face was different. The mischievous smile he'd worn since the moment I met him, the grin that was always performing, always playing, was gone. What replaced it was something free of any play. Pure.

"Let me teach you that mantra. Each time, move one bead as you make the sound. Meditate with your finger."

Ohm.

"Let go of all your thoughts. Focus only on the sound. Truly."

Ohm.

I tried to let go, but my mind kept replaying everything we'd talked about since I arrived. He'd said that Shiva takes many forms, sometimes fierce, sometimes gentle, even as half-male and half-female, each a reflection of the dualities that run through all things. Shiva embodied destruction, but also creation. The two were one and the same.

I thought of Siddhartha, who took many forms in his life, each marked by moments of death and rebirth. The child. The guru. The rich man. The ascetic. And at the end, standing on the bank of a river, finally understanding the sound of all things.

Ohm.

I watched Baba Lutlo as he chanted. I'd only known him a few days, but he'd shown me more versions of himself than most people reveal in a lifetime. The gang leader. The guru of thieves. The son. The father. The teacher. Like the god he venerated, he seemed to contain infinite forms within one body.

Then I thought of myself.

Ohm.

Drifting in the void of anesthesia and waking up unsure if I was still in the same reality.

Ohm.

Lying in the bloody dirt as Bruna cradled me, waiting for the ambulance.

Ohm.

Picking away at my guitar on a cold night in a half-built house, my kids with their mother on the other side of town.

Ohm.

Each time a part of me had been destroyed, something new had been created in its place. Neither better nor worse, but different, whole in the duality of light and darkness. I'd come to Varanasi to find the meaning of this sound, and by chance arrived in the midst of the world's largest celebration of light over darkness.

The city itself was a kind of technology. Not built for comfort or commerce but for a single purpose: to help people let go. Varanasi has been doing this work for over three thousand years. It predates Rome, predates Athens, predates nearly every city still standing on earth. And unlike those cities, which were built for trade or defense or political power, Varanasi was built to help human beings face the one thing none of us can avoid. Every ghat, every temple, every fire, every drum ceremony beneath the burning ground is part of that machine, refined across millennia, still running.

I pressed on the beads, one at a time, listening to the water rushing by, until for the briefest moment my mind settled into the space between thoughts. The river flowed and flowed, and yet it was always there. Always the same, and every moment new.

Ohm.

Ohm.

Ohm.

When I got home I threw away my shoes. They were covered in the grime and dirt of a city built to burn the dead. And then I was back in San Diego, back in single fatherhood, making breakfast and packing lunches. But the color of the light seemed different. Everything seemed interconnected in a way I hadn't noticed before. The Ohm at the moment of my destruction, its symbol of transformation, the many lives lived inside one life, the letting go in order to become. It was a philosophical journey as much as a spiritual one, and it had followed me home.
title: Chapter 11: The Sound of the River
