Chapter 12: Wayfinder

The ocean had been pulling at me my whole life. As a kid in Santa Cruz I'd stared at the surf posters on the walls of Long's Drugstore. In college I'd learned to ride the small waves off the San Diego coast. After the divorce Rich had handed me a board and said "Surf it out." After the amputation the picture of Mike Coots in the barrel had shown me what was still possible. The first time I surfed on one leg I couldn't stand up, my prosthetic catching the rail, the phantom pain screaming every time saltwater hit the socket. But I kept paddling back out, because the ocean was the one place where my body had always made sense to me.

Then a call came. A new show was being developed called Welcome to Earth, pairing Will Smith with explorers having remarkable experiences with natural forces. They asked if I wanted to tell the story of vortices by surfing the barreling waves of Hawaii's North Shore.

Oh shit.

Surfing off the coast of San Diego is one thing. Hawaii's North Shore is a different beast entirely. Riding within the heart of a barreling wave is the apex of the sport, requiring the perfect combination of skill, luck, and a willingness to put yourself in the most violent part of the ocean. It was far beyond anything I'd ever done. Hawaii is the mecca of surfing, where the sport originated among the royal families of Oceania before it spread across the world. The North Shore is where all the energy of the unbounded Pacific hammers the sharp Hawaiian reefs to forge a deadly connection between ocean and land. Mike Coots had his leg taken by a tiger shark in those waters. The waves tower like high-rises. People die there every year, and most of them aren't trying to surf on one leg.

But this was a chance to make good on the promise I'd made to myself in that hospital bed when I saw the picture of Mike on that wave. And if I pulled it off, maybe I could pay forward what that image had done for me, offering hope to someone else lying in a hospital bed wondering what was left.

I said yes.

Like a student who hadn't studied for a big exam, I spent the following months frantically preparing. I asked friends for guidance on barrel techniques. I watched hours of videos. I got up at dawn each morning to surf before the wind picked up. On the days I had the kids with me, I'd get home just in time to make them breakfast before school, still covered in sand and salt.

It wasn't enough. I still wasn't even close. Before I had cameras pointed at me in the highest-profile filming project of my career, I wanted to experience the North Shore firsthand. Not so I wouldn't embarrass myself, but so I wouldn't die.

The show's producer connected me to a legendary Hawaiian board shaper and indigenous leader who'd brought back many of the island's ancient customs. He was in his late sixties, but in photos he looked ageless, as if something about the waves kept him young. I watched videos of him shaping massive surfboards from traditional Hawaiian woods entirely by hand, and read about how he'd resurrected the once-forgotten royal Hawaiian practice of sledding down lava fields at death-defying speeds.

His name was Pohaku. I flew out early to Oahu to meet him.

I wasn't sure what to expect. A couple years before, I'd spent time filming a Lost Cities episode in Micronesia, where I'd met a tribal chief who required me to ingest a hallucinogenic kava drink while he stared into my soul before allowing me into a sacred location. Many Pacific islanders had a justifiable wariness toward outsiders. Their communities had been ravaged by colonialism, and they were suspicious of anyone who showed up saying they wanted to film. They wanted to see authenticity of purpose first.

So I wasn't exactly prepared when the first thing Pohaku said to me was, "Hey, fucker. You going to buy me dinner?"

He was older, bald, covered in traditional Hawaiian tattoos, and more than a little standoffish. I realized he saw me as a representative of National Geographic, the organization that had reached out to him numerous times before.

We met for dinner at the priciest restaurant on the island, and he showed up with his family and ordered plate after plate of steak and fish. If he was going to help, he would make damn sure it was worth his while.

I started telling him my story and how I'd been inspired by the picture of Mike Coots. He looked at me, sizing me up. It wasn't just my prosthetic that made him cautious. Any outsider who showed up thinking they could surf the North Shore would be met with suspicion. In winter, storms across the Pacific hurl massive waves of energy like stones thrown into a pond, the ripples charging across the ocean toward these unblocked little islands. They're unfathomably powerful, violent, and beautiful. Every year, surfers get crushed down into the reef and never come back up. If they're lucky, the responders eventually find their bodies.

Finally, Pohaku seemed to make up his mind. "Okay. We try tomorrow. Be ready early."

I was too nervous to sleep that night. I sat staring out my window at the crashing surf. Every wave on the North Shore is defined by the reef below it; they have names and histories. As the waves get bigger, the reefs that break them are further out in deep water. The ones broken by the outermost reefs loom over sixty feet high. The surf app said the waves we'd be facing tomorrow were over ten feet. The waves back home were half that size.

Early next morning, Pohaku picked me up and brought me to Rocky Point. There were no cameras. The sky was still the amber of sunrise. The water was clear and warm.

I'd brought a board my friend had shaped specifically for me, designed for the stability issues that come with having one biological leg. The ankle of my prosthetic was a large spring that didn't rotate, so I'd attached it to the strap of the board. If the waves ripped the prosthetic off, at least I'd find it attached to my board.

"Ok, let's surf," Pohaku said.

The waves were bigger than predicted. Twelve feet or higher. But I couldn't back down. I had to show I was willing to commit, no matter what.

The whitecaps of the North Shore are so organized by the reefs that there are secret channels, riptides you can use to pull you right out past the break. But you have to be able to read the water. If you don't, you get the shit kicked out of you. The waves are too powerful to swim through. You can try to duck under, but they're relentless. Mess up once and you won't just be slammed by one giant breaker, but by those right behind it. The risk of drowning is very real.

Finally, I got past the break. I sat breathing hard on my board. As I waited for the waves, I tried to get Pohaku to open up.

"I don't talk when I surf," he said. "I focus. The world is chaos, but in the chaos you wait for the moment. Focus."

The waves came in sets of three. A bunch of mellow ones would pass, and then the energy would change. It starts as a little rolling hill in the distance. As it draws closer, all that energy and mass is forced upward by the reef below, pushing the peak higher until it crests. That's the moment. If you're in the right position, you can ride the shoulder of that crest.

But you have to be strong enough to paddle to the right spot and fast enough to catch the energy while it's still building. You have to pop up onto your feet, or foot, and let go of all your inhibitions so you can exist in the eye of the vortex and ride it through its chaos. Hesitation will ruin you.

The first big wave came.

"No, wait," Pohaku said. "Behind it, outside! Paddle out, paddle out."

A bigger one was coming, and if we didn't get out of the way we'd be consumed in the whitewater. We swam with all our strength toward the back of the break, and as we rose over the crest of the first big wave, I saw more mountains bearing down. I paddled faster and barely made it over the next one as it hurled itself over the reef.

"This is the one. Go!" he said.

I paddled as hard as I could, but it passed me by.

"Next one, next one." At least he saw I was giving it everything. "Get deeper," he said, meaning get closer to the break before I started paddling. Fully commit, no hesitation.

The next big wave came. Fifteen feet high. Heart pounding, I turned my board into position and drove my hands into the water, paddling harder than I ever had. I could feel the momentum of the wave envelop me, and then came the drop: the moment where I popped to my feet as I slid down the face of the wave, riding the echo of a distant storm from far beyond the horizon.

Time seemed to slow. Everything melted away as I focused on the energy flowing beneath me and pushing me forward. It lasted only a second or two but felt much longer. Then the lip of the whitecap curled and crashed down upon me, punching me into the depths.

I hadn't surfed within the barrel. I'd been crushed by it. Suddenly I couldn't see which way was up or down. Everything was darkness. I was a rag doll in the churn. There'd been no time to take a breath before I went under. I felt my prosthetic slide against something hard. I was all the way down on the reef.

Get back up. Don't die down here.

I grabbed my prosthetic and the cord attaching it to my board, clinging for dear life as it pulled me upward. I emerged gasping into open air. No time to find Pohaku. An entire mountain range of whitewater was hurtling toward me. If I didn't get out of it, I'd be crushed again. I climbed onto my board, heart pounding, and started paddling.

I didn't get away. I took another pounding. Then another, and another, each one stomping me into the reef as if punishing me for having ventured into their territory. By the time I got out of the break, I'd been pushed a quarter mile from where I'd started.

Bruised, battered, and completely gassed. But alive.

I slowly paddled back to Pohaku. He looked surprised I hadn't given up.

"Okay brah," he said. "Now go again."

So I did. Failing and getting my ass kicked again and again until one massive wave crushed me under the weight of its lip, ripping the board out from under me and taking my prosthetic with it. Bobbing without my leg, I yelled to Pohaku that I had to swim in.

We were on a section of reef where there was no beach along the coastline, only rocks. He told me to swim around. I swam as best I could without two legs, relying only on the force of my arms. Finally I washed up on the sand, exhausted and dripping and legless, next to a group of tourists and some turtles nesting on the beach. The tourists stared at me with alarm. The turtles couldn't have cared less.

Pohaku walked over, covered in sand and water. He was holding my board in one hand and my leg in the other.

"Here you go brah. You a crazy fucka," he said. "Let's go."

That was the first time I met Pohaku.

The next time I went to Hawaii, a few weeks later, it was with a Nat Geo film crew. We were further into the winter swell season, and the waves were even bigger than before. Pohaku had arranged for two water-rescue legends on jet skis, Jeff O and Nolan, North Shore lifeguards with deep local roots. In Hawaii, water safety teams are a serious thing. To save people from the hardest waves, they have to put themselves right in the face of them, which means they're always a hair's breadth from crisis themselves. They were exactly the people you want around when it counts.

On the first day, I did everything I could to catch a wave. The increased swell made it harder to catch momentum by paddling alone, so catching the larger rollers often requires a jet ski to tow you into position. But jet ski or no jet ski, I failed again.

On the second day, I thought I'd caught one. A second later it crushed me and split my board in half. Pohaku got me another board from his house, but I continued to struggle.

Then Pohaku called over to Nolan on his jet ski. "Fuck it, brah. Throw me the rope." He got on and wakeboarded behind the jet ski into position, then whipped into the shoulder of the biggest breaker of the day. As it hit the edge of the reef below, it spiked upward and became a towering twenty-foot wave. He flew across its face, leveraging the speed to ride the shoulder and descend like a comet. He looked like a laughing Buddha, shaved head, infectious smile, projecting an aura of pure bliss. It was the first time I'd seen him without a hint of suspicion or stoicism.

The drones and cameras overhead captured his ride while an underwater camera operator caught the vortices that pearled along the body of the wave. It was the end of the day.

"All right, sucka," he said. "Let's go."

Exhausted and in awe, I was ready to get out. I had big, bleeding slices across my arm where the board had cut into me in the whitewater. Not ideal in the same ocean where that tiger shark bit off Mike Coots' leg.

By then, Pohaku and I were no longer strangers. He'd seen that whatever I lacked in skill, I made up for with gusto and a willingness to learn. He was starting to speak to me with candor and respect.

He told me that for him, life is chaos. The world is chaos. Everything is chaos. He'd been on his own since he was thirteen. He'd lived through a tumultuous life and had the scars to prove it. And yet he'd found peace.

"These waves are generated by storms from distant lands, and they arrive at our shore," he told me. "You don't get to choose when they arrive or how strong they are. You only get to choose what to do with them."

When I saw Pohaku riding that wave, I started crying. Not from sadness. From something I couldn't name at first. We had battled together for so long, and in the state of exhaustion that comes from days of getting crushed by the ocean, he suddenly showed me what I had been trying to reach. I was watching another guy surf, but it felt like I was on that wave with him, inside the joy on his face. And it wasn't about the wave at all. It was about the potential for that kind of joy residing within me, within anyone. He talked about the feeling as perfection. Pohaku had found it not in a shaman's ceremony or a cave or a desert, but in the water. The wave was where he went to find what couldn't be taken from him, and watching him ride, I understood that the joy I was searching for wasn't something I had to earn or prove. It was already there. It had always been there. I just had to stop bracing against the chaos long enough to feel it.

In March of 2020, just weeks after I'd finished filming in Hawaii, I gave a talk at Cambridge University, where decades before my father had taken us on his sabbatical. The university put me up in a tiny room that felt like a monk's cell, a small old bed, a simple desk beneath a window that looked out at the river where people were punting. I wondered about the other scholars who had shared that bed, people who had pursued nothing material in life but only knowledge. They were all explorers, including my father.

The talk itself had been years in the making, shaped by long conversations with Derek, who was now a professor of AI and cultural resonance in Amsterdam. He'd been my best friend since graduate school, the guy who'd hung the Sleep Study sign and carried me on labyrinth adventures, but he was also the intellectual partner I'd always turned to when I needed to make sense of what I was experiencing. Together we'd traced the connections between flow states, altered states, and the ecological landscapes that produced them, how each culture's doorway into the mind seemed to grow from the specific chemistry of the land it lived on. The morning of the talk I was nervous and I called my father. I went through the lecture with him, how cultures across the world had developed technologies of consciousness through the environments, ecologies, and entheogens available to them. The Ganges River. The waves of the North Shore. The mountains of Mongolia. The psychedelics of the ancient Americas. He gave me advice, but more than anything, it was the first time in my life we were peers. I had carried his rejection of my mother as if it were a rejection of me for so long, and standing in that tiny room overlooking the river where he had once walked, I realized he finally saw me as an equal. Not his wayward youngest but a fellow explorer of the same mysteries he'd spent his life studying from behind a telescope. His were at the galactic scale. Mine were at the human one. But we were asking the same question.

Standing in those halls where I'd watched him lecture as a kid, trying to explain things I was only beginning to understand myself, I felt closer to him than I had in years.

And then, seemingly overnight, the world shut down.

On the trip home, the security protocols were different. People wore masks and kept their distance. Everyone kept talking about a virus. By the time I landed, the era of Covid had begun. A great wave had come from a distant shore, and now we all had to decide what to do with it.

The cruel irony was that we were forced to experience a crisis that affected everyone in isolation. Most of the rituals I'd come to believe played a vital role in human well-being were communal by their very nature: the living caring for the dead, the shaman leading a collective mantra, weddings and music and dance. Ceremony and community go hand in hand. But now community was the danger.

The kids, now seven and ten, built a huge play fort of blankets and cushions that took over the downstairs living room and became our shared bedroom for the first months of the pandemic. While they still bounced between Kara's home and mine every other week, we had otherwise become a pod closed off from the world. I tried to make it as fun as I could, raising chickens and lizards and ants and whatever animals we could adopt. Charlie's endless positivity and Millie's humor and creativity created an incubator of joy that was, for a time, quite wonderful. Our little unit finally had extended time together without another trip on the horizon. But as the months wore on and life in the fort continued, it began to feel claustrophobic. Live long enough in a fort and you start to feel like you're under siege.

So, as I'd done all my life, I sought the outdoors. I'd take the kids into the Anza Borrego desert and we'd dig for fossils in the sandstone. When they were with Kara, I'd find my way to the sea.

In those early days of the pandemic, it was illegal to enter the water in San Diego. Police were stationed at the beach to prevent it. But every night, right around sunset, I'd sneak past them and into the ocean. There was a red tide, an algae bloom carrying bioluminescent plankton that lit up like stars each time they were churned by the waves. As I walked in, each step created a tiny supernova beneath my feet. I'd lie in the bioluminescence and feel the ocean hold me while the world talked about isolation at a scale none of us had imagined. Survival was not just about staying alive. It was about keeping the magic of life alive so that life was worth living. The ocean was where I went for that, the way I'd always gone to nature when everything else was wrong. Just me and the water and a galaxy of glowing microorganisms, lighting up the lonely nights.

As society started settling into the new reality, friends reached out and began joining me, seeking to reclaim a sense of community. One of them was Alex, whom I'd met a few years before under the strangest circumstances. After returning from Varanasi at the end of 2017, I'd taken the kids back to Death Valley for New Year's Eve, hundreds of miles off-road to the space where Bruna and I had begun the psychedelic journey that saved my life. But what started as a magical moment took a turn when the truck got trapped in the dunes, sinking into soft sand. We were stranded, our gear and tent some twenty miles away.

"Ok, kids, we can survive anything! What do we need? Water, a lighter, clothes, and my guitar. The adventure continues!" I exclaimed with false bravado, trying to convince myself we were going to be okay in the rapidly chilling desert night. Beneath the light of a wolf moon, we trudged through miles of open desert, using the sky as a compass like the Bedouins of old. Eventually our path crossed a dirt road that ran between the main pass and the hot springs. We built a fire from old driftwood scattered across the wash, then spent hours huddled around it as the temperature dropped, hoping someone would happen to drive through the middle of nowhere.

Miraculously, someone did. A distant speck of light became the headlights of a truck, and a twenty-something guy with a beard rolled down his window and offered to help. That was Alex. He'd just quit his job to pursue filmmaking, much like I'd walked away from the traditional path to search for Genghis Khan's tomb. Two leaps of faith, colliding in the dust. He pulled us out, and we parted ways. We didn't see each other again for years.

But about six months after Covid hit, Alex messaged me. He'd moved to San Diego and wanted to make some friends. He was a talented surfer who'd grown up navigating the cold swells of Northern California. So we began surfing together.

I woke up every morning in the predawn darkness. While Charlie and Millie slept in the fort, I'd slip out and drive through morning fog to the beach. Pandemic restrictions were still in place, masks required wherever we went. But all that melted away in the ocean. Alex would be there to catch the first light, barely peeking over the eastern horizon. We'd put on our wetsuits and walk down the long road to where the beach met a deep underwater canyon. In the darkness, we could just make out hints of how big the day's waves would be. Sometimes the sets were small and forgiving. Other days the canyon funneled swells that reared up taller than either of us. As the sun rose higher, the mist in the air painted the water in pastels, the last glimmers of the bioluminescent tide fading like the night beneath the vivid pinks and yellows of the new day.
One day, I told Alex about Pohaku and my growing belief that surfing was a way of tapping into something fundamental about the human experience. I told him about that picture of Mike Coots, euphoric in the barrel, and how it had inspired me.

"You should do it," he said. "You should get that barrel. We should film it."

That was the start of what we'd call the Barrel Project. At first it was just the two of us, me on my board and him bobbing with a waterproof camera we'd pooled money to buy. Then I reached out to Johnny Harrington, one of the camera operators I'd met during the development of Welcome to Earth. Johnny was an East Coast kid who'd grown up surfing hurricane swells off Rhode Island and had built a career in underwater cinematography from Shark Week to the far corners of the ocean. I watched him build a massive camera housing in my garage, a contraption he'd be taking into the same waves that had been crushing me, in waters where Mike Coots would show us the teeth marks on his skin from the tiger shark that took his leg, and where Pohaku spoke of his big brother being the shark itself. And there was Johnny, tightening bolts and checking seals, fully aware of what lived in that water, choosing to get in anyway. That was who he was. He had the kind of quiet, steady loyalty that doesn't announce itself, it just shows up when you need it. He and Alex would float in the cold winter waters for hours to get in position for each wave attempt, and between takes they'd give me pointers, teaching me how to turn, how to slow down, how to read the energy building beneath my board.

Since my prosthetic ankle didn't rotate, we started adjusting the angle of my foot to get more contact on the board. We used an Allen wrench to rotate the foot out, making it look as if I was walking like a bird. It was awkward waddling through the parking lot, but once I was on the waves, I felt free and almost superpowered.

A friend, Jeff McCallum, shaped some new boards for me, large enough to paddle further out for bigger waves but with enough stability to turn even without an ankle. One of the first financial backers of the Genghis Khan project caught wind of our endeavor and arranged for a training session at an exclusive surf ranch where pro surfers use artificially generated waves to fine-tune their skills. Once again, what began as a dream was becoming a reality. Bit by bit, it was becoming easier to feel the precise moment where the wave's energy would catch my board and I could pop up to ride its face.

By the winter of 2021, as Covid restrictions began to ease, we set our eyes on returning to Hawaii. We began watching for storms. Pohaku would map the weather from across the Pacific, tracking incipient systems, charting the wind they generated and the waves they'd create. We were on standby, ready to go. When the time was right, he'd let us know.

Weeks later, we were back on the North Shore with the most intense, beautiful waves in the world. As Pohaku and I spent more time together, he began showing me something beyond the waves.

He took me to his home on a hill overlooking the east side of the island. Under a jungle canopy that his backyard pressed against, he stood in nothing but board shorts, looking at a giant plank of ulu wood laid across two workbenches. He ran his hands along the grain as if feeling for what was inside the wood. He picked up an old planing tool from the bench, something that looked like a shuttlecock with two handles, and pressed it into the wood, sliding it up and down the grain with a steadiness that felt less like cutting than massaging. Little curls of wood spun up as he worked, like waves themselves. Pohaku shaped boards the way his ancestors had shaped them, from ulu, wiliwili, and koa, carved by hand with no measurements, sanded with coral blocks, finished with kukui nut oil. He'd buried his first finished board in a taro field to absorb the mana of the earth. When he was there working, the gangster-like banter that was his normal cadence fell away, and it seemed like he was transported into the dream version of himself, the weight of the modern world slipping into the shadows. Suddenly he was there in the tradition of his ancestors, and the board under his hands was the vessel that would carry it forward.

Pohaku was a wild man, an untamed wolf with a genuine heart. Down the side of his leg ran a tattoo of a papa holua, a hill sled, the symbol of an ancient Hawaiian practice where riders hurled themselves down steep mountainsides on massive wooden toboggans. The tradition had nearly disappeared, but Pohaku had revived it from memories of his own childhood, bringing the practice back into the living culture of Hawaii. For Hawaiians, tattoos aren't decoration. They're earned, lived history inscribed in skin. Carved into his body was a connection to his past.

One day we decided to paddle up the river into the jungle. He handed me one of his wooden boards to do it on. We paddled through the lagoon and into the river side by side, and as the banks narrowed and the jungle closed in around us, he began to tell me about his people. How they would fish up the islands. How they would take their outriggers up these rivers and into secret caves deep in the heart of the mountains. He showed me a long roll of paper he'd brought. It was a list of names.

"These are my ancestors," he said. "Going all the way back to the beginning. To the first canoes, the first wayfinders. To the shark, my family's god."

His roots were the ancient people who stood on the edge of the only world they'd ever known, looked across the sea to a distant horizon, and decided to voyage into the unknown. Thousands of years ago, they traveled by paddle and wind to arrive at this land that would one day, many generations later, find me paddling beside their descendant. That long list began with a single, brave crew, riding a canoe into nothing.

"Sometimes, when the big rains come down from the mountains," Pohaku said, "the locals will find an ancient rudder that got pushed out from a canyon by the storm. The first wayfarers brought their giant canoes deep into those caves." For those who knew where to look, the secret would never be told.

For Hawaiians, the ocean is a kind of mother. "We come from the water, and we'll return to the water." He told me that the ancient wayfinders could know where they were by feeling the direction of the swells, reading the deep heave and pull of the sea itself. He believed he'd been a shark in another life, and would be again after his death. He told me that one day, many years before, an unthinkably large wave nearly drowned him. As he drifted on the edge of death, he had a vision of a shark so vivid it catapulted him back into consciousness. He rode the next wave all the way back in.

Despite all the training and mentorship, I still hadn't been barreled. There were moments when the whole thing seemed ridiculous. We were chasing something entirely for fun and self-satisfaction at the end of the day, just like climbing the mountains of my youth, only now I was climbing mountains of water. As the waves got bigger I wondered if the risks were worth it. Maybe I'd dragged all these people into this pursuit on the tail end of a pandemic that had made everyone on the planet face their mortality. Maybe the whole thing was an elaborate way of not stopping, because stopping meant feeling the full weight of what was gone.

But we kept going. Again and again I'd be crushed under columns of water or my board would break and I'd be left floundering in the frothy wake. I'd return to a repair warehouse in San Diego where a couple of legends in the local surfing scene would get to work on my board. One time, one of the old surf shapers brought me to a back room and pointed to a poster on the wall of a young Hawaiian man riding a massive wave. "That's Pohaku, forty years ago." He looked so different as a young man, but the smile on his face was the same one I saw each time he caught a perfect wave.

We kept returning to the North Shore, even as it got harder and meaner with the changing of the seasons. One day, I was finally able to meet up with Mike Coots to surf, just as he'd said we would back in that first hug at the triathlon. Pohaku called Jeff O and Nolan to bring the jet skis, and together with Mike they started teaching me how to tow into bigger waves.

That day, Mike told me a story. When he was younger and still trying to make it as a pro surfer, he would strap a GoPro to his board and capture images of himself on the waves. But when he looked at the pictures, he saw that in each one he was grimacing, his face locked in terror. He decided to start smiling instead. The instant he made that choice, he became more in flow. Even after the shark bit off his leg, he kept choosing to smile. Not just as a surfer but as a champion of the very thing that had compromised him. He became a shark conservationist. He became part of the wave itself.

I thought of Pohaku, smiling like Buddha as he found perfection in chaos.

That day I told Mike something I hadn't said to anyone. That his photograph in the hospital had become a kind of mask for me. That I'd used his image of joy to paper over my own pain, to build the strong face that got me through the years of being El Robotico and the bionic explorer and the guy who jokes about snakes. But underneath the image was the loss I'd never fully looked at. I was out here trying to prove to myself that the promise his picture had made in that hospital bed was real, that the joy was actually possible, that I hadn't been making it up. Mike listened without flinching. He knew. He'd been the image before he'd been the man, and he understood what it cost to live inside someone else's hope.

And yet again I was realizing that it was the quest and not the destination that was going to give me what I needed. Just like Mongolia, where the tomb was never the point. The barrel wasn't the point either.

The day was coming to an end, but a distant storm had sent us one more wave. A single wave like any other and yet utterly unique, existing for a single, perfect moment.

I started paddling.

As the great swell surged upward, I rose with it and popped up on my board, just as I'd tried so many times before. But this time, I chose to smile.

The giant lip of water curled over my head as the slope of the wave's shoulder kept forming in a perfect Fibonacci curve. As the wave wrapped around me, the sound of the world disappeared into the roar of water that consumed everything outside the tunnel. It felt alive, as if I was inside a living body of water that was wrapping itself around me but maintaining this tiny pocket where I could exist in wonder. Time slowed. The light filtered through the wall of the wave in blues and greens I'd never seen before. I was inside the vortex, and for a moment that felt like it could have lasted forever, the chaos and the harmony were the same thing.

Then the wave consumed me entirely, threw me into the reef and spat me back out. But as I emerged from the froth, the smile hadn't left my face. I floated there giggling, looking for Pohaku, for Johnny, for Alex. They were scattered across the water. I lay on my back in the wash, exhausted and laughing, and let the ocean hold me.

Chapter 13: The Door in the Mountain

What actually happens after death?

That was the question in my mind as I drafted a letter for my kids to read if the unthinkable ever happened. It wasn't an idle exercise. A version of me had died in an accident that cost me my leg. Charlie and Millie had seen me broken, stitched back together, and forced to begin again. We all had been given a lesson in how fragile life really was.

And still, I was constantly heading back into risk. Helicopters, war zones, giant waves, venomous snakes, these had become the raw materials of my working life. The dream I'd chased since I was a kid had come true, and it had brought me into the company of the dead. From the outside, each expedition looked thrilling. From the inside, they blurred into tombs, skulls, and rituals, each one asking me to stare at mortality a little longer than was comfortable.

The rhythm of filming was orbital. Nearly half my days were spent on expeditions, Colombia, Peru, Israel, Jordan, Sudan, Micronesia, each a window into a distinct version of human existence. Then I'd rush back to San Diego and drop into single-dad mode, packing lunches, coaching softball, sneaking bills under pillows as the tooth fairy. Over time Kara and I had worked out a flexible calendar that made it possible, but it often meant being "on" seconds after landing. I was living two lives at once: explorer and father, each demanding everything. I'd fly home from holding the bones of sacrificed children in Peru and be at Millie's softball game by the next afternoon, sneaking a tooth fairy dollar under Charlie's pillow that night with dirt under my fingernails from a dig on another continent.

On the road, I wasn't alone. The crew that Lucy Van Beek had originally assembled had become my second family over the years. Joe led the technical side, humble and unassuming, the kind of person who never announced his brilliance but had built a team around him that could go into the most extreme environments on earth and invent ways of seeing through the impossible. His brother had coded an augmented reality prototype overnight on one of our earliest expeditions, and Joe had taken that same restless energy and scaled it into a full operation. Duncan was his right hand, quieter but just as relentless, and together they made LiDAR sing. Gary was the Scottish cameraman who'd jam with me on his guitar after brutal days in the field, and who I'd later watch wade into raging whitewater without hesitation for a shot. Graeme was our stoic safety coordinator who never showed alarm, which made it all the more terrifying when he finally did. We were a band of well-functioning misfits. Months in jungles and deserts forged the kind of trust you can't fake.

I'd keep my bags packed for each biome, stacked next to a pile of prosthetic parts and wads of cash from around the globe. But beyond the logistics and the jet lag was always the deeper question: what is being human really about?

In Colombia, we scanned Ciudad Perdida and followed ancient Tairona trails revealed by LiDAR through cartel country under military escort. And yet, in the middle of all that, I sat with a Kogi priest on a circular stone platform high in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. The Kogi are among the last pre-Columbian civilizations in the Americas still maintaining an unbroken ancient way of life. They call themselves the Elder Brothers of humanity and believe they are responsible for maintaining the balance of the world. The platform where he stood was the same kind that defined Ciudad Perdida itself, though the Tairona who built it were long gone. The Kogi were their descendants, a living culture inhabiting the ruins of their own past. He sat in his white tunic, his long black hair falling past his shoulders, tapping a stick into a small container of coca and lime, rubbing the mixture inside his cheek the way his people had for centuries. Modernity was rising all around him. Yet there he sat, high in the cloud forest, looking as his people had looked through the conquests and beyond, holding the space for the rest of us in what he believed was the consciousness of the universe. He held my prosthetic leg and thanked the sun. "We are of the stars," he said. "All things come from the sun."

A few days later I was on the busy streets of Santa Marta, where beaches were covered in people playing volleyball and soccer, and the world I had just been in seemed light-years away.

I'd fly home from wherever I'd been, unpack the spare legs and snake gaiters, and slip back into school pickup lines moments after the plane touched down. My kids had grown used to it. In many ways all of our lives were lived out of suitcases, their world passed between my house and Kara's, my world passed between expeditions and fatherhood. In this untethered time, they were my foundation, my greatest cheerleaders, my greatest responsibility, and my best friends.

So one night, with the kids asleep and my bags packed by the door for the next trip, I sat down at the kitchen table in the dark house and wrote them a letter. Life had piled up, the accident, Covid, and all those sessions in the big waves where I'd held my breath underwater as the ocean crashed over me until the point of accepting convulsions, and it was confronting. I wrote about everything I'd learned along the way. About how choosing to let go of my leg had taught me that perspective is something you can decide, not something that happens to you. About Pohaku's words, that the waves come from distant storms and you don't get to choose when they arrive, only what you do with them. I told them that more than anything, I hoped they'd learned that. And I told them to go back to the dunes together throughout their lives, not just with the memories we'd shared but to make new ones. That the desert would always be there for them, the way it had always been there for us. It was a strange and beautiful moment, writing to my children what the world had taught me, in a house where they slept above me and the silence was the same silence I'd played guitar through after the divorce, the same silence I'd filled with Jamie's music, the same silence that would fill again each time I left.

Then I packed my bag for Peru.

Every Lost Cities expedition was incredible in its own way. But of all of them, Peru is the place we returned to most frequently, and each time what made it onto the screen was only a fraction of what we experienced. For a few of my crew it's also where things almost ended.

Even before I set foot there, Peru had haunted me. Not just through the iconic images, Machu Picchu rising from the clouds, Johan Reinhard's photographs of a sacrificed Incan girl preserved in ice, but through something more personal: my friend Gil's footprints in the snow of the Cordillera Blanca, the last tracks he'd left before he disappeared. Gil, who had once told me that mountains strip the mind to its essence and force you to live in the moment. Whose tracks we had found with Tomnod's satellite eye, staring at a screen in San Diego while his body lay somewhere in the ice. Like a moth to flame, Peru both called to me and haunted me.

And then my father told me something I'd never known. When my great-grandfather got on a boat from China to the new world, he wasn't the only one. He had an older brother who got on a different boat, heading to Peru. I imagined those two young men hugging goodbye on the edge of a dock, each waiting for a boat to carry him to a place he could scarcely imagine. One went north, one went south. They never saw each other again, never knew what became of the other's life. But generations later, the northern brother's great-grandson would find his way to the southern brother's continent, carrying a prosthetic leg and a camera and a question about what it means to be human that neither of them could have imagined asking.

Our first expedition in 2017 set out to search for the origins of Machu Picchu. The crew flew in from London, we loaded mules with our porters, and began the long climb into the Andes.

It quickly became apparent that one of our porters, known simply as Elder, was actually a Paqo, a shaman to his community. He was a smaller man, fifteen or twenty years older than I was, strong and quiet, with the classic profile of his Quechua-speaking community carved into his face like the mountains themselves. At rest stops he played a flute that seemed to carry the breath of those mountains. Our Peruvian archaeologist, Andas, explained that his people believed their ancestors had literally emerged from the mountains, echoing the link between natural forces and civilizational origins that so many of the cultures I'd encountered described in their own stories.

We came to a circular rock dwelling, more like a mound, with a small opening facing the largest peak on the horizon. I knelt and peered in. Human bones were scattered inside, poking up through the dirt. The air was cold from the altitude, and the space smelled of earth the way an old cellar does. Andas explained that for the indigenous Andeans, the dead were not gone but transformed into another state within the cosmic cycle. These dwellings were where the living communed with them, and the spirits of their occupants still existed as part of the Pachamama, the Earth Mother. The past was not past here. It was present, just on the other side of that small opening. Elder pulled out a pouch of coca leaves and performed a ceremony, holding sets of three leaves into the sky and scattering them into the dwelling before us. The other porters followed his lead.

The coca plant, which the modern world has turned into a recreational drug, is key to some of Peru's most significant ceremonies. Before climbing any mountain, coca leaves are carefully held and scattered into the wind as Elder had done, paying respect to the invisible energy of the land. Shamans chew wads of coca leaves to open a mental and spiritual channel to Pachamama.

Watching Elder with his coca leaves, I began to see something I hadn't been able to name before. Each land had provided its people with their own way in. The forests had given mushrooms. The deserts had given cactus. The islands had given kava. The high Andes had given the coca leaf. It was as if the earth itself had been teaching us how to open our minds since before we had a word for consciousness. Years before, the ethnobotanist Wade Davis, whose work on the intersection of indigenous knowledge and the natural world had been an inspiration since my earliest days of exploration, had described the geographic distribution of psychoactive plants as a kind of map of human imagination. I was standing inside that map now, holding coca leaves on an Andean mountainside, feeling the pattern in my hands. But if all these cultures, separated by oceans and millennia, had independently found these doorways, what were they opening to? What was the source of the human imagination that had dreamed up everything we have ever created, every city, every song, every god, every act of care? I didn't have an answer.

We pushed higher, to sixteen thousand feet, then seventeen thousand. The air thinned to a knife's edge. One of the American archaeologists doubled over, vomiting from altitude sickness. We halted to acclimate. While the rest of the team settled into camp, I turned to Elder and asked if he would show me how he understood the deeper spirit of this land. Not for the cameras, but quietly, as one traveler to another.

A few days later, the crew had a rest day. Elder and I slipped away. We followed narrow trails past rivers and cliffs, until we reached a grand staircase of stone carved into the mountainside, rising like a vast, ancient amphitheater hidden in the folds of the valley. It was an archaeological site that would have drawn crowds if anyone knew it was here, but tucked away from the iconic ruins of Machu Picchu, it was completely empty. "Inca," Elder said, gesturing upward. The steps were worn smooth by centuries of feet, but no one was on them now. The altitude made the light crisper, the way it had when I first arrived in Lhasa years before. Elder climbed ahead of me, playing his flute, and as I followed the sound up that ancient staircase I felt like I was walking into a ceremony that existed in the echoes of everything around me.

At the top, a vast open space like an amphitheater looked out over the ruins descending below and the mountain rising on the opposing valley wall. Crumbled walls of ancient buildings sat along its sides. Elder led me to the back, where the overhang of the cave cast the stone into shadow. There, carved into the wall in the heart of the mountain, was a large stone doorway. It didn't open into anything, just stone against stone. But Elder said it was a doorway to other realms.

He handed me a vial of distilled San Pedro cactus juice, a powerful entheogen he had made from plants in his own garden. San Pedro is different from psilocybin. Where mushrooms pull consciousness inward and upward into visions and psychodrama, San Pedro opens outward. It is sometimes called heart medicine rather than mind medicine. I looked at the vial, then at the door carved into the stone behind him. I drank.

Elder's flute began again, repeating its melody over and over. It sounded oddly familiar, haunting, as if the sound were emerging not from the instrument but from through the door itself. He tried to explain in a mix of Quechua and Spanish that it was an ancient song, seven civilizations older than the Inca. As the tune echoed through the cave, its notes seemed to travel through the portal and come back changed.

The San Pedro settled into my body as a warmth that spread slowly downward, a gravitational deepening, as if I were being drawn into the earth rather than lifted out of it. The world didn't fracture into visions the way the psilocybin had in Death Valley. It clarified. The light became crisper. The stone became more present. I could feel the weight of the mountain above me and the roots of everything below, and the boundary between my body and the ground beneath me became something I could no longer locate. I wasn't dissolving. I was settling. The earth felt alive, patient, ancient, and what I felt from it was something I can only describe as compassion.

Elder gestured again to the door in the mountain. "Those civilizations exist through that portal," he said. To him it wasn't just rock. It was a threshold where past, present, and future overlapped, and Pachamama, the mother who holds all realms, was the ground beneath my feet.

After what must have been a few hours, we descended from the cave. Elder built a hut of eucalyptus leaves he pulled from the hills and made a small fire to heat rocks, generating steam inside the leafy enclosure. In the steam, my body felt as if it were being received by the jungle and the mountain at once. From somewhere in the distance, the haunting sound of a train horn echoed through the valley. I asked Elder again where the melody of his flute came from.

"This song goes back to the beginning," he told me through hand gestures.

Then I realized where I'd heard it before. Filtered through time and distance, adapted into local folk songs and then eventually into Simon and Garfunkel's "El Condor Pasa" on my dad's old records. A fragment of American pop music, carried across continents, was rooted in this very soil. Something that had entered my subconscious long before I knew its origins had been alive in this place for longer than anyone could count. When Andas had explained that the mountain was our ancestor, I'd understood him intellectually. Now I understood it in my bones.

I thought about the door in the mountain. It didn't open into anything physical. It was stone against stone. But people had carved it there because they believed something existed on the other side, something that hadn't gone away just because centuries had passed. The civilizations Elder spoke of through that portal weren't dead. They were still there, the way the melody of his flute was still there inside a Simon and Garfunkel song, the way the bones in the dwelling were still part of the Pachamama that held us all. Time wasn't a wall with the past on one side and the present on the other. It was a door, and the door was open if you knew how to stand in front of it.

No LiDAR could see what Elder had shown me. The land held something that couldn't be scanned or mapped, and the people who lived on it had known that for longer than any of us could measure.

The second time I came to Peru was in the height of the Covid pandemic, in 2020. The fate of the world felt uncertain, but the story I'd come for was even darker. Filming had continued as "essential work" because people needed content while stuck at home. So in a world of protocols, I found myself at eighteen thousand feet on the glaciers of the Cordillera Blanca, where I had lost Gil years before. We were tracing climate events locked in ancient ice to the coastal plains below, where archaeologists had uncovered the world's largest child sacrifice. In the same time period as Genghis Khan's conquest of Eurasia, the Chimu people of the city of Chan Chan, facing apocalyptic El Niño floods, had marched hundreds of their own children to a bluff overlooking the coastline, fed them the cactus hallucinogens Elder had given me, and cut their hearts from their chests as an offering to the Moon and the sea. I held their bones in my hands, next to the ceremonial blade that had done the deed. When I tilted it, its bell-shaped handle rattled. It was the most unsettling sound I'd heard on any expedition. That rattle was the last thing those children had heard before their hearts were cut from their chests. I held the blade and could feel it.

Days later, I was back home, rushing from my flight straight to Millie's first school play after the start of the pandemic. I arrived in my mountaineering gear, mud still on my boots, just in time to watch her step on stage in butterfly wings we'd made together weeks before. The play was about the cycle of life, which she was now experiencing, and those sacrificed children never got the chance to. I clapped harder than anyone when she bowed.

Each time I left Peru, I thought I had glimpsed its essence, only to return and realize I'd barely scratched the surface.

A few years later, while filming the most ambitious season of Lost Cities, I wrote that letter to my kids. Things had not been going smoothly. We'd faced Covid delays, civil wars bubbling up on location, and near-death accidents. The present-day world felt as if it were in chaos, but it was our return to Peru that forced me to truly reckon with aspects of existence I'd seen so many different cultures grappling with: death, impermanence, and forces of nature that must be respected because they are bigger than us.

It was 2022. Eoin O'Shea, our showrunner, saw an opportunity to find stories that challenged assumptions. Together we had crafted a season not just about lost cities but lost narratives, histories left in the margins, voices drowned out by the dominant telling of history. It felt like a return to the original motivations behind my first expedition to Mongolia: to find what was left out of the school books of my childhood.

In Peru we decided to focus on the lost story of the Chachapoya, who the Inca they once battled had called the Cloud Warriors. Their history had been all but erased by war and disease during the era of Spanish conquest, until their great mountain citadel of Kuelap had been rediscovered more than a century ago, a fortress so vast and intricate it suggested the presence of a powerful civilization. But where was the civilization? The few home sites around Kuelap didn't match the scale of the monument. Everything pointed into the cloud forest, terrain dense enough to hide any trace of the Chachapoya. It was the kind of mystery LiDAR was made for. And the stakes felt urgent: storms and landslides were rapidly destroying Kuelap, threatening to erase them from memory forever.

Written records were almost nonexistent. What little is known comes from the few descendants who still speak fragments of a language even more ancient than the indigenous Quechua. Fortunately, archaeologist Parker Van Valkenburgh had an ingenious hunch. By tracing surviving words from that pre-Quechua tongue and matching them to place names on a map, we could begin to see where to focus the LiDAR.

That July the team converged in Lima, then proceeded toward the cloud forest. Our caravan of trucks rattled along dirt roads to a small village where we met Juan Santillán, a soft-spoken farmer who also ran the local heritage office. The Minister of Culture had given permission for us to scan the enigmatic cliffs above Juan's village, which served as the Cloud Warriors' city of the dead. They were normally forbidden to climb, but our non-invasive tools had opened the door. For Juan, those cliffs held his ancestors, but even he had never scaled them. None of us quite knew what we would find.

Mules carried gear and tents into a dripping green world. We passed through lush forest with dangling, succulent red vines that felt cool against our faces. With each step the air grew thinner. When we made camp, the glow of our headlamps mingled with the starlight of a vast and cloudless sky. At dawn we followed the faint traces of an ancient Chachapoya trail to the funeral cliffs. High above us in the morning fog stood the rows of clay sarcophagi called purunmachus. In the dim morning light they looked like the teeth of the mountain.

The plan was simple: Juan and I would push as close as we safely could to the burials, hold a clean line of sight with a radio in hand, and guide Joe and Duncan as they flew the scanners from a safe and respectful distance.

We meandered upward, looking for paths of least resistance and hacking with machetes when we couldn't find them. The further we ascended, the fewer viable handholds there were, until we were climbing the only plausible route. A thought entered my mind that each step, each hold, had been used before by the ancient Chachapoya themselves as they made their way up to honor their dead.

On the far side of the upper edge, we came to an immense dropoff. We donned harnesses and started making our way up with ropes, Gary precariously shuttling cameras along our line. In the final stretch, Juan and the rest of the crew stayed below to give me a belay. I was alone.

I came to an alcove, and as I shimmied across it, I looked down. Inside was a pile of wavy, reddish-brown hair, a single human tooth, and some fragments of rope. I was among the dead. A few steps further, and I saw a thousand feet of air between me and the ground. A wave of vertigo rushed over me, but years of climbing mountains with my friends had prepared me for this.

I peered around the last corner, and there stood the sarcophagi.

A line of clay statues adorned the cliffside. Expressions had been painted onto their masks, and they were angled to gaze upon the sunset in the space between sky and earth. One was decayed and broken open, strands of hair and an embalmed skeleton visible through the crack. As the afternoon light turned to gold, the sun caught their faces and seemed to make them come alive, the warm hues dancing over the clouds and casting a glow on painted features that had been watching this same light for six hundred years. When the Sistine Chapel was painted and when man stepped on the moon, they were here. I wondered if their detailed, stoic expressions reflected the character of those entombed within, and what they made of me, a one-legged man from California perched on their cliff.

I was acutely aware of my own impermanence. One day I too would be reduced to a pile of hair and bone, and someday even that would dissolve into dust. Perhaps only my prosthetic would remain. But these faces would still be here, bodies naturally mummified in the arid Andes, eyes fixed on the horizon. As Maya once said, we will be long gone. And yet these mountains will still be standing here.

The sudden buzz of a drone shattered the silence. I radioed down to Joe and Duncan, making sure they hovered close enough to capture the cliff but far enough not to disturb the dead. As the hours passed, I pulled a sandwich, an apple, and a tiny chocolate from my pocket. My hands were covered in dust and dirt, and I was thinking about the fact that this was the dust of a city of the dead. Human bones lay within feet of me as I ate, and it was strangely normal. I was probably the first person to have lunch with those Cloud Warriors in six centuries. Interestingly, the ancient Andeans had lived with their dead, sometimes burying them in the floors of their homes, and in certain celebrations the dead would be brought back out, cleaned, and dined with to keep the connections alive. Sitting there with my sandwich amongst the sarcophagi, I was doing something their builders would have understood perfectly.

On the way down, more skeletons revealed themselves, packed into crevices, tucked into shadow. I brushed the dust from my clothes and paused. Was I wiping away dirt, or bone?

The next day, back in Juan's village, we gathered around the data as it came to life on screen. Juan stood beside me, his eyes widening. Soon the room filled, first the local team, then townspeople, until some were perched in the rafters, all waiting to see what the machines had found.

As the scans resolved, more sarcophagi appeared. Then, hidden high in the cliff, a cave beyond reach. Inside, the LiDAR revealed a vast scatter of bones: a mass grave.

I looked over and saw Juan crying. "This is my story," he said quietly. "This is my history." The room was packed, townspeople hanging from the rafters trying to see the screens. There wasn't a lot of conversation after, just hugs and laughter. And then, just like that, we left. I often wonder what it must feel like for those communities when we drop in like aliens with our drones and our screens, reveal something sacred about their own past, and then disappear as quickly as we came.

But this was just the first step. We had found the Chachapoya's city of the dead, but the mystery of where they had truly lived still lay ahead. That was what we planned to find out next. But fate had something else in mind.

On the far edge of their world lay the inter-Andean dry forest, a sunbaked canyonland more like Arizona than the lush Amazon it eventually feeds. Peruvian archaeologist Jeff Contreras had traced remnants of a vast network of ancient trading paths that once bound the Cloud Warriors to distant cultures of desert and jungle alike. Our goal was to follow those forgotten arteries from the Marañón River and see if they could lead us to the settlements they once nourished.

The descent from the cloud forest was like traveling through epochs of earth itself, each bend revealing a new ecology folding into the horizon. Ominous rainstorms built in the distance until the storm caught us, drenching the switchbacks. My stomach knotted as I thought of the accident that had taken my leg, how quickly a single turn of fate can change everything.

We reached the banks of the Marañón late. A worn-down hacienda at the water's edge became our shelter for the night, the only one for miles, with an empty pool filled with debris that reminded me of an abandoned hotel we were squatting in. It also happened to be the staging ground for a local doctor's birthday party. The crew was exhausted and nervous for the days to come, and the karaoke that was amusing at first quickly became grinding. I fell asleep to its dulcet tones while the river swelled in the dark.

By morning, the Marañón roared like a living thing. The rain had thickened the heaving current to the color of chocolate. We hurried through safety briefings, loaded our rafts, and pushed off far later than planned.

Tradition says no journey should begin without an offering of coca leaves to Pachamama, a ritual to remind us that we travel not just through landscapes but through living spirits, as Elder had shown me years before. But in our rush, we forgot. It seemed a minor oversight at the time. Later, it would feel like breaking a covenant.

We boarded the rafts and pushed off. The river had already swelled, but it seemed to grow angrier as we approached a critical turn where an enormous wall of stone forced the water in another direction, creating a vicious undertow.

Suddenly, a great gust of wind blew the camera boat in front of me off course, slamming them into the wall. Our raft collided with theirs, and they flipped. Gary, Adam, Graeme, and everyone else on that boat were dropped into the raging current, along with all our camera gear and most of our camping equipment.

Jeff and I stood on the bow, trying to pull anyone or anything out of the water. Most of the team popped to the surface in their life vests. But not Gary, Adam, or Graeme. I dropped to my knees at the edge of the raft, staring into the dark water, looking for any sign of them. Nobody came to the surface. Five seconds turned into ten. Then twenty. Then thirty. I debated diving in to try to pull them up. I hadn't taken a breath since they went under.

When we later reviewed the footage, it was closer to a full minute. Had I just watched my friends drown in front of me?

Finally, they burst to the surface, the pressure of their life vests forcing them upward. Gary's eyes were impossibly wide and dilated; he looked like an alien. Adam's gasps were ragged half-sobs. Graeme started swimming toward their flipped raft, but Gary was still floating in the current, a couple of hundred yards away.

"Gary, are you okay?" I called.

He didn't respond. I called again.

"No" was all he said.

Our director, Steve Sherman, had fallen in the water but was pushed out of the deeper current. He clambered atop the overturned raft. His drenched body looked strangely heroic as he screamed, "Get the drones up, get the drones up!" The main cameras were gone, and in the chaos everyone was focused on survival. But he was still focused on the story.

I held my oar out to Adam and used all my strength to pull him out of the water by the straps of his life vest. His usually solid frame slid into our raft like a wet noodle. He began to weep. "I thought I was dead," he said, over and over.

We got to the river's edge and everybody piled out into chaos. Gary had been pulled to shore by one of the other rafts, shivering, limping with a giant bloody bulge on his shin. Someone had a first aid kit and was tending to the wound. Adam was wrapped in an emergency blanket, crying. Even Graeme, our burly Scottish safety officer, was deeply shaken. He'd tried to help the others but had run out of air himself. The force of a focused eddy had pushed him down against the rocks on the bottom, so deep his ears popped from the water pressure. Radio chatter was constant as the Peruvian guides ran back and forth on the beach trying to gather whatever was floating downstream.

Gary looked at his bleeding leg.

"Somebody get me a cigarette," he said.

Graeme grabbed his satellite phone and started calling for help. Luckily, the accident had happened one bend before the truly inaccessible section of the canyon began. Amidst the chaos, our stoic Peruvian collaborator Jeff pulled out a handful of coca leaves.

"We forgot the coca offering!" he said. "We must thank the river. No one died." He dropped to his knees and offered the leaves to the water.

Eventually a few trucks made it down to a nearby bank on the last capillary of the road system. We returned to the shack where the doctor had celebrated his birthday. What followed was a kind of purgatory. Satellite calls flew to offices in London and DC, assessing the damage and trying to salvage the expedition. The safety of the crew was most important. But there was a good chance that if this expedition was shut down with the story of the Chachapoya incomplete, the financial blow could mean the premature end of Lost Cities.

I waited with Adam along the calmer section of the river, dangling a small fishing line. He just stared into the distance, spontaneously tearing up and saying, "I thought it was over."

That night I slept by the river with our Peruvian guides, trying not to think about the offices around the world that were balancing insurance, investment, and risk. In the morning, word came: we were standing down and going home. Heartbroken, we packed up and began the long journey back.

But as if the accident had been the breach of some karmic levee, bad news kept coming.

A call from home. My mom was sick, found unconscious in her house. I had to get to the hospital.

The next day, our ropes expert, one of the strongest and most agile people I've ever met, fell in the shower and broke his ribs.

The day after that, the drone pilot got Covid, jeopardizing our return home entirely.

When I was finally able to fly back, it was late July and the height of summer. I hadn't seen Charlie and Millie in weeks, but rather than going home directly, I headed to Santa Cruz to visit my mother in the hospital. She'd had a diabetic insulin spike and fallen unconscious. She was on the mend, but it was brutal to see her in a hospital bed like that.

On my first night back in San Diego with the kids, the fire alarm started blaring for no reason. Charlie and Millie looked up from what they were doing. And then, at that exact moment, a buffalo skull that had been tightly screwed to my wall for years fell off and shattered on the floor. Bones and teeth scattered across the room in a way that made the hair stand up on the back of my neck. The fragments looked like the remains I'd found in the cloud forest, the wavy hair and the single tooth in the alcove a thousand feet up. We stood there, all three of us, scared like little kids who had just heard a ghost story. The alarm stopped on its own. I went to sweep up the shattered bones and hair but couldn't throw them away. We put everything into a box and decided to bury it in the yard in a ceremony the next day. The kids slept in my room that night. The friends who were supposed to sleep over the next night, after hearing what happened, none of them wanted to come.

I grew up in a house of science. My father was an astrophysicist. I was trained as an engineer. I know how to measure things. But years of traveling through ancient landscapes had taught me something that didn't fit on a chart: that the past still breathes through us, that forces exist which don't care whether we believe in them, and that ignoring them doesn't make them go away. I don't claim to understand what happened on that expedition or in the days that followed. But I can't pretend it was all coincidence. So when the skull shattered on my floor the very night I returned, I couldn't help but wonder if we'd neglected something essential.

The words of our Peruvian guide kept playing in the back of my mind.

We forgot the coca offering.
title: Chapter 13: The Door in the Mountain

content:
Chapter 14: The Axis Mundi

A couple of weeks passed. Gary's leg healed. Adam stopped tearing up without warning. My mother came home from the hospital. The world righted itself, or seemed to, the way water settles after a stone drops through it. And somehow, despite everything, Lost Cities wasn't canceled. Preparations for filming began again. These were stories that would not be told otherwise. Time was against us now, since the network's commitment and funding came with an expiration date. If our luck didn't turn soon, the whole dream would unravel.

My thoughts kept returning to the chaos on the river. We forgot the coca offering. I thought of what the shaman had told me all those years ago on the Burkhan Khaldun: respect the old ways. In rushing to chase discovery, we had failed to do just that.

Our chance to correct the transgression came faster than we had anticipated. By September, the weather in Peru had improved. The rain had calmed, and the rafting team was available and willing. It was time to make peace with the river. And so once again, I found myself on the banks of the Marañón with the same team and the same goal, but with one major difference. This time, Jeff, our Peruvian archaeologist, hired a Paqo named Inti from the local village to present the coca leaf offering and ask the river for permission.

That night, as the rest of the film team, about ten of us in all, were charging equipment in the shack, I went alone to the river to sleep under the open sky. The shaman was there with the Peruvian boat crews whom, despite my broken Spanish, I had befriended during that strange purgatory after capsizing last time around. Inti was an unassuming man in unremarkable clothes. But something about his gentle presence reminded me of the elders I'd met before, in the Inca cave and on the mountain in Mongolia.

I sat with him and told him what had happened. Not just the accident on the water, but my mother getting sick, my friend breaking his ribs, the buffalo skull shattering on the ground.

"Is it a curse?" I asked him nervously.

He sat chewing a handful of coca leaves for some time, as if listening for a message only he could hear. Then, with translation from the younger boat crew, he spoke.

"It's not a curse. You're lucky. The river was swollen at that time, and dangerous. The raft flipped moments before you entered the section of river that you couldn't have gotten out of for days. No one died. Nothing permanently bad occurred. The signs are warnings: the fact that you felt it means you have a connection to the other side. Follow your intuitions, and respect the traditions."

Maybe the accident on the river wasn't a punishment. Maybe it was a gift. Maybe it was both, existing concurrently like matter and antimatter.

I slept on the river that night. A light rain came and went, and when I woke, an Amazonian Giant Yellow-Leg Centipede crawled out from under my sleeping bag. It had used me for warmth, but it hadn't bitten me with its potentially fatal venom.

Maybe I am lucky.

The film crew came to the riverbank, and beneath the rising sun, Inti gathered us to offer the coca leaf tribute to the river. We each took handfuls and poured them into the water, giving our respect to Pachamama as the ancient Chachapoya and Inca had done. I am not a religious person, but having been face to face with so many rituals of death, I don't presume to know what lies beyond. Maybe each land has its own spiritual force. Who am I to doubt it? Some team members dismissed the ritual as theatrics. But after all that had happened I stood in reverence and watched the leaves drift downriver until they were out of sight.

We loaded our rafts and began our journey down the same waters that had thwarted us only months before. This time we found our flow, like the waters of the river itself. Eventually the ancient trade routes we found with Jeff along the river gorge led us back into the cloud forest, where our LiDAR scans revealed endless terraces of Chachapoyan home platforms ascending every hillside. It felt like the anchor had been lifted.

By February of 2023, the season was nearly complete. We had traversed deserts, mountains, and oceans. It had been the hardest season yet, but also the most rewarding, not only professionally but personally.

One of our episodes had been filmed in Oman, and for the first time ever I'd been given the opportunity to bring Charlie and Millie out on location. Kara agreed to fly them out and stay. Over the years we'd grown from collegial co-parents into something closer to genuine friends, and it was on that trip that it clicked. On the way into the desert we stopped at a mosque and walked through ancient markets that gave off the air of an interplanetary waystation from Star Wars. Millie and I rode camels together, their giant laboring legs bending so she could climb on. I'd brought the kids' old ski goggles to fight off the dust storms, the same ones we'd worn in Death Valley years before. We slid down Arabian dunes on our backs the way we had on our sacred dunes back home, only now Bedouins and camels shared the moment with us. Charlie fished in the Gulf of Oman with a handline and some bread. The kids were older now, but their wonder hadn't dimmed, and they saw a humanity in the landscape that had nothing to do with the dramatic news stories they'd grown up hearing about the Middle East. Kara watched all of this, and I realized that even in divorce she had always been up for supporting us, and was happy to be a part of the adventure life that had also played a role in fracturing us. My two worlds had finally converged. I was grateful to have had that, before Lost Cities concluded.

The final expedition of the season would be to the jungles of Chiapas. It felt like a fitting finale, because this time we weren't searching for just another lost city. We were chasing the first city. The mythical birthplace of the Maya, a place called Matwil, whispered in glyphs carved nearly 1,300 years ago on the tomb of the great King Pakal in Palenque.

Years earlier, in Guatemala, I'd seen the abandoned cities of the Maya emerge from the jungle canopy, revealed by LiDAR. It was where I had first used the technology that would reshape my life. But in Guatemala, LiDAR had opened a window into the end of the Maya world, mapping the height of a civilization that would collapse under its own weight. Chiapas promised something else entirely: a glimpse of the beginning, if only we could find the legendary origin city.

I had spent years — decades, really — seeing civilizations through the lens of the cities they left behind. And everywhere I found the same pattern: people organized for survival purposes, but beyond food and water something else was at play. Rhythm became music. Marks became language. Ideas grew large enough to shape pyramids and causeways. Culture could not be explained by utility alone. If it could, our monuments would be nothing more than granaries and our songs little more than maps. Instead we sang songs whose meanings were felt more than explained, tones born from the landscapes we emerged from. This is what I had felt while playing music in the desert with Jamie, and when I had opened my mind in the psychedelic journey to remap my phantom pain away. It had felt as if I had touched the primordial source of imagination. In the hunt for Matwil, we would be searching for that source once again.

Chiapas is a truly magical part of Mexico, and the nearby city-state of Palenque, which perished in the eighth century, is uniquely important to both the Maya and Mayan archaeologists. It was there that the first fully deciphered dynastic history emerged from the glyphs, confirming that the Maya recorded real events, not just religious symbols. Beneath its ruins, researchers discovered the first large-scale Maya aqueduct system, revealing an advanced understanding of water management.

In Palenque, our research team introduced me to an archaeologist named Joel Palka. With his ponytail and rolled-up sleeves, he had a humble, gentle demeanor that belied the fact that he was one of the leading Mayanists in the world. There aren't many jobs for Mayanists, and there's not much money in it. This community of archaeologists is driven almost entirely by passion. Joel had once heard a tale of an ancient stele that had been reported down the river, sitting in someone's backyard, and went searching for it one afternoon with the excitement and confidence of a kid looking for secrets in a treasure hunt. He was focused on excavating sites dating to the earliest days of the Maya. But he'd never truly searched for the mythical origin city.

Over drinks, Joel walked me through the discovery that had made Palenque famous. In 1948, an archaeologist named Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found a hidden doorway at the top of a pyramid they called the Temple of the Inscriptions, named for the vast hieroglyphic panels covering its inner walls. "Over four years," Joel said, "his team cleared a rubble-filled stairway that plunged straight down into the heart of the pyramid. At the bottom, behind a triangular doorway, they walked into the burial chamber of K'inich Janaab Pakal, a Maya ruler who'd been dead for fourteen hundred years." The jungle pyramids, he explained, were revealed for what they truly were: not monuments of stone but cosmic tombs.

Joel's eyes lit up as he described what they found on the walls. An immense inscription of a Ceiba tree emerging from the underworld, carrying the ruler's soul to the stars above. And at the tomb's base, an enigmatic glyph deciphered decades later to mean "Matwil," an origin city where the gods were born and Mayan civilization began. The iconography described it as "The place of the Cormorants," a waterfowl the Maya believed could travel between the world of the living above the water and the underwater realm where souls emerge from and return to after death.

There were other mysterious glyphs throughout the temple complex, Joel continued, including an image of a "split mountain" next to the Mayan glyphs for "wind" or "breath." Taken together, they seemed to hint that the origin city of Matwil was in a "watery place of Cormorants" where a "breathing mountain" could be found and the gods of the Maya were born. Whatever that meant.

Joel told me of an artificial canal that ran directly underneath the burial chamber of Pakal's tomb. It was connected to a small tributary that led back to the Tulija River, and ultimately to the remote lake district of Metzabok, where he'd found scattered ruins of very early Maya activity. The indigenous Lacandon people who live there are descendants of the Maya who had moved back into that landscape in the wake of the collapse. If the mythical origin place were to be found, it seemed plausible it would be close to this lake district.

Our path was set: we were going to Metzabok.

We were excited to be following these breadcrumbs, but Joel cautioned us. "Once we get out on the lake system, we can't use any motors, only canoes. The Lacandon people don't want to wake the spirits that live beneath the water." He said the lake system was massive and labyrinthine, tucked away in deep jungle. There were local legends of anacondas, and frequent sightings of crocodiles.
