Instead we sang songs whose meanings were felt more than explained, tones born from the landscapes we emerged from. This is what I had felt while playing music in the desert with Jamie, and when I had opened my mind in the psychedelic journey to remap my phantom pain away. It had felt as if I had touched the primordial source of imagination. In the hunt for Matwil, we would be searching for that source once again.

Chiapas is a truly magical part of Mexico, and the nearby city-state of Palenque, which perished in the eighth century, is uniquely important to both the Maya and Mayan archaeologists. It was there that the first fully deciphered dynastic history emerged from the glyphs, confirming that the Maya recorded real events, not just religious symbols. Beneath its ruins, researchers discovered the first large-scale Maya aqueduct system, revealing an advanced understanding of water management.

In Palenque, our research team introduced me to an archaeologist named Joel Palka. With his ponytail and rolled-up sleeves, he had a humble, gentle demeanor that belied the fact that he was one of the leading Mayanists in the world. There aren't many jobs for Mayanists, and there's not much money in it. This community of archaeologists is driven almost entirely by passion. Joel had once heard a tale of an ancient stele that had been reported down the river, sitting in someone's backyard, and went searching for it one afternoon with the excitement and confidence of a kid looking for secrets in a treasure hunt. He was focused on excavating sites dating to the earliest days of the Maya. But he'd never truly searched for the mythical origin city.

Over drinks, Joel walked me through the discovery that had made Palenque famous. In 1948, an archaeologist named Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found a hidden doorway at the top of a pyramid they called the Temple of the Inscriptions, named for the vast hieroglyphic panels covering its inner walls. "Over four years," Joel said, "his team cleared a rubble-filled stairway that plunged straight down into the heart of the pyramid. At the bottom, behind a triangular doorway, they walked into the burial chamber of K'inich Janaab Pakal, a Maya ruler who'd been dead for fourteen hundred years." The jungle pyramids, he explained, were revealed for what they truly were: not monuments of stone but cosmic tombs.

Joel's eyes lit up as he described what they found on the walls. An immense inscription of a Ceiba tree emerging from the underworld, carrying the ruler's soul to the stars above. And at the tomb's base, an enigmatic glyph deciphered decades later to mean "Matwil," an origin city where the gods were born and Mayan civilization began. The iconography described it as "The place of the Cormorants," a waterfowl the Maya believed could travel between the world of the living above the water and the underwater realm where souls emerge from and return to after death.

There were other mysterious glyphs throughout the temple complex, Joel continued, including an image of a "split mountain" next to the Mayan glyphs for "wind" or "breath." Taken together, they seemed to hint that the origin city of Matwil was in a "watery place of Cormorants" where a "breathing mountain" could be found and the gods of the Maya were born. Whatever that meant.

Joel told me of an artificial canal that ran directly underneath the burial chamber of Pakal's tomb. It was connected to a small tributary that led back to the Tulija River, and ultimately to the remote lake district of Metzabok, where he'd found scattered ruins of very early Maya activity. The indigenous Lacandon people who live there are descendants of the Maya who had moved back into that landscape in the wake of the collapse. If the mythical origin place were to be found, it seemed plausible it would be close to this lake district.

Our path was set: we were going to Metzabok.

We were excited to be following these breadcrumbs, but Joel cautioned us. "Once we get out on the lake system, we can't use any motors, only canoes. The Lacandon people don't want to wake the spirits that live beneath the water." He said the lake system was massive and labyrinthine, tucked away in deep jungle. There were local legends of anacondas, and frequent sightings of crocodiles.

I'd learned my lesson in Peru, so the first thing we did was arrange a meeting with the last living Lacandon h-men, their shaman, to ask for his blessing. My production team had met an Italian anthropologist who had moved to the jungles decades ago to build a meaningful relationship with the Lacandon community, and she agreed to bring us to the village where he resided. After an introduction, the shaman lit nine little altars with incense and began a long series of chants. Each altar was for a specific god: a god for the mountains, the sun, the waters, even one small altar for the god of the white man. "Jesucristo," he said.

He told me that everything has a soul, rocks, trees, animals, people, and that all souls are connected and share a kind of energy called k'uh. Every time a soul died, the roots of the trees carried it to the sky to become a star, and every time a tree was cut down, a star would fall. When all the trees were gone, all the stars would fall and the world would be over.

To my relief, the shaman had run out of the fermented, ritualistic liquid made from spit he would normally have us drink, but he still gave us his blessing to enter the lake district. His warning to be respectful of the spirits brought to mind the message of the shaman on the Burkhan Khaldun, and the river in Peru. Respect the old ways.

We made our way toward the lake, driving deep into the jungle. Joel had set up camp on the shore of the lake district, right in the heart of the Lacandon community. We arrived after sundown. Joel's contacts among the Lacandon people had generously set up a little settlement for the crew. They'd even built small, whitewashed, air-conditioned boxes with no windows for me and Gary to sleep in. They were beautifully well-intentioned, but stepping inside felt like checking into a miniature holding cell. Gary took one look at his and said he'd rather take his chances with the mosquitos. I ended up sharing the crew trailer with him instead. Joe, meanwhile, had packed buckets of lemon-flavored mayonnaise in his suitcase, which became the expedition's most divisive provision.

Joe and Duncan filled a hut with our LiDAR-powered drones and computers and generators, transforming it into a processing lab where they could crunch the data. Joel was ready to take us out on canoes and had asked two Lacandon guides named Kin, meaning sun, and Boor, meaning small bees, to accompany our team. I'd spent years working on my Spanish and still sounded like an idiot more than half the time, but it didn't matter here. Lacandon Maya sounded nothing like the imported language of the conquistadors. The words had a deliberate, unhurried cadence, softened with sounds that reminded me of the indigenous languages I'd heard in the American Southwest, as if the land itself shaped how people spoke on it.

We started surveying the jungle, beginning with the place where Joel had found remnants from the earliest "preclassic" Maya. We piled into canoes, following Kin and Boor onto the lake and drifting through the fog with no sound but our wooden oars sliding along our canoes as they passed through still water. Suddenly, Kin grinned and pointed through the mist at some cormorants flying through the jungle.

Upon reaching the shore, we hiked through the jungle until we reached Joel's site. It looked like a pile of rocks. But he showed us where he'd surveyed and pointed out lines he thought could be the outline of a city. Joe and Duncan sent up the drone, and as the LiDAR penetrated the foliage, we saw that Joel was right: we were standing in what had once been a city.

But that was just the beginning. Joel hypothesized that if this were truly Matwil, the Maya's legendary origin city, it would be laid out in a way that honored their cosmovision. They believed that geography was symbolically aligned with the points of the compass. The Maya saw time as existing within this sacred wheel, where certain energies, patterns, and even events could recur at different points in the cycle of birth, life, death, and rebirth, each era at once unique and a reflection of those before it.

Specific colors embodied this vision: red for the east, the rising sun, and renewal. Black for the west, the underworld, and transformation. White for the north, wisdom, and the realm of ancestors. Yellow for the south, maize, and sustenance. In the middle was green or blue, representing the sacred Ceiba tree: the cosmic axis mundi binding the heavens, earth, and underworld together.

Joel said, "Maybe we should overlay this cosmovision of existence onto the lake system itself. That might give us clues where to look for the breathing mountain."

Overhearing this, Kin said, "Yes, we have a mountain that breathes."

What?

He explained that at the center of the lake system was the Red Mountain, Chak-Aktun: the sacred mountain that breathes.

At dawn, our crew started canoeing across the lake. Our long-haired Lacandon guides whispered in their ancient dialect as they led the way. The water was utterly still and reflective; it felt as though we were floating across a plane between worlds.

We passed a limestone wall covered in ancient rock art depicting countless handprints. "When souls die, they fly back to this lake and travel through that wall into the underworld," Kin said in a blend of Lacandon Maya and Spanish that Joel interpreted.

One evening as the sun set, the team left me alone on a canoe in the middle of the lake. They paddled to the horizon and went out of sight to film the scene from a distance. I stayed standing in the mirrored water. The warm air from the day still lingered, and it was creating a fog over the lake that thickened as the light faded. Bats flew overhead. Cormorants crisscrossed the shoreline, hunting the invisible. Then the moon rose over the shoulder of the surrounding mountains and the entire lake was cast in its light, a blueish tint in every direction. The canoe rocked gently on the still mirror, and I was afraid to move, afraid to disturb the peace around me. It felt like standing in a church and not wanting to make a sound out of respect. The liminal space Joel had described in the Maya cosmovision, the plane between the living and the dead, didn't feel like a concept anymore. It felt like the water I was floating on.

For the first time I felt I was understanding not just an idea about the origin of civilization but the feeling that could give birth to one. Not something someone thought. Something a place put into them. Every once in a while some chatter would chirp through my radio from the team in the distance, jolting the air like a plate dropping in the middle of a silent temple. I turned my radio off and sat in the blue stillness.

As we neared the other end of the lake, I looked down through the mangroves and saw the roots of trees reaching up from the depths. On the other side of the lake, there was a great hollow log. Boor handed me a big stick.

"Hit this log three times to tell the mountain that we are coming," he said. He spoke of the mountain as if it were not a landmark but a living being. I hit the log and a hollow drum sound echoed across the water, shattering the stillness of the lake.

We hiked a winding trail to the top of a mountain that overlooked lakes on all sides. Boor, speaking in Lacandon, communicated that he was happy his machete was "choosing to do its work well." In his view, even a machete could have agency. At the peak was a shaman altar containing little incense burners for all the gods.

Kin brought me to a small hole on the ground off to the side of the peak. He leaned down into the opening, and as we waited, a great wind passed over us, rustling the trees and sending ripples across the lake. A few seconds later, a strong wind came bellowing back, blowing his hair back.

"See?" he said. "The mountain breathes."

The belly of the mountain was connected to a cavity, creating a giant windpipe. The "breathing mountain" was in fact a large cave system.

While we sent the LiDAR drones up to survey the terrain, I donned my climbing gear and ropes and started working with Arcelia Garcia, a Mexican archaeologist who specialized in Maya dwellings, to plan an exploration of the cave.

"The Maya believed that caves were a portal to the world of the gods," she explained. "Look for natural features that could have been locations for offerings."

I packed a small bag with the essentials, strapped on a harness and my helmet, and got ready to enter. I'd learned over the years that filming in sacred spaces can take a long time, so I also made sure I had a pee bottle hidden in my pack. There was no way I was going to use the home of the gods as a bathroom.

Together, we descended into the hole, dropping through razor-sharp limestone into the narrow passageways that would take us into the heart of the mountain. The edges of the rock seemed to protect the entrance like guards at a front gate, tearing at our clothes and skin as we squeezed through. As I rappelled into a darkness broken only by my headlamp, I was struck by fear, not of bugs or spiders, but of bats. The bugs in that environment don't have enough energy to move fast enough to pose a threat. But the fungal spores that grow on bat guano can silently infect humans, dooming them to slow and painful lung damage that could take decades to manifest. I moved as carefully as I could, lowering myself deeper into the belly of the mountain that breathed above us.

The passageways narrowed and widened and narrowed again. The air grew cooler and heavier. I could hear Arcelia's breathing behind me and the drip of water somewhere in the distance, but otherwise there was nothing. No wind, no light, no sound from the world above. We were inside the mountain now. I felt like a boy entering a sacred space, nervous that I might offend a sleeping giant. Every sound I made, every scrape of my prosthetic against the rock, felt too loud. This was the portal the Maya had carved their door for, the same threshold I had stood before in Peru with Elder. Only this time I wasn't looking at the door. I was on the other side of it.

Far beneath the hole, we entered a cavern whose ceiling was covered in so many stalactites it felt like the lid of an iron maiden, ready to slam shut at any moment. The ground beneath them was littered with debris, and when I knelt to examine it, my headlamp glinted off a tiny fragment of a ceramic pot. I called Arcelia over.

She knelt beside me and held the fragment under her light. Her hands were shaking.

"Oh my God, this is it," she said. "This particular type of ceramic, with its waxy, red-painted covering, was from the earliest days of the Maya."

That tiny fragment told a story of a ritual in the heart of the Maya mountain gods themselves. Someone had come down here, through those razor-sharp guards, carrying an offering into the darkness. We made our way back out slowly, shaking off the bat guano, blinking as the daylight hit our eyes.

We crossed the lake back to our camp. Joe and Duncan started processing the LiDAR data from the survey of the mountain. As the computers ingested all the data points to convert them into layered maps, the hum of the generator became the soundtrack of our conversation.

Finding that pottery fragment in the heart of the mountain was confirmation that early Maya activity existed beyond the site Joel had first discovered. He theorized that since the Maya built in accordance with their cosmovision, the mountain could be the axis mundi around which everything was oriented, which would mean other sites of interest at different locations, laid out on the compass with the breathing mountain at its center.

As the generators hummed and the computers crunched, we spent the next few days taking our canoes out to the banks along the edges of the lake system. At each bank, I'd grab my machete and search the undergrowth for anything worth surveying.

One of the highest mountains in the region was located near the northwest shore. We loaded our gear into canoes and hiked to the peak, where the only path forward hugged a sheer cliff face. As we shimmied precariously by, we passed a perfectly square hole carved into the wall of the cliff itself.

Joel said, "For the ancient Maya, rocks from different places had specific powers. Maybe someone carved this square out and brought it elsewhere to transmit the power of this mountain." We surveyed the peak but didn't find anything else.

By the time we returned to camp after days of searching, data was finally emerging from Joe and Duncan's lab, stripping away layers of jungle and revealing buildings that had lain undiscovered for thousands of years.

We saw that next to the breathing mountain was a large plateau we couldn't reach on foot, since that part of the jungle was covered with razor-sharp vines. On that plateau was a pyramid. But unlike every other one discovered in the Maya world, this one had three sides, not four.

"What the hell is that?" Joel said in disbelief. Then he noticed what looked like an early prototype of structures Mayanists believe to be solar observatories. Could this be the blueprint for the great observatories of Palenque?

Finally, we looked at the LiDAR map of the breathing mountain itself. When we removed all the layers of trees on the mountainside, we realized the entire mountain had been terraformed. There were indentations at specific points of elevation, as though the mountain had once been carved into a great stepped pyramid.

At this point, the expedition was near its end and we were exhausted. I'd been pricked by cactus, cut by vines and rock, and fallen ill. The team doctor, a talented, no-bullshit woman named Gio, was doing her best to keep us patched up, but she was fighting a losing battle. There was a strain that went beyond the physical, an uncanny feeling that the world of the dead lay just beyond reach.

Gio and I had become close over the course of the expedition. On the night of the full moon, as the rest of the crew went to sleep, we walked through the jungle toward the water's edge to see its reflection across the mirrored lake. She handed me a book.

"This is a very important book," she said. "I think you should read it."

I thanked her but put it in my bag without opening it.

In the final days, Joel kept pushing Joe and Duncan to run sunrise-sunset simulations of the lake system. "This entire lake system is one big solar observatory," he said. "All these buildings in the data have been laid out in a specific pattern around the breathing mountain. Let's run simulations of different days of the year to see if the path of the sun will align with that pattern." His logic made sense, but none of the dates we tried lined up.

"Try the solstice." Nothing.

"Try the equinox." Nothing.

Finally I asked if there was any other date we could try, and Joel had a eureka moment.

"Try August 13th."

Joe and Duncan plugged it in and the simulation played out before us. We saw that right as the sun set on the night of August 13th, it passed directly over the northwest point where we'd found that mysterious square carved out of the cliffside. Joel gasped.

"What happened on August 13th?" I asked.

"It's the beginning of the current 5,125-year creation cycle in the Maya calendar."

I felt the same rush of discovery I'd experienced atop the Burkhan Khaldun. This had to be it. A place where it all began.

A lifetime earlier, my first search for identity had taken me to the Burkhan Khaldun, where, watching Amaraa bow to the sky at the four compass points, it was like glimpsing the moment that mountain became the birthplace of the Mongols. Now, after passing through my own cycles of death and renewal, I found myself once again on a sacred mountain where the points of the compass held cosmic significance, and where a great civilization had been born.

Years before, on a mountain lake in China, a girl named Maya told me that long after we were gone, the mountains would remain. Much later, an Elder in Peru had told me that on the other side of that cycle, we originated from the mountains. Like the Hindu concept of Samsara, the cycle of life, death, and rebirth that Baba Lutlo had illuminated on the banks of the Ganges, the Mayan cosmovision perceived time as cyclical. The wheel turns, and the living stand where the dead once stood, and someday others will stand where we are standing now.

On the flight home, I pulled the book Gio had given me from my bag. Its cover read The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying. I turned it over in my hands, read the first few lines of the jacket, and put it back. Something in me wasn't ready. I was afraid of it in a way I couldn't explain, the way you're afraid of a door you know leads somewhere you can't come back from. I slid it into my bag and stared out the window at the Pacific, thirty thousand feet above the water that Pohaku said we all come from and return to. I didn't know yet how soon I would need it.
title: Chapter 22: The Axis Mundi

content:
Chapter 23: Shadowlight

Whenever I called, Jamie Shadowlight would show up. She'd arrive in her long fake-fur-lined sweater coat, carrying her violin, which she called Excalibur, in one hand and her pedal bag and battery-powered amplifier in the other, complaining that she needed roadies. If the kids were home they'd run out and greet her like she was a wizard. She'd tell them to bring the gear in and then gift them something random that had been gifted to her, monarch butterfly earrings, dream catchers, little talismans from people who loved her. Leo would come with his synth drums. I tried to bring home an instrument from wherever I'd been, a Syrian oud from Egypt, a Sudanese tambur, and fumble my way into their sounds. Each culture had its own tuning, as if channeling the resonant frequencies of the land it had emerged from.

One night there was a power outage and the whole city went dark. Charlie and Millie and I had just come back from a camping trip high in the Western Sierras, and the kids had smuggled a few tiny frogs from a meadow into a container hidden in the RV without telling me. Without an ecosystem that matched theirs, we'd built a terrarium to keep them alive. That night Jamie came over and taught the kids how to move the flame of a candle with their minds. One flicker and they were convinced. They ran upstairs eventually, and Jamie and I began to play.

Even without power, everything worked. We'd built our setups with the intention of playing deep in the desert, battery-powered and portable, sometimes just the two of us, sometimes with Leo. On nights like this we'd spend time searching for open tunings, not the traditional tuning of strings but rather hunting for the harmony and resonance that matched whatever moment we were in. The long echoes of her reverb would transform her violin into a whale's call, and then it would flutter up into heights that felt at first like a butterfly and then an eagle that swooped back around my melodies, which began to flow like a dance with hers. She let me realize a part of myself that could enter a true flow state, tapping into something that didn't require my mind but rather my feeling. In the dark house, with the city blacked out and the candles burning and the frogs chirping in their terrarium, we played for hours. Charlie and Millie drifted off to sleep upstairs while the sounds filled every room. I think about that sometimes. My kids grew up with this music rising through the floorboards of their home, these strange, beautiful, unexplainable sounds seeping into their dreams. Whatever Jamie and I were tapping into on those nights, they were absorbing it without trying, the way I'd absorbed my father's universe from the back rows of lecture halls. I didn't plan it. But the magic was in the house, and they grew up inside it.

Months later, the octagonal drum arrived unexpectedly from Bulgarian filmmakers who'd heard our music. Jamie had already dreamed it. She'd described it to me, the shape, the size, the sound it would make. It was only when the light caught its silhouette from behind, its tensioning strings casting a shadow across its broad body, that she realized it was the drum from her dream. From then on we began every session with that drum in my hand. She said it opened the portal. I believed her. Years later I would learn that shamanic drumming across cultures converges on roughly the same tempo, around four beats per second, which happens to match the theta brainwave frequency associated with deep meditative and trance states (ref: Hove et al., 2016). The drum wasn't just atmosphere. It was tuned to the brain's own operating frequency, and humans had figured this out thousands of years before neuroscience had a name for it. When we played, the pain of whatever I was carrying from the road stopped, and something older took its place.

On the outside, Jamie's composure was that of a great shaman, steady and knowing. But in the lab, as we called my living room, we laughed like little kids, passing a bottle of whiskey or tequila back and forth between riffs. She was a pirate in so many ways, a rebel who had cast off society's expectations in pursuit of something more pure. A wandering musician who valued freedom over everything. She was my spirit twin.

But one week after I returned from Mexico, her text wasn't an invitation to grab our instruments and open the portal.

"I just came back from the doctor," her message read. "They found a tumor. I have six months to live." She was forty-seven years old.

The news hit like a physical blow, literally knocking me to my knees. I was frozen in the doorway, staring at the text in disbelief, then screaming into the phone. Life had been moving so fast. The last time we had really spent quality time together was nearly a year before, on my birthday. We'd found a secret dried lake bed in the desert by scouring satellite imagery and BLM maps, and driven out with a small group of friends and the kids. We played music until the sun rose, Charlie and Millie singing into delay-heavy mics, barefoot on the cracked ancient mud. As the winds picked up that night, Jamie sat around the campfire and held the group with her violin harmonies, which sounded like ancient whales flying over the ancient lake. She was so vibrant then. How could this be happening now?

I called Eoin, who had flown in from London to direct the voiceover recordings for the season we'd just filmed. He understood immediately and canceled the studio slot. Shortly after, I walked through the doors of the hospital where my children had been born and my leg had been removed.

Dozens of Jamie's friends surrounded her bed in a simple hospital room, overflowing into the hallway. She was in a hospital gown. When she saw me, she called me over and was blunt. "They said I'm dying." She looked scared but fierce, a cornered warrior making her stand. In that moment I resolved to help her navigate what was to come, just as she had helped me in my own battles.

And so a new kind of journey began. A juggling act of doctor appointments and emergency room visits against a backdrop of frequent moments of synchronicity and beauty. She was a pure musician who had never given value to money, yet donations and food flowed in from the community that cherished her. The love was profound but overwhelming, pouring in like a waterfall. By default, I became the primary coordinator, much as Bruna had done for me years before, but I wasn't alone. Michelle offered her home on the cliffs overlooking the Pacific as the staging ground for the fight. The cliffs felt timeless, and the house was a Spanish-style home filled with artifacts from around the world — ritual masks, drums, feathered dresses. An entire garden was dedicated to organic fruits and vegetables that we'd pick straight from the earth. Jamie didn't have a place to live once she could no longer gig for rent, and we needed somewhere large enough for her community to flow in and out of. Michelle's place was just that, and her dog, which had been dyed like a swirled rainbow candy cane, would wander in at the most intense moments and plop down on Jamie's feet, breaking whatever tension the room was holding.

Santiago, a Colombian guitarist, became my right hand through the hardest stretches. He was all passion and loved Jamie like a sister. We called ourselves the guardians of the temple. Even in the ICU, exhausted beyond reason, he'd hit on a doctor as she walked through the ER, and when she gently rejected him he asked her for warm blankets. But beneath the charm he was steady and thoughtful, a person of deep conviction, and I needed that as I began making decisions at a life-and-death scale for Jamie when she could no longer find the words to articulate what she wanted. Others brought instruments and played with an authenticity and beauty that Jamie appreciated more than anyone. When I needed to travel, or on my weeks with the kids, the tribe jumped in. It was hard. It was a year and a half of hard. But there was beauty and magic and humor woven through it, and the community that gathered around Jamie was as much a part of her healing as any medicine.

Inspired by her will and determination, we chose to believe in the fight. We tried to find foods that could help her body resist the transformation, oils and tinctures she would rub into her skin. But she always returned to sound. I would carry her singing bowls into the infusion centers, awkwardly explaining to the doctors that we needed to resonate the medicine first, per her command. They'd look at me and I'd shrug. She had always been someone I admired, but now I followed her around in awe, a dutiful attendant to a powerful queen. She moved through the world in those final months like a demigod, and I doted along behind her, racing to make sure everything was as good as it could be. Music, resonance, harmony through gongs and tuning forks merged with infusions and IV drips in her room. When she had strength, we would walk down to the cliff's edge overlooking the Pacific and sit staring out at the horizon. She was fierce in her determination to live every second to its fullest, even as her body began to wither away. It seemed as if the weaker her physical form became, the stronger her spirit grew.

There were long nights when she dipped in and out of hospice and I sat by her side. They gave me a pamphlet about what to expect. It read clinical, stages of decline laid out in medical language, but as I turned the pages I realized it mirrored what I'd been reading in the Tibetan Book of Living and Dying. The same progression, the same thresholds, described in different vocabularies separated by centuries. It seemed to me that all cultures, all philosophies, all religions had been formed around this same experience, the one thing every human being will go through. The pamphlet and the ancient text were both guidebooks for the same journey.

But there were moments where reality forced unwanted reckonings. At first I resisted. I kept telling myself, you must bend the spoon by truly believing the spoon is bent, drawing on the lessons of my own battle with phantom limb pain. But over the course of that long year, Jamie dipped toward the edge so many times that my refusal to contemplate her death began to waver.

It was in those moments that she began having conversations with beings invisible to me but very real to her. Musicians coming to play music. Her mother, who'd died before they could reconcile. Whether these were chemical reactions of a brain in delirium or the veil between realms truly thinning, I don't know. But she was tiptoeing between here and the beyond. I watched as she worked through the various aspects of an unfinished life, letting go of feelings left unsaid. Then one night, even though we had only ever been like family, she held a wedding for us, with the invisible spirits as our only witnesses. I thought of the large painting that hung in the atrium of where she was staying, a portrait of a family of Mongolian reindeer herders that felt like a haunting window into a past life we may have shared. And now, in this life, we were bonded right as I was about to lose her back to the other side.

I told myself I should be prepared for this. Everything I'd seen and lost should have made me ready. But still, it was scary. Death is scary.

Finally, a year after it was given to me on the eerie, fog-covered lake of the Maya jungle, I opened the Tibetan Book of Living and Dying and began to read it to Jamie as she dozed in and out of consciousness. The ancient Tibetan knowledge keepers had mapped the terrain of existence with almost scientific precision, and its pages read like a guidebook. I would alternate with passages from the other book of my life, Siddhartha, which had been handed to me on a lake in the shadow of a great mountain. I had read it many times, but now it assumed a far greater significance. Jamie told me that Siddhartha had been her father's favorite book. She had loved him dearly. The word "Ohm," which had ferried me from the wreckage of my accident to the banks of the Ganges, now soothed us both.

Everything felt connected. Even the cliffside estate that had become the basecamp for her journey was tied to what I was experiencing. Years ago, on that very same ocean bluff, archaeologists had discovered the intentional burial of a nine-thousand-year-old couple. As I walked the grounds with Jamie through the seasons of a year and we looked out over the ocean, I couldn't shake the feeling that we had slipped into a dream that tied the ancient past to the present and future. Synchronicities abounded, and as we watched whales breach in the shoreline waters, Jamie would smile and laugh at all the magic she saw around her.

I can't claim to know what happens before or after life. But sitting with Jamie through those long nights, I kept thinking about all the cultures I'd encountered that had arrived at something similar — this sense of a cyclical rhythm to existence, where death is not an ending but a return. I didn't know if I believed it. But I took comfort in it as I watched it unfold before me.

While Jamie's body grew weaker by the day, her internal power seemed to grow. She started living only by her stage name, Shadowlight, her physical form fading away with the name she'd been given at birth. She refused to stop creating music, even as her body failed her. One day, when the exhaustion was visible in every line of her face, she held our octagonal hand drum in the air and began to sing. It felt primordial, like the low drumbeat I'd heard years ago beneath Mongolia's sacred mountain. As she reached the crescendo, sunlight filtered through a prism on her window, casting a rainbow over her.

She looked at me and smiled. "It's fun, you know? All of it."

I laughed. "Yeah. But why is it that the hardest moments often bring the best memories?"

"Because when you have no options left, all that's left is your imagination. And in that space, everything can be magic."

On June 6th, 2024, Shadowlight transitioned into the beyond. It happened in the soft glow of the morning light, on the mesa overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The boundaries between life and death dissolved. The light in the room felt thicker, like you could mold it with your hands. The words of the last song she sang to me kept playing in my head.

Together we'll dance across the universe.

There was a giant stillness for a time. I returned to Charlie and Millie first. They had been waiting for me patiently through a year and a half of this battle, but it had been hard on them too. At one point Millie had said she was so sad that Jamie was dying, but that they were still alive and needed me too. She was right, and hearing it from my eleven-year-old daughter cut deeper than anything.

After eighteen months of fighting alongside Jamie, I was bewildered and exhausted. But there was also a sense of magic everywhere, as if the thick light I'd felt in the room when she passed continued to hang in the air in the days and weeks that followed. I couldn't explain it. The world looked the same but it didn't feel the same. Something had opened and hadn't closed back.
title: Chapter 23: Shadowlight

content:
Chapter 24: Dancing Across the Universe

Then I was invited to climb Mount Cayambe in Ecuador. As the furthest point from the Earth's axis of rotation, it's the fastest-moving location on the planet. It would be the tenth annual fundraising climb with the Range of Motion Project, an organization providing prosthetics to those in need. In Guatemala, where I'd regained my mobility after being fitted for my own prosthetic, I'd watched an amputee on the street because he didn't have that same opportunity. This climb would provide a chance to fight that injustice.

But I also had a quieter motivation. In my state of mourning, I hoped to scatter Shadowlight's ashes at the summit, where she could dance faster than anyone else through the cosmos.

The organization paired me with a climbing partner: a twenty-year-old indigenous Ecuadorian amputee named Carlos Garcia who, thanks to their efforts, had been fitted with a prosthetic earlier that year. He didn't own a phone, so we were only able to talk once before the day of the climb. But I learned he'd grown up in a remote part of Ecuador, had lost his leg at sixteen in a car accident just as I had, and had lived on crutches for the three years that followed until ROMP helped get him a leg.

We couldn't have come from more different worlds, but very shortly we'd climb together to the top of the planet.

As I learned more about the mountains of Ecuador, I read about Alexander von Humboldt, a nineteenth-century explorer who'd reached the top of a peak called Chimborazo, not far from Cayambe. There, he saw a world that was truly interconnected, where the smallest gust of wind on the coast would affect the peaks of a nineteen-thousand-foot volcano, cascading onto the rainforest below, demonstrating what we know today as an ecosystem. Two hundred years later, I was about to climb that same range with Shadowlight's ashes, searching for that same interconnectedness at the peak.

On September 24th, 2024, a few days before I set out, I celebrated my eighth birthday. Not the anniversary of my birth but the date I lost my leg and was reborn. My leg-o-versary. I held Charlie and Millie tight that day, grateful for the life we had been given together. They'd grown into their own people. Millie could ground me with her determined power and dry wit, and Charlie had a joyful wisdom beyond his age, but the bond we shared felt more enduring than anything I'd encountered in my explorations.

When I arrived at the ROMP headquarters in Quito, I finally met Carlos in person. He was soft-spoken, but his smile was infectious. When we hugged, it felt like we'd known each other far longer than a few months.

Prosthetic feet lined the shelves, each destined to change someone's life thanks to our upcoming fundraising climb. On the wall opposite those shelves was a mural of a tree composed of the painted thumbprints of everyone involved with this effort. The clinic workers asked me to paint my thumb and add my print to the wall.

As I pressed my thumb against the paint and then against the wall, I was reminded of a story I'd read about a cave in Borneo. Archaeologists had discovered a thirty-one-thousand-year-old skeleton within. Analysis revealed that it belonged to a boy whose leg had been amputated below the knee, just like mine had. It was the oldest medical operation in the human record. Remarkably, there was bone growth indicating the young amputee lived for many years after the loss of his leg. Someone had cared for him. A community had chosen to keep this child alive when they didn't have to, thirty-one thousand years before prosthetics, before medicine, before writing, before cities.

Nearby caves held hundreds of ancient painted handprints, likely made by those who cared for him. I looked at my thumbprint on the wall, still wet, and I thought of those handprints in Borneo. I thought of the handprints in the Joshua Tree cave and on the limestone wall at Metzabok where Kin said souls fly back to the underworld. The same gesture, repeated across thirty-one millennia. We were here. We cared.

I thought of the amputee in the Guatemalan village, balancing on worn crutches while I walked past on carbon fiber. I thought of the man begging near the base of Cayambe, eight years on crutches because no one had helped him. Ninety-five percent of amputees in the world will never receive a prosthetic. But thirty-one thousand years ago, before cities, before writing, before agriculture, a community in a cave chose to care for a child who had lost a limb. They didn't have to. Nothing about survival required it. They chose to. That was the oldest story in the human record. Not conquest, not war, not the building of monuments. Care. The choice to help someone who cannot help themselves. That was what made us human then, and it was what the thumbprints on this clinic wall were trying to do now.

As we acclimatized, Carlos and I developed a close bond. We bought matching alpaca wool jackets in a local market and wore them everywhere. I came to see him as a little brother. Even the name "Carlos" was the Spanish translation of my own son's name, Charlie. As I helped him prepare for the ascent, he helped me improve my Spanish.

We met the other climbers, who apart from our local guides were mostly amputees from around the globe. One had survived a mass shooting in Aurora. Several had lost their limbs in car accidents. There were war veterans and Paralympians. The founder of ROMP, Dave Krupa, was an amputee himself. I'd never been around a group like that before. As we prepared for the summit, we opened up to each other, sharing our stories of how we'd come to be there and why we were climbing. After the accident, I'd forced myself to adopt a mindset of absolute positivity. But among this community, and after all that had transpired with Shadowlight, that stance was morphing into something more honest.

Ten days later, we drove to the base of Cayambe. The plan was to travel by vehicle to a mountaineer's refuge at sixteen thousand feet, then stage our climb over a few days. As our caravan approached the village at the foothills, we passed an amputee begging on the streets. He was stunned as our crew of amputee athletes jumped out to greet him, asking for his contact information so we could help get him a new leg. He'd been begging on crutches for eight years, unable to work. For most of us, it was a reminder of why we were climbing. For Carlos, it was like looking in a mirror.

We drove into the clouds until the buses could go no further, then transferred into smaller trucks. As we piled out, Johnny Harrington sent a drone up for aerial footage, but it suddenly tumbled from the sky. On recovering it, we realized it had crossed the 0.000 latitude line marking the equator, and the shift in the Earth's magnetic poles had scrambled its systems. Marveling at the invisible but very real divide between North and South, we heard the cries of Andean condors circling above us.

Carlos and I jumped into the back of a truck, and as we drove to the refuge I pulled out my guitar and started singing. We made up a song, Dos Hermanos Estas Muy Loco, two crazy brothers. But as we passed the treeline and rose above the clouds, the mood changed, and our silly song shifted to something more emotional.

The truck reached its stopping point at the base of the glacier. We jumped out to gaze at the peak, unobscured by clouds. As I stared at the impossibly massive glacier reflecting the sun like a lighthouse beacon, all my emotions came pouring out. Something about the grandeur of the mountain shattered whatever walls I'd built up, and in its presence I started weeping. I cried for Jamie, for Gil, for the part of me I'd lost in the accident and all that I had received in return, for all who had donated to help amputees they would never meet, for the love I had felt as Jamie took her final breaths, and for the beauty of the world I was part of.

When I looked over at Carlos, I saw he was weeping too. A year ago he'd been on crutches and had never seen snow, and now he stood on two legs, breathing thin mountain air near the top of the world. We didn't say anything. Our language barrier had made much of our communication physical, and in that moment we didn't need anything other than each other's embrace. We wiped our tears and made our way to the stone cabin with its bunk beds and battered windows.

We huddled there for several days, letting our bodies acclimate, venturing out to practice glacier climbing with crampons and ice axes, singing along to my guitar each night, reading notes of encouragement from those who had come before us on prior climbs.

On the day the climb was due to begin, Dave gave a speech about the very first ROMP climb, ten years before. That group had trained and waited just as we had. But the night of the climb, a huge storm came through, stopping them in their tracks. What mattered, he said, was that they were all together.

We were slated to begin at ten that night, since the glacier becomes unstable under high sun. After a restless nap we woke at nine, ate our dinner and filled our water bottles. But just as we sent our last messages via satellite phone, the weather turned. The wind started pounding the windows as seventy-mile-per-hour gusts rattled the small stone building. We delayed. The hours ticked by. I checked my bag to make sure Shadowlight's ashes were there.

The storm kept growing stronger. Carlos, Dave, and I waited in that little room. Around midnight, two hours past our departure time, one of the Andean guides came in. "Guys, come on down. We're going to have a team meeting."

They had climbed partway up to check conditions. The winds were overwhelming and the snow was wet. The summit attempt was off. We'd reassess at three in the morning.

Stunned silence. But I thought about Dave's speech. What matters is we're all together. I grabbed my guitar, and as the storm howled through the chimney, we started singing Lean on Me. The lights blinked on and off and windows rattled, but we sang on.

Lean on me, when you're not strong. I'll be your friend. I'll help you carry on.

Around three in the morning, I woke to use the bathroom and stepped outside. The wind wasn't howling anymore. The stars were out. The storm had passed entirely.

Half an hour later, we were climbing up the rocky escarpments. The cold was bitter, the darkness absolute. Then dawn's first light peeked over the horizon, and we saw that the storm had laid a pristine blanket of snow across the mountain. In the distance, the peaks of Cotopaxi and Chimborazo rose out of the clouds.

As we climbed straight up the side of the volcano, I heard Carlos whispering a mantra with every footstep. Si se puede, si se puede, si se puede. Yes, I can. Yes, I can. Yes, I can.

I was at the front of the rope line, eager to reach the summit before the sun got too high. But our guide pulled up short, concerned by a vast wind drift. He started digging to see what lay beneath. Sheets of ice layered beneath heavy blankets of powder. Avalanche risk. We tried another direction. More of the same.

We all looked at each other. The golden rule of climbing is that you must respect the mountain. The mountains will be here long after we're gone. They were there after Gil died, and they'd still be here if we all perished in an avalanche. We had climbed as high as we could.

But any disappointment disappeared when I looked at Carlos. He pulled a feather from his pack, held it up to the sky and said, "Who needs legs when you can fly?"

I took Shadowlight's ashes from my pack and scattered them into the wind. For a moment, we danced together across the universe, higher and faster than anyone else on earth. Then she was swept away, to become part of the vast ecosystem that stretched out below us.

We made our way down the steepest part to a flat. As the team pulled out food to snack on, a snowball from Dave smacked Carlos in the side of the head. He looked shocked for a second, then started laughing. He grabbed a fistful of snow and threw it back. Then I joined in, and so did Dave and all the others: a massive, joyful snowball fight on the side of a glacier at seventeen thousand feet.

Afterward, as we descended, we looked back and saw that right where we had cut off our climb, an avalanche had rumbled down from the peak. We'd made the right call.

Hours later, we reached the trucks and drove toward the foothills. We stopped at the equatorial line and everybody jumped out to take a photo. Right before the flash, a big guy from Colorado who'd lost both legs in combat called out for everyone to turn around. We pulled our pants down and mooned the camera.

As we milled about, everyone drifting back toward the trucks, an older Ecuadorian man from the refuge walked straight toward me. He looked weathered, worn down in the way of mountain people. He was holding an intricately patterned mask with two faces. I thought he was trying to sell it.

"I don't have any money on me," I said in clumsy Spanish.

"No, no. For you," he said, placing it into my hands.

"Why are you giving this to me?"

He pointed up to the mountain. "Recuerda." Remember the mountain.

Then he walked away without asking for anything. Not even a photo. The night before, I'd told my crew to leave the satellite link we'd brought for the community to use as a resource. Maybe he'd seen that. I rejoined the group and asked our Ecuadorian drivers what I'd been given.

"It's the Diablo Huma," one said, making a funny face. "The two-faced ghost!"

Carlos corrected him. "No, that's what the Catholic conquistadors renamed it. Its real name is Aya Huma." Aya, he explained, meant spirit in the indigenous Quechua language, and Huma meant guide. The mask was a spiritual symbol from the earliest cultures of the land, the heart of Andean cosmology. Its colors represented the full spectrum of existence, and the faces on each side represented the duality of all things: good and bad, past and future, shadow and light.

I thought of Jamie.

The Aya Huma is seen as a protector in life's rites of passage, a guide whose whip reminds us that life is a dance through dualities, always in balance with the living earth.

On the flight home, I held the mask in my lap and thought about Carlos pulling that feather from his pack. Who needs legs when you can fly? I thought about the thumbprints on the clinic wall and the handprints in Borneo, thirty-one thousand years apart, saying the same thing. We were here. We cared. I thought about Jamie holding the octagonal drum above her head with the last of her strength, a rainbow cast across her face, telling me that when you have no options left, all that's left is your imagination, and in that space, everything can be magic.

I thought about my children, who I'd be shooting arrows and cheering for at softball games within hours of landing. My love for them had long become the most primal rhythm of my life. They were transforming as well, entering into the flow of their own lives, each with their own challenges and triumphs ahead of them. Challenges I couldn't yet imagine.

And I thought about the mask in my hands, the spirit that watches over us as we stumble from light into shadow and back again. The two faces, looking in both directions at once. Shadow and light. One face looking forward, one face looking back.

The plane crossed the equator, and the world kept spinning beneath us.
title: Chapter 24: Dancing Across the Universe

content:
Chapter 25: The Boy and the Butterfly

I was in the Field Museum when the phone rang. I'd gone there to prepare my mind for an expedition to Borneo, where a team had found the remains of a 31,000-year-old child in a cave among some of the oldest rock art on earth. A boy whose leg had been amputated below the knee, just like mine. The researchers called him TEBO1. The oldest evidence of care in the human record. His bones showed years of healing, meaning people had kept him alive, fed him, carried him, chosen his survival when letting him go would have been easier. Around the burial were hand-print stencils pressed into stone by the people who made that choice.

No one really knows what our mindset was like thirty-one thousand years ago, so I was wandering the Pacific exhibits, looking at old outrigger canoes and a video of a ceremony where they deactivated a canoe by taking it apart, the belief being that the canoe itself was alive and had a spirit. I was trying to imagine what it was, at the dawn of our species, that made that choice possible. Whether care was something we invented along the way, or whether it was part of us from the start, woven into whatever it is that chose existence over emptiness.

I was inside that thought when Deena called.

Nervously calm. Charlie was with ski patrol. Did he have any allergies? She was going to the mountain now and would call back in moments. The phone hung up and I sat convincing myself that it was likely nothing. A sprained wrist maybe.

Then the phone rang again. A much more urgent Deena handed me to the patroller. "All I can tell you at this time is he's breathing and has a pulse."

---

When I was eight years old the earth moved and I learned that the ground is not solid. When I was seventeen my father left and I learned that not even my foundations were permanent. When I was thirty-five a vehicle rolled and I learned that the body is not mine to keep. Each time something was taken, and each time what replaced it was larger than what was lost, though it never felt that way at first. The larger thing came later, and always from a direction I wasn't looking.

My father used to explain, in the language of astrophysics, that in the first moments after the Big Bang, nearly equal amounts of matter and antimatter collided and destroyed each other. For every billion particles that annihilated, one extra particle of matter survived. From that tiny surplus, that sliver of something over nothing, everything that exists was born. Stars, oceans, civilizations, music, the particular shape of my son's grin. All of it, from an imbalance so small it shouldn't have mattered.

I carried that idea for decades without understanding it. It sounded like science. It turned out to be the truest thing anyone ever told me.

That winter, Charlie and I drove the 395 every Friday night. Nine hours north through the dark, past the hot springs and dry lake beds, into the mountains. He'd ski with his Mammoth Mountain freeride team, something he'd worked tirelessly to join. Every other weekend Millie would join. Her passion was ice skating and she would spend hours at the mountain's rink. I'd drop them off and find a stretch of the Owens River and wade in alone.

Shadowlight had died months before. The world had gone quiet, not empty but resonant, like the pause between movements in a piece of music that's still vibrating with what just ended. I kept feeling her in synchronicities I couldn't explain and had stopped trying to, as if she hadn't vanished but changed state. The Aya Huma mask hung on my wall at home, its two faces looking in opposite directions, one forward, one back, both belonging to the same head.

The river carried whatever I brought to it. I watched the winter arrive and peak and fade in the movement of the water, as the spawn came and went and the bug hatches turned with the weeks. Long ago Gordo had taught me to read a river. Now it felt like the river was reading me.

Charlie and I talked on those drives, about the things that surface when the road is dark and there's nowhere else to be. One night he asked what I thought happened after we die. I told him about sitting with Jamie in her final months, how I'd read to her from the Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, about the stillness between thoughts and what it might open into. She'd been focused on healing, not dying, so those readings were rare and hard. But after she passed, I kept feeling her, as if she'd merged back into the fabric of everything and was somehow orchestrating little moments of magic to let us know she was good.

"I've noticed that too," Charlie said quietly.

He asked what I thought about reincarnation. I told him what I'd learned in Varanasi, that the rituals on the Ganges were designed to release you from the cycle entirely, to skip straight to nirvana. He looked out the window for a long time. The headlights of oncoming cars washed over his face and disappeared.

Then he said he understood that as a concept, but he liked living so much, why would you skip the cycle if you liked being in it?

He was fourteen. He spoke with a steadiness that made me forget his age.

The week before his accident was the best week of the year. Miracle March, late-season storms, the mountains buried in powder. We chased first tracks before dawn. Then I left for Chicago, and Charlie stayed with his teammate Piper wanting to squeeze the last ounces of winter for the last snowflakes before the seasons changed. Piper's mother Deena was baking cookies with them the night before his own journey would begin.
---

Cold Chicago air. A taxi. The hairs on the back of my neck. Then the call from the life flight, and through the phone the mechanical rhythm of a ventilator breathing for my son, the beep of his heart monitor. My mind went through the phone and I was there with him, seeing the stretcher, the tubes, the aircraft. A thousand miles between us and no distance at all.

I had held the bones of the dead across the world. I had chanted over the dying. I had lost my own leg and rebuilt myself from what was left. None of it could protect me from that sound, the most brutal call of my life.

What I found in Reno was a manufactured sky, tiny lights on a blue ceiling designed to soothe injured brains, and beneath it my boy. Tubes, bandages, a pressure bolt in his skull. Piper holding his hand, having been first to reach him on the mountain. Kara there too, divorced a decade, but in that room just his parents, holding each other, shaking. The doctors' words. Brain bleeds. Coma. Diffuse axonal injury. Severe traumatic brain injury.

I looked at him and wondered if what made him him was still in there.

And I recognized, with a familiarity that was almost unbearable, that the wheel had turned again. The ground had shifted. Something was being destroyed, and something was about to be created from the wreckage, but only if something held. Only if whatever tips the balance toward life over absence, love over entropy, was strong enough to carry him through.

I got to work. In the days that followed, Kara and I found a unity that surprised us both. She cleaned his nails and picked adhesive from his hair while I argued with nurses about circadian rhythms, and frantically researched medications and protocols, desperate for any sense of control. Whatever had separated us as partners, this bond needed nothing else attached to it. We were different kinds of caregivers, and our son needed both.

Johnny Harrington had moved into the house just weeks before the accident, after a breakup with his girlfriend. The night it happened we went out and bought a cheap sleeper couch and set it up in the guest room that had already been half recording studio, half storage. He was pretty depressed. It had been his girlfriend of seven years. But this wasn't new for the house. There were always friends staying for extended stretches, and it added to the spice of life. Along with Johnny came his fishing rods, his surfboards, and all his camera gear, piled in the corners like he was setting up a base camp. I knew from my own experience that the best chapters often start from the hardest ones, and I had a feeling this was going to be great.

Instead he found himself helping me carry Charlie up and down the stairs when we brought him home, holding his weight on the landings, steady and uncomplaining, the same quiet loyalty he'd shown bobbing in the cold water off the North Shore. He didn't ask what was needed. He just did it. Over the weeks and months that followed, Johnny became like a brother to me and an uncle to the kids. He was one of the handprints on the cave wall. But he wasn't the only one. Deena and her daughter Piper, who had been there since the mountain, Piper holding Charlie's hand and Deena counting him down from ten. Owen, his teammate, who never stopped showing up. Kara and her partner Diana, who held the other half of his world together. Rich and Katrina and Pearl, the neighbors who had been family since before the kids could walk. Derek and Qasim, my brothers, who dropped everything and came. Each of them chose to be there when they didn't have to be. Thirty-one thousand years ago, a community kept a child alive. Here was the same instinct, the same choice, playing out in a house in San Diego with a cracked guitar and photos taped to the walls.
title: Chapter 25: The Boy and the Butterfly

content:
Chapter 26: The Protocol

We built the only thing we could, the environment his brain would wake up into. We silenced the monitor alarms inside his room, routing them outside. I fought to protect his sleep, pushing back each time they wanted to wake him for 3 AM assessments to scream "can you hear me!" at his blank face. His circadian rhythm had shattered along with everything else, and I knew from the neuroscience and from the nomads that the body heals in cycles of dark and light, not under permanent fluorescence. Each morning I opened the curtains and let the desert sunrise fill the room. Each night I sat beside him in the dark, staring up at a single painting on the wall of a wolf looking up at the moon.

I slept in that chair every night. I hadn't known I was going on this journey, and the only clothes I had were what I'd packed for a two-day trip to Chicago. As the days stretched into weeks, I researched each day's micro-progressions through the darkness, synthesizing everything I could find, then when the attending physicians made their morning rounds I'd meet them in the hallway in the same clothes I'd been wearing for three days and deliver a full briefing of what had happened overnight and what I wanted to adjust. Surprisingly, they accommodated me. I wasn't going to be passive about this. But as the routine continued, my clothes began to smell and I looked increasingly like someone who should be a patient, not an advocate. I didn't want my son's first real memories of his rebirth to be that his father stunk. I would have to do something about that.

He came back in layers, and each layer taught me something I had spent my life approaching from the outside.

The body first. Days of nothing, then a finger. The body holds maps the conscious mind has lost. I knew that from my own phantom limb. Now I watched my son's body feel for its own edges in the dark.

Then imagination. Deena, eight national cross-country titles, an Olympic bronze, a career built on the principle that the mind enters a reality before the body follows, sat alone with my unconscious son and counted him down from ten. Through the Mammoth Mountain Inn, out into the snow, all the way to one. She asked him to pick up a handful of snow and bring it to his lips. Charlie's lips moved. His brain was shattered and he could imagine. Imagination wasn't some higher function that arrives after the basics are restored. It was the deepest layer, the one that was there before language, before motor control, before memory. It was the capacity that every culture I'd ever explored had built their temples and their drums and their ceremonies to access. And it had survived the catastrophe because it is the most fundamental thing we have. The power to step into a reality that doesn't yet exist was alive in my son before he could open his eyes.

Then care. I called out to the world, not for sympathy but for visualization. Picture him whole. Baba Lutlo called from the Ganges, Pohaku from the North Shore, the Dalai Lama sent mantras, a goat was slaughtered in Pakistan. The light in the room thickened with something I could feel but not measure. Charlie would later tell me he felt it in the coma. The love reached him.

I hung photos and messages on every wall until the room looked like a cave, its surfaces covered with the marks of the people who refused to let go. I hadn't planned to reenact something thirty-one thousand years old. But there I was, pressing images to walls in the dark, doing exactly what had been done in Borneo around the body of a child someone chose to keep alive. The instinct was older than language. It was the oldest thing we do. The thing that builds everything.

Deena and Piper drove me to a place I'd found online in Reno — not so much a store as someone's home that had turned into a music shop and thrift store. An old man with a long white beard sat on the front porch to welcome us in. It was the first time I'd left the hospital since it all started, and stepping out of that vortex into a world that was not in a state of emergency was honestly strange. We walked through a collection of old guitars. There was a beautiful one covered in inlays, but something about an old cracked one sounded deeper. Piper pointed to it. "That one," she said. I agreed. The guitar played more beautifully than any I'd held, as if the fractures were what gave it its voice. The strap was white Lakota buffalo leather, and holding it I felt Jamie reaching through. I played softly through the pain next to him, wondering if he could hear the sound of my melodies.

They wanted to restrain his arms at night. I refused. A brain this open would absorb whatever surrounded it. I would not let fear be the first thing written into his new life.

Then breath.

The first attempt to take him off the ventilator failed. Thirty minutes in, his lungs couldn't sustain it on their own and the machine kicked back on. We stood listening to the mechanical rhythm resume and I felt something in me threaten to give way entirely.

The next day we try again.

Piper is at his hand. Kara at his foot. Deena against the wall, doing what she does, sending what she calls a beam of light. I stand next to his head. I don't plan it. I just start chanting. The same sound Bruna chanted over me in the dirt. The sound I chanted over Jamie as she crossed the threshold. Now over my son, as he fights his way back through the same door, moving in the opposite direction. Toward life.

Ohm. Ohm. Ohm.

His body struggles. We hold our positions, each of us doing whatever we are called to do. Minutes pass. Then his breathing begins to change. The rigid cadence of the machine softens into something uneven and imperfect and unmistakably his own. His lungs, remembering what they were made for.

An hour passes. Nobody moves. Nobody speaks except me. We stand where we are, in the positions we chose, as if leaving them would break whatever is happening. I keep chanting, whispering to him between the Ohms that he is a phoenix, that this is his rebirth, that everything on the other side is waiting for him if he is ready. The doctors come in and sit him up. I hold my breath as they reach for the tube. What comes next is violent and holy in equal measure. Fluids and bile erupt from him as the tube slides from his throat. His body convulses with the first unassisted coughs, raw and guttural, the sounds of a body reclaiming itself. I have witnessed three births in my life, my two children and a camel I helped deliver years before. This is the fourth. Not a gentle arrival. A rupture. The boundary between one existence and another torn open by force, and on the other side of it, something breathing that was not breathing on its own moments before.

His eyes open. The room is full of alarms and voices and the bustle of nurses adjusting monitors. Through all of it, they ask him to try to move his hand.

His thumb goes up. Barely. Unmistakably a thumbs up.

Piper grabs Kara's arm. Deena drops her head. I hear someone behind me exhale for what sounds like the first time in an hour.

Even now. Even with a brain shattered across every axis, still unable to speak or see clearly or remember his own name. His first act in this new life is to tell us it is going to be OK.

"You're the guy with the backpack. Derek."

That's what he said when they asked who I was. I told him I was Albert, his father. He raised his eyebrows, his only expression, before he fell back to sleep.

I didn't make it to the hospital garden before the sobs overtook me. I stood in the hedges and cried the hardest I had cried in my life. My son didn't know my face. What could be worse.

But he kept coming back. Each day a little more. For weeks, his eyebrows were his primary language, two tufts of hair bouncing up and down. It was how he said yes, how he said I'm here, how he told you he understood before his words came back. A little wave of approval from above his eyes.

He scanned the photos on the walls for hours. He asked questions so basic they were almost primordial, why is he washing his hands, as if encountering the mechanics of existence for the first time. I watched him and saw the story of humanity I'd spent my career trying to understand. My son was meeting the world the way we must have as a whole. Without assumptions. Without a map.

The doctors warned us to expect anger. But from his first conscious moment, Charlie kissed the nurses on the forehead. Even paralyzed on one side, seeing double, his deepest layer was gratitude and care. As if the injury had stripped away everything acquired and what remained was the foundation itself.

The first time he said anything about where he'd been, he still only had a handful of words. Just that he'd seen a ton of light. And a feeling he called "stoke." Then he passed back out.

It wasn't until weeks later, as the connections in his brain slowly re-emerged, that more came. A white void. A park bench to his front and right that felt like part of his own skin. Brightness that wasn't coming from anywhere, just present. And a feeling he struggled to name, not a love between things, but the love that things are made of.

He told me this in a hospital gown, the way he'd tell me about a dream. No weight to it. Just what he saw.

I didn't say much. I went back and read my own account of the moments under anesthesia when they cut my leg away, the avalanche of chaos resolving into something I could only describe as an embrace from the universe itself. We had used almost the same words. We had been to the same place. And what we found there, independently, without consulting each other or any tradition or any text, was that in the vast chaos of everything, there is something that holds. Something slightly stronger than the destruction. Not by much. But enough. And it makes everything.

As the feeding tube was removed, then came the food. I was obsessed with feeding him the right things for a rebuilding brain, the same instinct that had led me to struggle with chicken legs on a camping grill years before while Millie caught her first fish, the same instinct that had me sneaking iodized salt into Kara's food when she was pregnant. Deena and I filled shopping carts at a local organic market with blueberries, nuts, yogurt, cod liver oil, and mountains of salmon. Salmon for breakfast. Salmon for lunch. Salmon for dinner. More salmon. An old cleaning lady surveyed our supplies and nodded. "This is the good stuff," she said. "The stuff her mother would give them."

At first Charlie's brain couldn't register when he was full. The wires for satiation didn't work yet. So he ate and ate and ate, and I kept feeding him more omega-3s and blueberries and cod liver oil. One day he turned to me, confused, and said he didn't know why his belly was so big and that his skin was burning. It was stretching. Months later, back in San Diego, he walked into a poke bowl shop. The woman behind the counter asked what he wanted. He looked her dead in the eye and said, "Absolutely no salmon."

"Passion is life," he told me one afternoon, barely able to get the words out. Then slept. He'd given himself his own mantra.

When Millie arrived she walked in like nothing was wrong, the kind of denial that is also strength. She and Charlie had traveled between two homes their whole lives, each other's fixed point through every upheaval. That night she called me sobbing from the room at the Ronald McDonald house where she and Kara were staying while I slept in the hospital. The next morning she was at his side feeding him salmon, playing cards on his legs.

She took him to the garden. Pulled off his shoes. Pressed his feet into the grass. "Wiggle your toes, Charlie." His legs moved for the first time.

I watched my daughter, fierce, private, processing it all in a journal she showed no one, and saw myself at her age, navigating upheaval without a protocol, finding her own way. And I watched my son, joyful, determined, twelve breaths on a resistance inhaler when they asked for ten, eyebrows raised in quiet pride, his lungs collapsed in the accident and yet still choosing to exceed the requirement. I saw a different mirror. Two children carrying forward the pattern I'd been tracing across civilizations and continents, each in their own way, neither needing me to explain it to them.

He cleared rehab in a week. They'd expected a month.

What followed were six months of watching a human being get built. Not rebuilt, there was nothing re- about it. I took him to the redwoods, then home, where I turned everything I'd ever learned into a single purpose.

Late at night I'd sit at the kitchen table building a protocol from every corner of my life. Circadian science and nomadic sleep rhythms. Breathwork to hyperoxygenate the brain drawn from shamanic traditions. Music from the frequencies of Varanasi's drum temples. And alongside the ancient, the cutting edge: I used every tool available to search and synthesize the latest medical research on neuroplasticity and brain recovery, combing through studies and clinical data, trying to make sense of it all and build a framework that wove the old wisdom and the new science into a single approach. The same convergence I'd spent my career exploring in the field, ancient knowledge and modern technology aimed at the same mystery, was now aimed at my son's brain.

At 2 AM, with Charlie asleep beside me — we shared a bed for three months — I'd close the laptop and listen to him breathe and think about how strange it was that everything I'd searched for in distant places had been preparing me for this room.

He rebuilt in phases and knew it. "Third grade," he'd say. Then weeks later, "Fifth grade." His mind felt like a phone with the apps cleared, fast, free, absorbing everything. I watched and recognized the pattern from my studies of how civilizations emerge. Connection first, always. Then awareness. Then language. Then the complex unbounded wonder. The guitar I had found for him now sat next to him every day. He had rewired his fingers to his brain by plucking at it each day, bit by bit, and the progress was truly remarkable. Within weeks he went from not being able to stand on his own to doing steps on a slackline, first one or two, then a handful more, then sixteen in a row, hanging in the air. Each day felt like it was filled with triumphs and miracles.

Life started to feel like we had built a training center for human development, precise times at 8 AM and 8 PM to wake up and fall asleep, rituals of mindful reflection, intention and gratitude on either end of the day. A game of chess and tea at the foot of the bed before making our way downstairs. A heaping breakfast of more salmon, eggs and antioxidants. Yoga, juggling, slackline, visualization meditations, reading, helmet research, something in nature that made us feel joy, then back home for more salmon and supplements to reset and do it all again.

FOR ALBERT: EXPAND THIS CHAPTER

This is the payoff for the entire book. Everything you learned in the field — shamanic breathwork, nomadic sleep rhythms, music frequencies, Varanasi's drum temples — converges here in your son's recovery. Currently compressed into a few paragraphs. It needs to be the richest chapter in the book.

  • What specific breathwork techniques did you use? How did you connect them to shamanic traditions?
  • The music frequencies — what were you playing at his bedside? How did it connect to what you learned with Jamie and in Varanasi?
  • The neuroplasticity research — what studies mattered most? What did you synthesize at 2AM?
  • How did you structure the visualization meditations? What was Deena's role?
  • The nomadic sleep rhythms — what did you learn from the gers that applied here?
  • The diet protocol — more detail on the science behind the choices
  • When did you realize everything you'd searched for in distant places had been preparing you for this room?
title: Chapter 26: The Protocol

content:
Chapter 27: The Return

He wouldn't kill a bug. He would sit and stare at an ant for an hour, watching in wonder as it made its way through the world. Monarchs migrated through that summer and Charlie would hold them on the milkweed, watching eggs become caterpillars become chrysalises become flight.

Millie had stayed with her mother through the critical months. She had school, and friends, and the normalcy someone in the family needed to hold. But as Charlie stabilized she came back over, and the distance teenagers build between themselves and their siblings simply fell away. They'd sit in the garden watching the monarchs together, two kids in metamorphosis, his dramatic and visible, hers quiet and private, unfolding in the pages of a journal she showed to no one. I'd watch them from the kitchen window and understand that whatever protocol I'd designed for Charlie, Millie was doing her own version of the same work without anyone building a framework around her.

He wanted to fly. Couldn't understand how backflips became stairs with supervision. I bought RC cars that did triple flips and we'd launch them at the bay most afternoons, the only flight he could touch.

On his three-month anniversary, driving home from one of those sessions, the sunset filled the sky. Charlie looked out the window a long time.

"That's the feeling. That's what it feels like. The other side."

He called his mother and told her he loved her. Turned to me and wept, not from sadness but from the sheer weight of being here. The gravity and the gratitude, inseparable.

Weeks later he shared a passage from his journal with me:

I love you old Charlie, but it's time for me to keep moving and finally I can let go.

He'd arrived at it alone. The same understanding I'd clawed my way to through phantom pain and psychedelics and watching Shadowlight release what she carried. My son found it at fifteen in a notebook because it was already in him. It had always been in him. The surplus. The margin. The thing that doesn't annihilate.

Six months. What grew back was what had been there all along, the way a river runs beneath ice all winter, waiting.

He returned to school with an even deeper drive and top marks, fueled by a need to show himself what his brain could still do. His neurologists said miracle.
