He told me the closest thing he feels to the love from the other side is sitting with someone in a hospital going through their own darkness, and being there to give them hope.

As Charlie's recovery progressed, he learned that so many people who go through traumatic brain injuries go through them alone, without community, without a protocol, without anyone pressing photos to their walls. It bothered him deeply. He turned to Johnny, who was still living with us, still showing up every day, and asked him to start filming the journey. Not for vanity but because he wanted to share it with anyone lying in a hospital bed wondering if they'd come back.

Then he was invited to give a public talk about his experience coming back from what he called "the other side." He agreed without hesitation. He came to me for advice on how to give a speech. I told him the best speeches start like a campfire, open with something that makes people laugh, and they'll follow you anywhere.

He disappeared for a few minutes. I could hear him typing in the next room. Then he walked back in with a look on his face I couldn't read.

"Dad, I asked the internet for a joke about brain injuries."

"And?"

"It said: 'There is absolutely nothing funny about brain injury. Do not make jokes about it.'"

He held a straight face for about two seconds. Then we both lost it. We laughed until we were crying, until my stomach hurt, until neither of us could talk. A fifteen-year-old kid who'd come back from a coma, asking the internet for permission to laugh at the thing that almost killed him, and the internet saying no.

"I'm opening with that," he said. And he did. I sat in the audience crying with joy as my son walked onto a stage and made a room full of strangers laugh about the thing that almost killed him. It was one of the proudest moments of my life.

At six months we sat down for a proper interview. He was radiant. But when skiing came up, his face changed. Another impact could compound everything. He cried.

I knew that grief. I'd stared at the space where my leg had been.

Then he stopped. Got quiet. Said he'd been thinking about why he loved skiing. He could pinpoint it. He was ten. We were on a double black diamond. We were giggling.

"This has always just been about having joy together. And we'll never lose that."

We packed the car.

We drove north on the 395, the same road, the season turned. Snow replaced by sage, ice by wildflowers. The same world carrying different weather.

Past Sky Rock where the Paiute carved their spirals into volcanic stone, and hillsides where we had searched for obsidian in theirs. Past the turnoff to Death Valley. Past the little lake where he and Millie once pulled trout for breakfast, back when the hardest thing in our lives was a family learning to hold together in a new shape. Past Mount Whitney, where I'd climbed with Gil and learned that every peak is just a vantage point for the ones beyond.

When Mammoth appeared Charlie sat forward. No fear. Only home. For me it was harder. I was driving into the landscape of the worst phone calls of my life, and also into the place where my son had become who he was.

He found his teammates Piper and Owen. Then the patrollers who saved him, and afterward said quietly that maybe what he wanted was to become one of them. Not the glory. The care. We stood in the empty locker room. The smell of wax in the walls. He looked at the space where his old life happened and I stood behind him knowing that doorway, having spent years in my own versions of it.

We went to Chair 6, right in front of the main lodge where his team had met every morning, right next to the runs where he and Millie had learned to ski. There was no looking away from it — the site of his accident sat front and center in the amphitheater of the mountain. I felt the fear, the animal pull to never let him near a mountain again. But we chose not to surrender this place to its worst moment. We loved this mountain. We would find a new way to see it, even as no part of me could watch him fall again.

At the summit, bare granite, the range unfolding as he looked outward.

That night at dinner I told him plainly a hard reality. That the path he'd imagined for himself in competitive skiing needed to change. That another impact could compound everything, and the next one could be the last. His eyes glistened but he held my gaze. I'd spent my entire life refusing to accept limitations. Now I was asking my son to accept his.

We walked into the valley. The buck moon rose so bright we thought it was the sun, enormous, unhurried, flooding everything with silver. Wolves howled in the distance. We howled back, all of us, and the grief and the fear and the six months of willing a brain back together poured out into the sound and dissolved.

The next morning we went to the river.

The water wound through the valley, rolling over rocks and pooling in deep bends. Summer. Green banks, bugs catching the morning light above the current.

We pulled on our waders and stepped in.

I had spent my career walking through the ruins of civilizations that rose and fell, the Maya cities that emerged from jungle and were eventually swallowed back into it, the Mongol empire that stretched across continents and returned to grass, the Chachapoya fortresses crumbling into cloud forest, the temples of Varanasi still burning above the river that carries everything away. Each had emerged from imagination and returned to earth. But none of them were really gone. Their fingerprints were everywhere, in the languages we speak, the roads we travel, the rituals we perform without knowing their origins. They had not vanished. They had transformed. The wheel had carried them forward.

And standing in the river with my son, I understood that the same force that built those civilizations and the same force that brought Charlie back from the void was the same thing my father had described in the physics of the Big Bang. The margin. The surplus. The tiny fraction of harmony that outlasts the chaos, not by much, by almost nothing, but by enough. Enough to build a star, a city, a song, a family. Enough to press a handprint into a cave wall. Enough to keep a broken child alive.

The capacity to care. To imagine. To choose creation in the face of destruction. It was there thirty-one thousand years ago in a cave in Borneo, and it was there now, in a river in the Eastern Sierra, in the grip of a boy holding a fishing rod with hands that six months ago couldn't hold anything at all.

We didn't know what to call it. We both called it love, because there was no better word, though it is bigger than that word and older than any language that contains it.

Charlie cast his line. The current took it downstream, past rocks, through shafts of morning light. We stood in the cold water, my one real foot and the carbon blade beside it, his legs that six months ago couldn't hold him, and we didn't speak. The river moved over us the way it moves over everything, with the patience it has always had. Carrying what is given. Returning what is needed. Containing all of it, every season, every voice, every version of the boy beside me and the man I used to be.

His line went taut. I watched the rod bend and the current pull and something electric travel up through the water and into his hands, a bolt of life from beneath the surface, ancient and immediate and entirely new. Charlie looked at me and grinned.

Something both new and ancient, something alive, on the other end once again.
title: Chapter 27: The Return

content:
Epilogue

I write from the rim of Ubehebe Crater in Death Valley. Millie picks at her basket of Easter eggs while Charlie works on a speech for school at the little table inside our RV. I had dusted it off after years of disuse. They have grown older, and with all that had happened these past few years, these moments together seemed more and more rare. We are days away from returning to Mammoth on the one-year anniversary of the day Charlie almost died. On the shoulder of this volcano, I look out at a desert landscape that holds so much for us, in memories, and now I know, in memories yet to come.

It's impossible not to feel the echoes from this very spot. The toddler version of Millie in her ladybug costume and Charlie in his space outfit, looking for magic rocks while we pretended we were on the moon. The time we stood on this peak with a pirate flag, owning the loss of my leg as a thing that made me a pirate, in rebellion against any victim narrative that was threading its way into my head. Today Charlie and Millie ran into the sun-baked river wash with the innocence of play that took us back to our earliest days here.

I thought of the moment we had first arrived, years before, to this exact location. Divorce had just broken the expectations of the family that would be, and I had loaded our first rented RV with every toy I could find — model rocket kits, camping stoves, guitars, mac and cheese packs, carpets, umbrellas, armchairs — in a dazed state of anxiety, trying to imagine a life remapped into the unexpected. We headed north on the 395, that sacred road that has transected my entire life, and took the turn into Death Valley. I had no music saved, and had never imagined a place with zero connectivity, but as we entered the geological wonderland the outside world fell away with the signal. Suddenly we were in silence. I drove as the kids played in the bed in the back, fighting and screaming as much as they were laughing. But the silence hurt, to be honest, letting my thoughts mask the deeper truths beneath them.

That night, after searching for an open campsite in desperation — looking for a place to belong — we found ourselves at the Mesquite camp high over the vast scape that rolled out in front of us, with mountains rising to the sky and sand storms swirling into desert tornadoes that danced across the dried lake beds like giant ghosts. The wind picked up as the sun set, and we hunkered into our little spaceship on wheels. Charlie, Millie, and I pulled out toy planes and cars to build our own make-believe world from nothing more than imagination and the love we had for each other.

The storms came up the valley and whipped around our camp, shaking the suspension and rocking the bus back and forth like a child in the arms of a parent. Then the storm passed and the stars emerged. I pulled out a stargazing app to track the constellations, and the only music we had heard in days began spontaneously playing, an ethereal celestial score to match the magic, as if brought to us from the stars themselves. That became the soundtrack of our lives. A cosmic dance in the desert.

What we found that night, and in the cycles of time since, is something I have had to learn through the same forces that shape the dunes and the mountains. That beauty is in the storm.

I think of Jamie, and the Salurian, the secret dried lake bed where we played music under the stars. I think of the adventures I have been given, the worlds I have seen, and the many chapters of humanity I have witnessed in the ruins of ancient cities, in the caves and temples and mountains where our story began. And I think of all those who have come before me, and all that will be.

Last night, just the three of us, we stood on the dunes as the sun dropped and the first stars appeared in that liminal space between day and night. Charlie looked out across the sand and said, "We are living in a moment that will soon pass into a cherished memory." These days have meant more to me than my human eyes can contain. But the cycles will continue. My children's children's children may play on these dunes long after I have come and gone. They will look for the tiny pupfish that swim in the primordial spring waters in the hottest place on earth, and play in the sand that has meant so much to us.

Days later, we drove north.

One year after his accident, we returned to Mammoth. Charlie rode down the mountain that had almost killed him, his community surrounding him like a flock of birds flying down the slope. It dawned on me that this was all just for fun, this silly thing we were choosing to do, slide down a giant mountain covered in snow in the face of death, just for fun. We got to the bottom and he stood there, all of us looking at each other, tears in our eyes, laughing as if we were in awe that it had all actually happened. He told us he was grateful, and recalled the moment he had spent in the coma, where he saw a universal love as what transcended everything. Then he made us all do a silly dance, and we wiggled like worms on the snow. We got back on the lift for as many laps as the day would allow.

Afterward, he taught his mother to ski. Kara, who had lived in fear since the day of the accident, who had never once stood on skis, asked to learn. Not because anyone pushed her, but because her son had gone to the edge of existence and come back glowing, and she wanted to understand what he'd found there. She wanted to choose love over fear. Charlie taught her with the seriousness of a professional instructor. She wobbled and laughed.

We stood around them on the bunny slope, this strange, beautiful, imperfect family, and I thought of the handprints in the cave. We were the handprints. We were all TEBO1. Every one of us, choosing care over convenience, choosing to keep each other alive, choosing to accept help when we need it, choosing the tiny surplus that builds the world.

The wheel had turned. It would turn again. And instead of wondering what was before and what comes after, I wonder if that's even the question. In the vortices of what is, impermanence bows its head to the infinite.
title: Epilogue

content:
Chapter 1: The Accident

Millie caught her first fish in swim diapers. She was three years old.

I'd been tending the grill under the weathered beach umbrella that lived permanently in the bed of my truck, half-watching Charlie and Adam's son chase each other along the water's edge. She'd been asking me to help her fish, but I was hunched over the tiny camping grill trying to keep it from tipping as I turned the chicken legs I was making them for lunch. As a single father of two small kids I was obsessed with getting as much protein into them as possible so they'd grow up strong, the same instinct that had once led me to follow Kara around with tiny packets of iodized salt to sneak into her food when she was pregnant because I'd read it was good for brain development.

Every time I looked up from the grill, Millie was one step further along on her own. She'd gone down to the shore, pulled a ghost shrimp from the sand with a PVC pipe tool I'd made her, baited the hook on her Elsa-themed fishing rod, and cast it into the shallows. Ghost shrimp look like tiny lobsters, their pinching claws nearly the size of their bodies. She'd done the whole thing by herself because Dad was busy trying not to set the chicken on fire. The next thing I knew she was running toward me with a fish in her hand.

"Dad! Dad, I got one!"

Charlie ran over to see. She held it up, smile stretched from ear to ear, and tried to get the hook out of its mouth. I knelt beside her and thought: I have a fishing buddy. That was Millie. Three years old, swim diapers, Elsa fishing rod, and already fierce enough to do everything herself.

It had been a good day. The kind I'd learned not to take for granted. Not the kind of day where you expect your whole world shifts. I'd only been back a few weeks from filming inside the tomb of China's first emperor for National Geographic, and in a few months I'd be mapping hidden pyramids in the jungles of Guatemala with lasers fired from drones. But my marriage had ended the year before, and now I was a single dad splitting weeks between two houses, trying to hold the thing that mattered most together with whatever hands I had free. On this Saturday afternoon, the most important discovery in the world was a three-year-old girl with a ghost shrimp and an Elsa fishing rod.

And then, a week before this perfect day at the bay, Bruna. We'd known each other for months, circling without quite landing. But that first kiss opened something I'd sealed shut. For the first time since the divorce, I could see a version of the future that wasn't just me white-knuckling it alone.

She showed up as the afternoon heat started to lift off the water. She walked across the grass and went straight to the kids, scooped Millie up, made Charlie laugh, dropped into their world as if she'd always been part of it. I watched her hold my daughter and felt something crack open in my chest. Maybe the empty chair at the table wouldn't always be empty.

Adam invited us back to his parents' place as the evening came on, a farmhouse out east of the city, where the late-summer heat was still rising off the ground. The kids jumped in the pool while Adam's father poured chilled wine on the patio. The last of the daylight caught Charlie's face as he climbed out of the water, and I remember thinking how much older he looked, steady in the eyes that most six-year-olds aren't. He'd absorbed the upheaval of the last couple years and come through it with something extra, or more likely it was always there and life was polishing it into focus.

A few moments later I looked over and saw Adam loading the kids into the "Rhino", a squat four-by-four, half tractor, half dune buggy.

"Quick ride, they'll love it!" he said with a smile.

Bruna stayed behind. I climbed into the passenger seat with Millie on my lap and Adam's daughter next to her. Charlie and Adam's son were buckled in back. We headed up a dirt track behind the house, Adam steering in playful arcs, dust kicking up behind us. The kids laughed with excitement, or maybe that was me.

One turn. Another.

The third, I felt before I understood. A lurch. Momentum tipping just a hair too far. Everything slowed. The Rhino tilting. My foot shooting out. One leg against two thousand pounds of metal and gravity.

Going. Going.

Ground rushing up. Metal meeting bone. Thunder from underwater.

Then silence. Dust. A ringing that swallowed everything.

I couldn't see. I couldn't move. My body suspended in something thick and formless, fighting to surface. Where are the kids. Where are my kids.

The ringing faded. Through the haze, Millie's face. Terrified. Screaming through the dirt. Breathing. At least breathing.

I couldn't turn my body. I couldn't find Charlie.

"Where's Charlie? Is he okay?"

Adam above me. "Charlie's alright!" Then he looked down. "Oh my god." He said it again. And again.

Adrenaline did something superhuman to him. He lifted the vehicle with one arm and dragged me free with the other. That's when I saw what was left of my leg. My foot jutting at an angle that doesn't exist in nature. What had been my shin was now open flesh and a million splinters of bone ground into the dirt.

"Get the kids out of here."

He ran them inside. I was alone.

No pain yet. Just the sky, and a silence so total the world seemed to have stopped to look at what I'd become. I saw myself on horseback, galloping flat out across the Mongolian steppe, dust blooming behind us, the crew yelling and whooping, my body part of the horse and the horse part of the earth and all of it moving as one thing. The purest physical joy I'd ever known. Gone, now, with the bones in the dirt.

And the smaller things. Charlie explaining the constellations to his sister on a camping trip, his mind always quietly cataloging the world. Millie standing on my feet in a deeply worn and tattered princess dress while I held her hands and we danced to her favorite song on endless repeat in a house that still didn't have drywall.

I'd just started to believe it was all going to work, and now my body lay in a shattered pool of blood and dirt that seemed to say I would never walk again.

Then I heard someone running up the dirt driveway towards me.

Bruna dropped to her knees beside me, shaking. She took my head in her lap. Her eyes locked on mine with a concern so intense it narrowed the world to just her face. Then she started chanting.

"Ohm. Ohm. Ohm."

I could feel it in her body against my skull. My jaw was clenched so tight the sound barely got through, what came out of me wasn't a word, more like a groan shaped into something just close enough. But I held onto it. I'd seen that symbol before, on a medallion a Sherpa had pressed into my hand in Tibet years ago, and on the kitschy tapestries that hung in every college dorm room I'd ever been in. But I hadn't understood it then, and I didn't understand it now. It was just sound. And it was the only thing holding me together, as the pressure from my wound crept closer past the barriers of shock and threatened to pull me under.

"Ohm... Ohm..."

Five minutes. Maybe thirty. Time had stopped meaning anything. The heat was still rising off the ground. My children were inside a house they had never been to wondering what had happened to their father, would they be ok? And a woman I'd known for barely a month was holding me together with her hands and a sound older than history.

When the sirens came, the paramedics moved fast. As they wheeled me toward the ambulance I saw Charlie and Millie in the doorway. Charlie had his arm around his little sister. Even then, even at six, he was already the one keeping things together.

"Don't worry," I told them. "It'll all be okay."

The doors closed. Outside, the last of the daylight was splitting into bands of gold and shadow across the hills. The kids were about to have their first sleepover, unplanned, while their father got rushed away in a stretcher. The pain broke over me. I gripped Bruna's hand and slipped between consciousness and darkness, the world I knew falling away behind me.

Ohm.

In the weeks to come, my leg would be amputated below the knee. The life I'd known would be gone. I had spent my career as an explorer, searching for the tomb of Genghis Khan across the sacred mountains of Mongolia, mapping hidden Maya cities with lasers fired from the sky, holding the bones of the ancient dead and wondering what they could tell us about the living. I thought I was searching the world for answers. I didn't know yet that the world was about to search me.

What followed would take me places I never expected. Into jungles where lasers would reveal civilizations hidden for a thousand years, and onto waves that would teach me more about the human mind than any laboratory. Into the ancient practices that shamans and scientists were only now discovering operated on the same neural pathways. To the burning ghats of India, where a city older than Rome had been engineered for a single purpose, and the cloud forest cliffs of Peru where hanging rows of the sarcophagi looked towards the endless sunrise. To the bedside of a dying friend and the bedside of my own son. And to a question I didn't yet know I was asking.

What is it, at the bottom of everything, that holds?

Somewhere in the darkness of that ambulance, as the sirens wailed and Bruna's hand held mine and the pain came in waves that threatened to take me under, a memory surfaced from somewhere I wasn't looking for it. A road through the pines. A trading post. I was eight years old in the passenger seat, and my father was trying to explain something about the beginning of everything. How in the first instant after the Big Bang, nearly everything that was created was immediately destroyed. Matter and antimatter annihilating each other in equal measure. But not quite equal. For every billion particles that cancelled out, one extra particle of matter remained. From that margin, that sliver of something over nothing, everything that exists was born.

I hadn't understood what he meant. Not on that drive through the pines, not in the decades that followed. But the ambulance was carrying me now, a small spaceship of blinking lights and strangers' hands, hurtling through the darkness between one life and whatever came next. My leg was shattered. A sound I didn't understand was still vibrating in my chest. And somewhere in between what I had been and what I was about to become, I was about to find out.
title: Chapter 1: The Accident

content:
Chapter 2: The Shifting Ground

Santa Cruz, California, 1989. I was eight years old. We were coming home from Peace Choir rehearsal, a pack of tie-dye-shirted kids who sang atomic countdown songs in front of grocery stores. That's when the world literally changed under our feet.

My mother was driving the hand-me-down Oldsmobile we called "the Boat" because riding in it felt like bobbing at sea. Jane sat up front in her sideways ponytail and neon pink MTV sweater. I was in back, staring at dry lawns and rows of Craftsman houses in the fading light. We passed Long's Drugstore with its posters of surfers riding huge waves, then turned toward our street on the edge of the canyon.

The car wobbled like we'd hit speed bumps. I saw people running out of their houses but didn't understand why. The Boat's suspension had swallowed most of the shaking.

We pulled up to find my brother Ed frozen in the driveway. He was usually the one with all the answers, two years older, top-ranked in the state for math, he had always been the family genius. But right then he looked scared.

"You didn't feel it?!"

He'd been watching the World Series when the Loma Prieta earthquake erupted ten miles away. Living in the Bay Area, we'd been warned for years about the coming "Big One." It gave me nightmares. But now it had actually happened and I'd missed it. In a strange way, part of me felt robbed of the chance to finally face something I'd dreaded for so long. Inside, the house looked like a snow globe someone had shaken and set down. Everything was on the floor. Cracks ran along the walls.

My mother stopped us from going in. Growing up in Hong Kong, she'd been an actress in the same film studio as Bruce Lee, and maybe that helped her keep her composure, or maybe it was something harder, a childhood born in the wake of war and rebuilt from scratch in a country where she couldn't easily communicate with the neighbors. She'd followed my father to this small California town, sewed most of her own clothes out of habit, scrimped every penny, and somehow held our family together through moves that spanned the globe. She was a tough cookie.

Whenever I asked for a snack or toy car at a store she'd scowl and aggressively demand "Shung!", save, in Mandarin. There was some benefit to English being her second language though. The TV shows and movies we watched were never filtered for content the way my friends' were, and I absorbed things that other kids my age probably shouldn't have, but did anyway with a grin.

When I needed her, she was there. I remember her sitting at the kitchen table beside me, patiently teaching me Roman numerals for a test I was terrified about, her hand over mine on the pencil. Now she held us back from our own front door, calm as stone.

Jane stood beside her, the oldest of us and naturally the most composed. If Ed was the genius, Jane was the rock. I, however, was the problem child, ironically nicknamed "xiao poo" at birth after a volcanic bowel movement ended my first few days of terrorizing the family in an undiagnosed bout of extreme constipation. It gave me a chip on my shoulder, but as the youngest there wasn't much I could do about it.

My father was an astrophysicist who spent his days covered in chalk dust, modeling the creation of planets and the properties of dark matter. He didn't sit us down and explain the cosmos. He just lived inside it, and we absorbed what we could from the periphery. I grew up in the back rows of lecture halls, too young to follow the mathematics but old enough to feel the enormity of what was being discussed. Sometimes the audience was rapt, but inevitably there would be a few snoring through convulsive whips of a head struggling to stay upright in a chair. But there was always an air of cheeky wonder and discovery amongst his community of nerdy explorers of the universe who communicated more in puns than anything else. His world included people like Stephen Hawking, whose ex-wife Jane was my sister's namesake, and whose voice machine I once begged to press. We couldn't follow the math, but something seeped in anyway, the way music does when you're not paying attention.

My fondest memories with him are the camping trips. He'd take us into the Sierra Nevadas with his graduate students, driving through giant pines to clearings where they'd set up telescopes and point them at the sky. I remember the smell of the green A-frame tent my brother and I would pile into, the trees so tall they made us feel like ants.

One evening, a bear broke into one of his friend's cars and we needed to get something from the trading post down the road. My father asked if I wanted to come with him. In a family of five where my brother and sister were older, wiser, and held more power in the dynamic, and I was the little poop youngest, having my father to myself was rare. We drove down that long stretch of road as the pines rose up on all sides, and we talked the way we almost never did, just the two of us, about small things and big things all the same. He told me he was proud that I'd hiked for miles without complaining. We talked about the waterfall where we'd slid down natural granite waterslides into a swimming hole. I remember wishing the drive would never end.

Then I asked him why he loved the stars. It took a moment for him to respond. Maybe he was deciding how much to explain. Then he told me his thoughts on everything. The Big Bang. Matter and antimatter. A tiny margin that made the difference between nothing and all of it. The stars, the mountains, the trees outside our window, the origins of life, us.

I didn't understand most of what he said. I was eight years old, and the numbers were too big and the idea was too strange. But I remembered his voice saying it, and the road unwinding through the pines, and the feeling of having my father to myself for once, and all of it fused together into something I carried without knowing I was carrying it.

Under the stars that night, he pointed out constellations and let me look through the telescope. He tried. He always tried up there.

That night after the earthquake, with the house too damaged to enter, he went inside just long enough to grab supplies and came back with the old tent and the little green camping stove that had followed us everywhere, ramen on the autobahn, first meals in new houses, the one constant that meant "home" when nothing else stayed the same. He also came back marveling that the row of National Geographic magazines on the shelf had shifted into a perfect wave pattern from the quake. The rest of us saw a disaster. He saw physics. We set up in the backyard, just like Yosemite or Joshua Tree, only this time under the shadow of disaster.

As night fell, the aftershocks came. I lay sandwiched between my brother and sister as the earth beneath us rumbled and shifted. And then a distant neighbor grabbed a megaphone and started calling out ratings for each tremor like an Olympic judge.

Five point four! Four point three!

Others joined in from yard to yard. Just like that, the shaking became something to celebrate rather than fear. Our fences no longer divided us. Overhead, shooting stars streaked across the sky. We clapped and called out scores, and in that strange, shattered night, we became a community.

In the days that followed, my siblings and I lived in the canyon behind our house. There was a sand cave on a cliff that Ed and I had found a way into, and we'd sit inside scraping pigmented sand from the walls, mixing it with water to make paint, then covering the stone with what we were absolutely certain were accurate representations of ancient cave drawings. They washed off by the next rain, but that didn't stop us from making more. Ed always went all in on my ideas, whether it was the cave art or building a fort or the Little Dipper, a roller coaster we constructed from junk and nailed me into for the maiden voyage. I loved him for that. Jane supervised with the calm authority of someone who would rather not explain to our mother how the youngest got launched off a cliff. Even now, the smell of chopped fennel takes me back to that canyon.

I grew up surrounded by stories of people who had crossed oceans and started over. My father's father, the son of a Chinese immigrant who'd worked the salmon canneries of British Columbia, had earned his way to Harvard and spent his life bridging East and West. Canada gave him the Order of Canada for it, the country's highest civilian honor, a medal that hung on his wall in a room where he never once brought it up. When we visited, he'd call me his little rascal and let me sit beside him while he read. There was a steadiness to him that I didn't find anywhere else.

It was my grandmother who told me, years later, about my father's brother. He'd been killed during the Cold War under circumstances that remained classified. The records were sealed. She never believed the official story. She said it quietly, the way you say things that have never stopped hurting. Whatever that loss did to my father, it went deep enough to shape everything that followed.

On my mother's side, the stories were just as heavy. Her mother had been a nurse in the war, their family from Nanking where the worst of the atrocities had occurred. Her father had walked across a thousand miles of war-torn China as a journalist to reunite with his family, arriving nearly dead. When they met, it was a love born in the fog of shifting giants. My mother was the oldest of five, and when she was born she was given the name Tali, meaning new beginning. She carried that role across the ocean when she followed my father to America, her family thousands of miles away. I'd hear her calling her siblings late at night, the phone cord stretched from the kitchen to the hallway for privacy, speaking rapidly in Cantonese I couldn't follow.

My parents gave me the middle name Yu-Min, citizen of the universe. Maybe it was an echo from the worlds they had arrived from. Maybe they hoped I could feel at home wherever I went, intergalactic or not. Looking back, I think they were hoping for something they hadn't been able to find themselves.

When I was twelve, my father arranged a sabbatical in Cambridge. "We're going where the apple fell on Newton's head!" he'd say, eyes gleaming. He dragged all of us across the Atlantic and suddenly we were living in a world made of old stone. I remember the first morning, cobblestones under my sneakers, the smell of damp air, buildings that had been standing since before my country existed. My father walked ahead of us through a courtyard and I saw him differently than I ever had. He wasn't the distracted man at the dinner table. He was someone who belonged here, part of a tradition of people trying to understand the fundamental nature of things. In the lecture halls, I sat in the back and listened to conversations I couldn't follow about the origins of the universe, the nature of time, the possibility that the Big Bang was not a single event but part of an endless cycle. Most of it went over my head. But it fascinated me, and sitting there I felt both admiration and maybe a little bit of fear that I would never live up to the bar he had set.

The Soviet Union had just collapsed, and my parents having an obsession with us seeing a bigger world than they had known used whatever travel money the university would give to drag us to every ruin, monument, and museum within reach, sometimes three in a day. Freshly burned buildings from a coup attempt in Moscow. The rubble of the Berlin Wall. Amphitheaters of Greece and cathedrals of France. My passport filled with stamps from nations that no longer existed. My father seemed to regard it all as tiny blips on the grand timeline of existence. The collapse of governments mattered less to him than the birth of stars.

We were constantly transplanted, all five of us living out of a suitcase from one adventure to the next, following my father's pursuit of knowledge across borders that were still falling in the wake of the Cold War. By day we'd hop from lectures on the universe to ancient ruins, then desperately search for the cheapest motel we could find to keep the circus going on an academic salary. At night, Ed, Jane, and I would pile into whatever dingy room we'd landed in, all five of us crammed together, and jump from bed to bed until our parents yelled at us to stop. It didn't matter what country we were in. We were having the time of our lives. The ground was always shifting, but as long as all five of us were in the room, it didn't matter.

On weekends my mother would push open the heavy door of some village church and pull me inside. She wasn't religious at all, but these places felt like portals into fairy tales. Set into the cold stone floors were life-sized engravings of medieval knights in full armor, swords at their hips, hands pressed together in prayer, lions curled at their feet. Some were seven hundred years old. We'd kneel on the stone, tape down sheets of paper, and rub sticks of dark wax across them in long even strokes. The image would appear slowly, first the outline of the shield, then the chainmail, then the face of someone who had lived and died centuries before I was born, emerging under my hands. Sprawled across a tomb in a country far from either side of our ancestry, I felt something I couldn't have named then. These knights had nothing to do with us, and yet they had everything to do with us. They were part of the same long story, a version of humanity that had lived and fought and prayed and been buried under stone, and here I was, a twelve-year-old kid from California with my mother beside me, running my hands over the traces they'd left behind. It was the closest thing to time travel I'd ever felt.

In Cambridge itself I tried desperately to fit in. I'd made a best friend, or thought I had, until he told me a girl couldn't like me "because of the color of my hair." He said it casually, as if reporting the weather. It was the first time I understood that the thing that made me different wasn't something I could fix by trying harder. That ended the friendship, and something else with it. The feeling of almost belonging, which I'd carried from school to school and country to country, hardened into something quieter and more permanent. My parents enrolled me in a Scout troop, and on those hiking trips I discovered what the wilderness could do for a kid who didn't belong anywhere else. In the wild, the question of where I fit just stopped mattering.

Then we moved to Palo Alto and the whiplash was total. One day, cobblestones. The next, the internet being born in garages. I can still recall the first time an AOL disc arrived in the mail. My friends and I slid it into our family computer and magically we were chatting to strangers not really knowing why we were even there. A company called Google was started in my high school teacher's daughter's garage. My brother and sister seemed to fit in fine. My sister became captain of the wrestling team. My brother was taking classes at Stanford by his sophomore year and even was taken by Steve Jobs' estranged daughter to the Sadie Hawkins school dance. I, on the other hand, was the smallest kid in my class by far and had the social life to match. At lunch I'd hover with my tray, scanning for a table that might let me in. Friday nights I'd sit in my room building model airplanes, the oldies station crackling in the background, watching Dances with Wolves and wishing I could disappear into the ancient world the way Kevin Costner's character had. I had friends but no best friend. Just barely on the outside, never quite knowing the trick to getting in.

I filled the solitude by going backward. I devoured survival stories like Hatchet. I convinced a hunting-obsessed neighbor to bring me deer hides so I could tan them the way early humans had. One day he showed up with a bloodied garbage bag that weighed over 50 pounds, and stank of death. I couldn't have been happier. Unfortunately, I skipped the crucial step of cleaning the remaining flesh before pouring the entirety of my mother's salt tin over it. For weeks our shed reeked like a coyote's den. There probably weren't too many other kids in Silicon Valley with a backyard full of rotting deer, but I was committed to the craft.

Then came another ragtag Scout troop of oddballs like me, led by two Harley-riding dads from welding labs. One had "love" and "hate" tattooed across his knuckles. The other was simply named Gordo, although he was more jolly than plump. And with them came the Sierra Nevadas.

Gordo tried to teach me to fly fish. For a year I caught nothing. I'd cast my line and watch it drift downstream, reel it back in, cast again, nothing. As we got older we would hike further and further into the wilderness, each trip I'd bring my rod, and he'd try to show me how to read the water.

Then one day it shifted. The river wasn't just a surface anymore. I could see beneath it, the shadows that had been rocks became fish. I cast and waited. The rod came alive and the line snapped tight and the water was electric in my hands.

From then on I was hooked. Whenever we made camp I'd catch trout and feed my friends. By sixteen I was an Eagle Scout, organizing hundred-mile trips over granite passes and through epic valleys. The stone spires rose up on all sides of us, like the cathedrals I had seen years before. We navigated by topo maps, hanging food in trees to keep them away from bears, once eating rattlesnakes when a bear got our rations anyway. We had only what we carried and we left no trace. The wilderness was the one place where everything felt timeless, neither ancient nor modern, just beyond time. I'd felt it first on those Scout hikes in England, but here it went deeper. My mother's world and my father's, the person I was at school and the person I was at home, it all just fell away. In nature I was part of something so much bigger than all that.

Jane left for college first. The week before she went, she took me on a long hike, just the two of us. We sat on a hill overlooking everything and she told me things were going to change, but it was going to be okay. I believed her because she was Jane. Then Ed. Their rooms went quiet one at a time, doors left open to hallways where nobody walked. I'd come home from school to a house that felt a ghost of itself.

My mother had always played the piano, not just in crisis but in everything, joy, boredom, the long afternoons when the neighborhood kids came for lessons and the house filled with beginners stumbling through scales. It was her language when English failed, and in the good years the house was full of it. But the music was changing. What she played after midnight carried a weight that hadn't been there before.

My father wasn't getting louder. He was getting quieter. He'd come home late, eat alone, disappear into his office. The camping trips stopped. The puns stopped. So instead of fighting, he withdrew.

Then one night it became real. There was a fight, louder than usual, and I sat in my room listening through the door, not knowing when to come out or what I would do if I did. By the time I finally opened the door, he was gone. I don't know if he said goodbye to anyone. I don't think he did.

My mother was at her piano. She was playing Chopin's Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2. Not for him. Not for me. For herself. The way a musician on a sinking ship plays not to save the vessel but because music is the only language large enough for what's being lost. I stood in the hallway and listened. I was seventeen years old.

The truth is I don't remember much about the days that followed. It was so traumatic and so awkward in the wake of the silence that my mind just let it go. I know the morning came. I know the house was different. But what it looked like, what we said to each other, whether we ate breakfast or sat in the kitchen not eating, I can't tell you. My memory gave that morning back to protect me from it.

My father and I didn't speak again for ten years. For a long time I'd dream about that night, different versions where I'd say all the things I couldn't say, where I'd catch him at the door, where he'd turn around. He never did. And the silence just kept stretching.

The ground had shifted beneath me before, in the canyon behind a shattered house, on a night when the neighbors scored the aftershocks and the stars shot across the sky. Now my father's car was gone from the driveway, and I watched as my mother played Chopin in the dark.
title: Chapter 2: The Shifting Ground

content:
PROLOGUE

I have held the bones of sacrificed children in Peru and rushed home to watch my daughter's school play in butterfly wings. I have galloped across the Mongolian steppe on horseback and slept in a Mazda hatchback in a university parking lot. I have chanted Ohm in the dirt while my shattered leg bled into the earth, and I have chanted it again, years later, over my dying friend, and again over my unconscious son as doctors pulled the breathing tube from his throat.

My name is Albert Lin. For the past fifteen years I've hosted a show on National Geographic called Lost Cities, in which I use lasers fired from drones to reveal civilizations hidden beneath jungles and deserts and oceans. I've mapped the tomb of China's first emperor, uncovered Maya pyramids in Guatemala, and searched the sacred mountains of Mongolia for the lost burial site of Genghis Khan. These are the parts that make good television.

What doesn't make television is the rest. That I launched the whole thing while living in my car with a poster of Genghis Khan taped to a borrowed cubicle wall. That my father is an astrophysicist and my mother was an actress in Bruce Lee's film studio in Hong Kong, and that neither of those facts explains me as well as you'd think. That I once wrestled a nomad on the Mongolian steppe and won by a move I remembered from high school, and had to perform an eagle dance while fermented mare's milk was poured down my back. That in 2016, on a perfect Saturday afternoon, a four-wheeled vehicle rolled onto my leg and I lost everything below the knee, and that the woman I'd been dating for barely a month held my head in her lap and chanted a Sanskrit syllable she'd never been taught, and that sound became the thread I followed through everything that came after.

I am an engineer by training. I believe in measurement. I also believe that a shaman in Peru once saved my expedition by offering coca leaves to a river, and that a drum tuned to four beats per second opens something in the human brain that neuroscience is only now learning to name. I have seen things I cannot explain and I have stopped trying to explain them.

This book is about the places I've been and the question I didn't know I was asking until everything had been stripped away. It spans earthquakes and empires, prosthetic legs and psychedelic ceremonies, the inside of a hyperbaric oxygen chamber and the inside of a mountain that breathes. It is about my children, who taught me more about being human than any ruin or ritual. And it is about a piece of physics my father told me when I was eight years old, on a drive through the pines, that I spent thirty years failing to understand: that in the first instant after the Big Bang, matter and antimatter annihilated each other in nearly equal measure, but not quite. For every billion particles that cancelled out, one extra particle of matter survived. From that margin — that sliver of something over nothing — everything that exists was born.

I didn't know what he meant. I'm starting to.
title: Prologue (Draft A - First Person)

content:
PROLOGUE

I have held the bones of sacrificed children in Peru and rushed home to watch my daughter's school play in butterfly wings. I have galloped across the Mongolian steppe on horseback and slept in a Mazda hatchback in a university parking lot. I have chanted Ohm in the dirt while my shattered leg bled into the earth, and I have chanted it again, years later, over my dying friend, and again over my unconscious son as doctors pulled the breathing tube from his throat.

My name is Albert Lin. I'm an engineer. I was trained at the University of California, San Diego, to see the world through instruments — electron microscopes, satellite arrays, LiDAR scanners that fire a million laser pulses per second to reveal what's hidden beneath jungle canopy and ocean floor. For the past fifteen years I've hosted a show on National Geographic called Lost Cities, in which I use those tools to uncover civilizations that vanished centuries ago. I've mapped the tomb of China's first emperor, revealed sixty thousand Maya structures buried under Guatemalan jungle, and searched the sacred mountains of Mongolia for the lost burial site of Genghis Khan. Along the way, a crowdsourced satellite platform my friends and I built from a university cubicle was used by six million people to search for a missing airliner. My father is an astrophysicist who models the creation of planets. I grew up in the back rows of his lecture halls. Measurement is in my blood.

I say all of this not to impress you but because you need to know it before I tell you the rest. Because the rest doesn't fit on any instrument I was trained to read.

In the course of this work, I've sat with a Kogi priest in the cloud forests of Colombia who held my prosthetic leg and thanked the sun. I've drunk San Pedro cactus juice from a shaman's vial in a cave in the Peruvian Andes and felt the boundary between my body and the mountain dissolve. I've watched a neuroscientist wave Halloween-store severed limbs at my stump to trick my brain out of a pain that didn't technically exist. I've played music in the desert with a dying violinist whose octagonal drum turned out to be tuned to the same theta brainwave frequency that shamans discovered thousands of years before neuroscience had a name for it. And I've sat at my son's bedside at two in the morning, building a recovery protocol for his shattered brain from a collision of ancient breathwork and cutting-edge neuroplasticity research, and I could not tell you where the science ended and the sacred began.

None of this is what I expected. I was the kid who built model airplanes alone on Friday nights in Palo Alto while the internet was being invented in garages down the street. I was the graduate student who hunted rabbits on the campus lawn with a blowgun made from lab supplies. I was the guy who lived in his car with a poster of Genghis Khan taped to a borrowed cubicle wall, eating architecturally engineered salad bar towers to save money. If you had told that person he would one day lose his leg in an accident, learn to surf on a prosthetic, host a television show watched by millions, hold the bones of the ancient dead across five continents, and end up believing that a Sanskrit syllable and a frequency older than language were the most powerful technologies he'd ever encountered — he would have asked what you were smoking. And then, eventually, he would have tried it.

I am a person who measures things. I also believe that a shaman in Peru once saved my expedition by offering coca leaves to a river, and that the most important discoveries of my career were made not by the lasers but by the people who had been living with those discoveries for centuries before I arrived with my instruments. These two facts do not contradict each other. They are the same fact, seen from different sides of a door carved into a mountain that doesn't open onto anything — except everything.

This book is about the gap between what my instruments could see and what I found in that gap when I stopped measuring. It spans earthquakes and empires, prosthetic legs and psychedelic ceremonies, the inside of a hyperbaric oxygen chamber and the inside of a mountain that breathes. It is about my children, who taught me more about being human than any ruin or ritual. And it is about a piece of physics my father told me when I was eight years old, on a drive through the pines, that I spent thirty years failing to understand: that in the first instant after the Big Bang, matter and antimatter annihilated each other in nearly equal measure, but not quite. For every billion particles that cancelled out, one extra particle of matter survived. From that margin — that sliver of something over nothing — everything that exists was born.

I was trained to measure the world. What I found is that the most important things survive the measurement. They are the things that hold when everything else is annihilated. A sound older than language. A choice to care for a broken child in a cave thirty-one thousand years ago. A fifteen-year-old boy giving a thumbs-up from a hospital bed because his brain, though shattered, remembered how to love before it remembered his father's name.

I didn't know what my father meant on that drive through the pines. I'm starting to.
